May  30,  1895. 


Dear  Friend:- 


Your  kindness  in  favoring  our 
Library  regularly  with  your  publications 
is  highly  appreciated,  and  our  Trustees 
tafce  pleasure  in  sending  you  herewith,  in 
return  for  the  same,  their  Year  Boole  for 
1895  . 

Kindly  place  upon  your  mailing 
list  the  "Historical  Library  of  American 
Y.  M.  C.  A.s,  Springfield,  Mass.",  and 
send  to  it  in  exchange  for  our  Year  Bool: 
the  Annual  Report  and  catalogue  of  your 
institution. 

Hoping  for  a  continuance  of 
past  favors  ,  1  remain  , 

Sincerely  yours. 

J  .  To  Bowne  .

Special     Y.  M.  G.  P.     Notice. 


THE 


-«* 


Bilhorn  Telescope 


ORGAN. 


A    REMARKABLE    INVENTION. 


The  above  cut  represents  the  most  complete  Baby  Folding  Organ  in  the  market.  Its 
tone  is  sweet,  rich  and  powerful.  Quickly  folded  and  easily  carried  by  one  hand.  The 
body  is  made  of  three-ply  oak  veneering,  thus  making  it  light,  strong  and  durable,  also 
neat  in  design.  When  open  the  organ  stands  just  right  height  for  a  common  chair.  The 
book  rest  is  arranged  so  as  to  accommodate  sheet  music  or  any  size  hymn  book.  It  is 
made  up  in  single^and  double  reed.  Weight,  23  and  24  Ibs. 

The  double  reed  is  provided  with  a  mute  swell,  thus  allowing  the  operator  by  a  single 
move  of  the  hand  to  arrange  organ  so  as  to  use  it  in  single  or  double  reed,  soft  and  sweet 
for  solo  woik,  or  full  power  for  chorus;  besides,  it  has  a  knee  swell. 

Just  the  thing  for  in  and  outdoor  meetings,  street,  gospel  wagon  and  tent  work,  Sab- 
bath School  class  rooms,  visiting  the  sick,  imprisoned,  and  for  general  Christian  work. 

SEND    FOR    FULL    DESCRIPTIVE    CIRCULAR: 


Bilhorn  Bros,,  56  Fifth  Ave,,  Chicago,  111, 


See  what  Dr.  J.   W.  Chapman 

ALBANY,  N.  Y. 

The  Bilhorn  Telescope  Organ  is  a  model  of  neat- 
ness, sweetness  and  power,  and  is  the  admiration 
of  all  who  have  seen  and  heard  it.  It  is  powerful 
enough  for  the  church,  sweet  enough  for  the  sick 
room,  and  will  be  invaluable  to  Evangelists,  Mis- 
sionaries and  Christian  Workers  everywhere 

The  single  reed  weighs  23  Ibs.  and  costs  $2.=>,00. 
The  double  reed  weighs  24  Ibs..  and  costs  $30.00. 

Its  music  is  as  sweet  as  that  of  the  most  expen- 
sive organ.  "  It  is  a  thing  of  beauty  and  will  be 
a  joy  forever."  J.  WILBUR  CHAPMAN. 


and  Rev.  B.  Fay  Mills  say: 

PAWTUXET,  R.  I. 

The  Bilhorn  Telescope  Organ  is  an  exceedingly 
valuable  invention  ;  one  of  the  last  that  makes 
men  wonder  why  it  had  not  been  invented  before 
and,  at  the  same  time,  how  it  could  have  been 
invented  at  all. 

It  is  full  of  melody  and  .power  and  indescrib- 
able sweetness.  It  is  better  than  many  of  the 
larger  organs,  and  yet  weighs  only  23  and  24  Ibs. 
and  costs  only  $25.00  and  $30  00.

BIENNIAL  REPORTS  OF  THE  AGENTS  OF  THE 
INTERNATIONAL  COMMITTEE. 

1893-180-4=. 


BIENNIAL    EEPOET    OF    BICHABD    C.    MOBSE, 

General  Secretary. 
I. — In  direct  relation  to  the  Committee  and  its  administration  of  the  work: 

1.  At  each  of  its  regular  monthly  meetings  the  Committee  has  received 
reports  from  the  sub-committees  on  Finance,  the  General  Field  Work, 
the  College,  German,  Physical,  Educational,  Office  and  Publication  De- 
partments, and  also  on  the  Foreign  Work.     All  the  meetings  of  the  Com- 
mittee   and  its  sub-committees  have  been  attended  by  the  general  or 
office  secretaries,  to  whom  has  been  referred  the  detail  work  necessitated 
by  the  action  there  taken,  including  instructions  to  the  secretaries  on 
the  field  and  in  the  office. 

2.  Conferences  of  the  Committee  and  its  secretaries  were  held  in  New 
York  September  12-17,  1893,  and  September  7-11,   1894.     Each  depart- 
ment of  the  work  was  carefully  reported  and  considered,  and  each  secre- 
tary obtained  a  clearer  understanding  of  the  work  of  his  associates,  and  a 
more  comprehensive  view  of  the  administration  of  the  work  by  the  Com- 
mittee.    The  arrangements  for  these  conferences  form  part  of  the  duties  of 
the  General  Secretary. 

3.  The  annual  dinner  meetings  of  the  Committee  with  its  secretaries 
and  friends  of  the  work  were  also  arranged  for  by  the  General  Secretary, 
and  held  in  New  York  November  23,  1893,  and  November  22,  1894.     In 
other  cities  similar  dinner  meetings  have  been  arranged  for  as  follows : 
St.  Louis,  December  5,  1893  ;  Brooklyn,  November  21,  1894 ;  New  Haven, 
December  4,   1894;  Hartford,  December  29,  1894.     In  response  to  the 
courteous  invitations  of  Messrs.  W.  W.  Spence,  of  Baltimore,  for  April 
18,  1893,  and  J.  J.  McWilliams,  of  Buffalo,  for  November  14,  1893,  some 
of  the  members  and  secretaries  of  the  Committee  attended  parlor  recep- 
tions of  friends  of  the  Association  in  those  cities. 

At  Scranton,  October  30,  1894,  two  secretaries  of  the  Committee  were 
guests  of  the  Social  and  Civil  Club  of  that  city  at  its  dinner  meeting. 
At  all  these  meetings  the  international  work  in  its  various  departments 
was  quite  fully  presented  by  members  and  secretaries  of  the  Committee, 


10 

and  the  results  have  confirmed  the  Committee  in  its  estimate  of  the  great 
value  of  such  meetings  in  promoting  the  appreciation  and  support  of  the 
international  work. 

II. — In  relation  to  the  Board  of  Trustees: 

The  Board  of  Trustees  held  its  annual  meeting  March  13,  1894.  Mr. 
Jonathan  N.  Harris  positively  declining  re-election,  Mr.  Samuel  Colgate 
was  chosen  president,  and  Mr.  John  S.  Bussing  was  re-elected  treasurer. 
The  General  Secretary  of  the  Committee  was  reappointed  recording  sec- 
retary of  the  Board. 

The  treasurer  received  on  April  9,  1894,  from  the  heirs  of  the  estate  of 
Mr.  Sidney  Dillon,  a  fund  of  $25,000,  to  be  known  as  "The  Sidney  Dillon 
Fund, "  the  income  of  which  is  to  be  applied  toward  the  support  of  rail- 
road departments  organized  among  the  employees  of  the  Union  Pacific 
Railway  system  at  points  along  its  lines. 

III. — At  the  Columbian  Exposition: 

The  exhibit  of  the  Young  Men's  Christian  Association  attracted  very 
general  notice.  The  portion  relating  to  the  educational  department  re- 
ceived high  commendation,  and  the  whole  exhibit  was  ranked  among 
those  worthy  of  special  mention  and  attention. 

The  World's  Congress  of  the  Associations  was  held  on  Association  Day, 
October  6th,  in  the  Memorial  Art  Palace,  Chicago.  Important  papers  were 
read  and  addresses  made  by  Elbert  B.  Monroe,  Chairman  of  the  Interna- 
tional Committee  ;  Lord  Kinnaird,  of  the  London  Committee  ;  President 
John  M.  Coulter,  of  Lake  Forest  University  ;  William  E.  Dodge  and 
Cephas  Brainerd,  of  New  York  ;  C.  M.  Hobbs,  of  Denver ;  E.  L.  Shuey, 
of  Dayton,  and  L.  D.  Wishard. 

IV. — In  relation  to  the  State  Conventions  : 

In  response  to  the  request  of  the  various  State  Committees,  arrange  - 
ments  were  made  for  the  representation  of  the  Committee  at  sixty-five 
State  and  Provincial  Conventions  held  during  the  years  1893  and  1894. 
The  names  of  these  representatives  are  given  on  another  page,  in  the  list 
of  these  conventions. 

V. — In  relation  to  the  secretaries,  agents  and  correspondence  of  the  Commit- 
tee and  its  sub-committees  : 

Correspondence  has  been  maintained  with  each  visiting  secretary  and 
agent  in  pursuance  of  the  instructions  of  the  Committee  and  its  sub- 
committees. 

The  Committee  has  been  obliged,  as  in  former  years,  to  employ  the 
services  of  special  agents,  in  order  to  respond  favorably  to  requests  for 
help  which  it  was  out  of  the  power  of  the  regular  force  to  render.  The 
following  gentlemen  have  rendered  satisfactory  service  in  this  capacity  : 

Logan  H.  Boots  resigned  as  a  regular  agent  in  the  Summer  of  1893,  but 
has  continued  to  aid  the  college  work  in  various  ways  on  special  occasions. 
He  was  succeeded  by  E.  Lawrence  Hunt,  who  devoted  nearly  a  year  to 
the  college  department,  making  an  extended  tour  among  the  institutions 


11 

on  the  Pacific  Coast.  A  similar  visit  was  subsequently  made  by  C.  C. 
Michener.  W.  H.  Sallmon  made  a  visit  of  several  weeks  among  the 
colleges  of  the  Maritime  Provinces  in  1893,  and  at  the  close  of  the  fol- 
lowing year  he  began  a  like  tour  among  the  colleges  of  Ontario  and 
Quebec.  Gilbert  A.  Beaver,  Percy  C.  Leslie  and  John  L.  Marshall,  Jr. , 
also  aided  the  college  work. 

C.  W.  Curran  and  E.  R.  Hicks  each  devoted  several  months  to  the  rail- 
road department  during  1893,  and  C.  H.  Moorman,  several  weeks. 

J.  B.  Squire,  C.  M.  Copeland  and  C.  S.  Ward  rendered  important  ser- 
vice in  the  West.  L.  B.  Moore  helped  in  the  colored  department,  and 
A.  L.  Biggs  and  James  Garvie  in  the  work  among  the  Indians.  Col. 
Von  Knoblesdorf  aided  the  German  work. 

VI. — Conference  at  the  office  of  the  Committee: 

Personal  calls  at  the  office  for  consultation  by  officers  and  friends  of  the 
Association  from  all  parts  of  the  country  have  multiplied,  various  prob- 
lems arising  in  relation  to  the  extension  of  the  work  have  been  considered, 
and  the  experience  accumulated  in  the  correspondence  and  visitation  of 
the  Committee  and  its  agents  have  been  placed  at  the  service  of  the 
friends  who  were  in  search  of  counsel. 

VII. — Correspondence : 

With  the  contributing  friends  of  the  international  work  correspondence 
has  been  carried  on  as  usual.  But  the  Committee  has  found  it  necessary, 
owing  to  the  additional  duties  of  the  General  Secretary,  to  distribute  to 
his  associates  some  of  the  financial  solicitude  and  responsibility  required 
of  him  in  previous  years.  In  answer  to  united  prayer  and  effort  the  Com- 
mittee has  been  enabled  to  provide  for  the  necessary  expenditures  of  the 
years  1893  and  1894. 

VIII.  —  World's  Conference: 

Following  the  instructions  of  the  Indianapolis  Convention,  the  Com- 
mittee issued  credentials  to  delegates  to  the  World's  Conference,  held  in 
London  June  1-7,  in  connection  with  the  Jubilee  of  the  parent  English- 
speaking  Association  in  that  city.  Proper  observance  of  the  Jubilee, 
June  6th,  was  also  promoted  extensively  by  the  Committee  in  this  coun- 
try, a  call  being  issued  to  all  the  Associations  to  commemorate  the  anni- 
versary. 

It  was  recommended  at  the  suggestion  of  various  friends  that  contribu- 
tions be  made  by  the  Associations,  and  those  interested  in  their  work, 
toward  a  permanent  fund  in  support  of  the  work  of  supervision  and  ex- 
tension as  intrusted  by  the  conventions  to  their  International  Committee. 
Over  Si,  500  have  been  contributed  to  this  fund,  and  has  been  invested  by 
the  Trustees  of  the  Committee. 

As  a  tribute  to  Sir  George  Williams,  the  honored  founder  of  the  London 
Association,  an  appropriate  memorial  address  was  prepared  and  pre- 
sented to  him  in  Exeter  Hall  on  Jubilee  Day,  June  6th,  in  the  name  of  the 
Associations  of  North  America.  It  was  signed  by  the  members,  trustees 
and  secretaries  of  the  International  Committee,  and  by  the  chairmen  and 
secretaries  of  the  State  and  Provincial  Committees.  The  address  was 


12 

carried  to  London  by  the  largest  American  delegation  (175)  ever  present 
at  a  World's  Conference. 

IX. — Personal  visitation : 

The  General  Secretary  has  attended  (1)  the  General  Secretaries'  confer- 
ences at  Louisville,  May,  1893,  and  Cedar  Kapids,  May,  1894 ;  (2)  the 
Students'  Summer  schools  at  Northfield,  in  July  of  1893  and  1894,  and 
several  of  the  State  Conventions. 

In  addition,  conferences  were  held  with  Association  officers  in  a 
number  of  cities,  and  several  anniversary  and  other  addresses  were 
delivered. 

He  attended  the  World's  Conference  in  London,  June  1-7,  reading  the 
paper  assigned  to  him  upon  the  work  of  the  American  Associations. 

X. — He  has  also  continued  to  serve  upon  the  Graduate  Committee  of 
Yale  University,  and  as  a  trustee  of  the  Association  Training  Schools  at 
Springfield  and  Chicago,  and  has  co-operated  with  the  National  Council 
of  Great  Britain  as  its  corresponding  secretary  for  America,  and  with  the 
International  Central  Committee  as  its  American  honorary  Secretary. 

XI. — In  relation  to  the  office  and  office  secretaries  of  the  Committee  : 

Each  addition  to  the  visiting  force  of  the  international  secretaries 
increases  in  many  ways  the  volume  of  correspondence  and  work  neces- 
sary at  the  Committee's  office. 

Erskine  Uhl  is  in  general  charge  of  the  details  of  office  work.  He 
also  acts  as  recording  secretary  of  the  Committee,  and  co-operates  with 
the  General  Secretary  in  relation  to  the  sub- committees  and  the  dispatch 
of  their  correspondence  and  work. 

P.  Augustus  Wieting  has  given  general  oversight  to  the  Treasurer's 
books  and  accounts,  attended  to  a  portion  of  the  correspondence,  helped 
in  preparing  and  revising  circulars  and  other  material  for  the  printer, 
collected  and,  in  conjunction  with  Mr.  Ninde,  edited  the  matenal  for  the 
Year  Books  of  1894  and  1895.  He  has  also  had  general  charge  of  a 
portion  of  the  details  connected  with  the  International  Conventions  and 
the  annual  dinner  meetings  of  the  Committee.  Charles  E.  Lyman,  the 
bookkeeper,  has  rendered  a  faithful  and  efficient  service  during  the  past 
two  years. 

John  Glover  has  had  entire  charge  of  the  delicate  and  responsible  cor- 
respondence connected  with  the  secretarial  bureau  of  the  Committee, 
keeping  the  list  and  register  of  the  general  secretaries  and  physical 
directors  upon  the  whole  field,  receiving  and  recording  notices  of  the 
various  secretarial  changes,  responding  to  applications  for  information 
from  Associations  seeking  secretaries  and  from  secretaries  or  candidates 
for  the  secretaryship.  A  large  share  of  his  time  is  taken  up  with  personal 
interviews  on  such  matters  with  callers  at  the  office.  This  varied  and 
difficult  service  he  has  rendered  most  acceptably,  seeking  and  receiving 
the  co-operation  of  his  associates  as  this  was  needed. 

Since  April  1,  1893,  77  men  have  found  positions  as  general  secretaries 
and  physical  directors  through  our  aid. 

At  the  office  personal  intercourse  or  correspondence  was  held  during 


13 

the  year  with  259  others  that  were  not  prepared  to  undertake  the  work, 
or  that  found  places  in  it  through  their  own  efforts. 

On  April  1,  1893,  18  vacancies  were  on  record  as  needing  our  help  ;  204 
applications  have  been  added  to  these,  making  222  altogether,  for  State 
Secretaries  and  their  assistants,  for  general  secretaries  and  their  assist- 
ants, and  for  physical  directors.  Of  the  222  vacancies,  we  assisted  in 
filling  77  ;  115  were  filled  through  the  action  of  others,  and  30  now  stand 
on  our  books. 

Of  the  vacancies  that  we  helped  to  fill,  5  were  in  Canada;  1  in  New 
England  ;  27  in  New  York,  New  Jersey  and  Pennsylvania ;  19  in  States 
west  of  these  ;  and  25  at  the  South. 

George  L.  Leonard  acted  as  office  College  Secretary  until  November, 
1893.  Since  then  he  has  had  charge  of  a  large  part  of  the  general  business 
details  of  the  office,  succeeding  Curtis  M.  Thorpe,  whose  resignation  was 
reluctantly  accepted  after  ten  years  of  very  efficient  service.  Mr.  Leon- 
ard has  given  special  attention  to  the  publication  list  and  work  of  the 
Committee,  and  has  also  wisely  conducted  a  portion  of  the  financial 
correspondence. 

H.  S.  Ninde,  as  editor  of  the  "Hand  Book,"  and  thoroughly  familiar 
with  the  best  methods  in  all  departments  of  the  work,  has  rendered  in- 
valuable service  in  the  editing  of  the  pamphlets  and  publications  of  the 
Committee,  and  in  attention  to  that  section  of  the  Committee's  corre- 
spondence which  relates  to  supplementing  by  counsel  and  the  most  recent 
information  the  instructions  and  intelligence  concerning  the  work  given 
in  these  publications. 

Clayton  S.  Cooper  succeeded  Mr.  Leonard  in  the  college  work  at  the 
office,  and  has  efficiently  conducted  the  large  correspondence  and  at- 
tended to  the  numerous  other  details  connected  with  this  department  of 
office  work. 

BIENNIAL  KEPORT  OF  THOMAS  K.  CEEE, 

Secretary. 

My  report  of  two  years  ago  closed  in  the  city  of  New  Orleans,  where  I 
spent  two  weeks  conferring  with  the  brethren  in  regard  to  their  work, 
and  starting  a  canvass  which  has  since  resulted  in  securing  the  money 
necessary  for  a  building,  now  in  process  of  erection.  I  then  visited 
Mobile,  conferring  with  the  State  Secretary  and  having  a  meeting  with 
the  local  Association.  I  held  similar  meetings  in  Montgomery,  Savannah, 
Charleston  and  Atlanta,  visited  Florida  in  the  interest  of  Association 
work,  spent  two  weeks  in  Augusta,  and  assisted  in  securing  pledges 
for  a  sufficient  amount  to  pay  the  debt  upon  the  building,  which  would 
otherwise  have  been  lost  to  the  work  of  the  Association.  At  Chattanooga 
I  conferred  with  the  brethren  in  regard  to  their  State  and  local  work. 

I  attended  the  Secretaries'  Conference  at  Louisville  and  the  Interna- 
tional Convention  at  Indianapolis,  arranging  for  many  of  its  details.  I 
attended  a  meeting  of  the  International  Secretaries  at  Indianapolis,  and 
two  subsequent  ones  held  in  New  York.  I  visited  Pittsburgh  a  number 
of  times,  and  conferred  with  brethren  interested  in  the  State  and  local 
work.  I  held  meetings  with  the  Associations  at  Mount  Vernon,  Yonkers, 
and  Poughkeepsie,  N.  Y.,  and  Montclair,  Jersey  City  and  Orange,  N.  J. 


14 

I  attended  a  district  conference  in  New  York,  and  have  visited  and 
spoken  or  given  a  stereopticon  exhibition  at  most  of  the  branches  of  the 
New  York  and  Brooklyn  Associations,  visiting  many  of  them  a  number 
of  times. 

I  spent  a  number  of  days  in  Chambersburg,  Pa. ,  and  secured  the  funds 
necessary  for  the  employment  of  a  secretary,  and  reopened  their  rooms 
and  started  their  work  anew.  I  visited  Toronto  and  arranged  for  a  re- 
organization of  the  work,  and  inaugurated  a  canvass,  which  has  since 
resulted  in  the  payment  of  a  considerable  part  of  the  burdensome  debt. 
I  visited  Boston  and  conferred  with  the  president  and  secretary,  and 
visited  a  number  of  other  places. 

I  attended  the  New  Hampshire  State  Convention  and  met  with  the 
State  Committee,  and  conferred  with  the  New  Hampshire  secretaries  and 
with  the  local  board  of  the  Dover  Association.  I  attended  the  Conven- 
tion of  the  Maritime  Provinces,  conferred  with  the  Provincial  Committee 
and  visited  a  number  of  Associations  in  the  Provinces. 

I  arranged  for  and  helped  to  secure  the  Association  Exhibit  at  the 
Columbian  Exposition,  and  also  helped  arrange  for  the  Association  Con- 
gress in  the  same  connection  and  attended  it. 

I  carried  on  an  extensive  correspondence  preparatory  to  and  f ollowing- 
the  Week  of  Prayer  in  November. 

By  request  of  the  Committee,  but  at  no  expense  to  its  treasury,  I  at- 
tended the  Jubilee  Conference  at  London  in  June,  1894,  served  as  chair- 
man of  the  business  committee  throughout  the  sessions,  furnished  cable 
reports  to  the  American  press,  arranged  for  a  breakfast  to  the  entire 
American  delegation,  and  so  far  as  I  could  promoted  the  comfort  of  the 
large  number  of  Americans  in  attendance.  I  attended  the  conference 
of  British  secretaries  at  Margate  after  the  meetings  in  London,  and 
visited  Paris  and  participated  in  the  ceremonies  connected  with  the 
decoration  with  the  Cross  of  the  Legion  of  Honor  of  Mr.  James  Stokes, 
a  member  of  the  International  Committee.  I  took  part  in  the  meetings 
of  the  Paris  Association  and  co-operated  in  securing  the  payment  of 
the  entire  floating  debt  on  the  Association  building,  amounting  to  $32,600. 
This  large  sum  was  given  by  Mr.  Stokes  and  Mr.  Andre,  whose  previous 
generous  gifts  had  rendered  the  building  possible.  I  conferred  with  the 
French  National  Committee  and  the  board  of  the  local  Association. 

Much  of  my  time  during  the  past  two  years  has  been  given  to  office 
work,  chiefly  in  connection  with  the  finances  of  the  International  Com- 
mittee, and  also  with  the  finances  of  local  Associations,  helping  them  to 
carry  debts  on  buildings,  to  plan  canvasses  for  buildings  and  current 
expenses,  and  in  many  other  ways  helping  secretaries  and  Associations 
in  details  and  administration  of  their  work. 


BIENNIAL    REPORT    OF    C.    K.    OBEE, 

Field  Secretary. 

The  first  part  of  1893  was  spent  in  the  Southwest  visiting  city  Associa- 
tions and  co-operating  with  State  Committees,  in  Louisiana,  Texas,  Arkan- 
sas, Missouri  and  Kansas. 

About  March,  1893,  under  direction  of  the  International  Committee,  I 


15  v 

transferred  the  Southwestern  work  to  Mr.  Gates,  and  took  up  the  work  in 
the  West  and  Northwest,  with  my  residence  at  Chicago,  to  which  field  I 
have  since  given  continuous  attention. 

This  field  includes  twelve  groups  of  Associations,  those  of  Illinois, 
Michigan,  Ohio,  Indiana,  Iowa,  Wisconsin,  Minnesota,  Manitoba,  North 
Dakota,  South  Dakota,  Nebraska,  and  the  Indian  Associations,  chiefly 
located  on  the  reservations  of  the  three  last  mentioned  States. 

The  five  last  mentioned  groups  were  unprovided  with  the  steady  super- 
vision of  State  Secretaries,  and  for  lack  of  such  attention  were  deteriorat- 
ing and  in  many  places  discouraged  in  their  work.  Consequently  my  time 
has  been  given  chiefly  to  this  part  of  the  field,  and  with  the  following 
results  : 

1.  The  Manitoba  Associations,  which  had  attempted  beyond  their  re- 
sources to  keep  a  Provincial' Secretary  in  the  field,  were  aided  in  the  re- 
adjustment of  their  work,  whereby  their  efficient  Provincial  Secretary, 
Mr.  Copeland,  has  been  retained  by  them  for  such  part  of  his  time  as 
they  can  provide  for,  and  the  Brandon  Association  has  been  enabled  to 
keep  a  general  secretary  for  part  of  his  time,  the  balance  being  given  to 
the  Provincial  work,  especially  during  Mr.  Copeland's  absence. 

2.  The  North  Dakota  Associations  have  been  encouraged  to  organize  a 
State  work,  and  have  engaged  part  of  the  time  of  Mr.  Copeland  as  their 
State  Secretary.     The  results  are  already  most  encouraging. 

The  State  Committee  contemplates  an  arrangement  with  the  Fargo  As- 
sociation for  a  supplementary  work  in  the  State,  similar  to  that  of  the 
secretary  of  the  Brandon  Association  in  Manitoba.  This  plan  makes  pos- 
sible a  steady  field  supervision  of  the  work  in  Manitoba  and  in  North 
Dakota,  and  at  a  comparatively  moderate  expense,  where  neither  group 
of  Associations,  nor  both  combined,  would  be  able  otherwise  to  employ  a 
traveling  secretary. 

3.  Ihe  Nebraska  Associations  have  been  aided  by  visitation  and  by  con- 
ference and  correspondence  with  their  State  Committee.     They  have  been 
helped  to  secure  such  part  of  the  timo  of  Mr.  Copeland  and  of  Mr.  Ward, 
of  Grand  Rapids,  Mich. ,  for  field  work  in  the  State  as  they  could  provide 
for,  and  additional  time  of  these  secretaries  has  been  furnished  them  by 
the  International  Committee  to  meet  critical  situations  and  important  de- 
velopments. 

4.  The  Indian  Associations  have  been  visited,  and  an  Indian  Traveling 
Secretary  of  the  International  Committee,  Charles  A.  Eastman,  has  been 
secured  and  put  into  the  field  for  this  work. 

5.  To  give  steady  supervision  to  these  weaker  groups  of  Associations, 
and  to  supplement  wherever  necessary  the  work  of  their  State  Commit- 
tees, the  plan  of  resident  field  supervision  by  the  International  Com- 
mittee already  undertaken  in  the  South,  the  Southwest  and  the  Central 
West  has  been  extended  to  the  Northwest,  and  Mr.  Copeland  has  been 
retained  in  that  field  for  this  work. 

In  the  locating  of  Field  Secretaries  by  the  International  Committee  for 
a  closer  and  a  more  continuous  relation  to  the  Associations  of  a  particular 
part  of  the  North  American  field,  it  is  not  contemplated  that  these  secre- 
taries shall  become  exclusively  sectional  in  the  segregation  of  their  time 
to  their  special  fields,  but  that,  while  the  interests  of  the  Associations  in  a 


16 

particular  section  shall  be  his  special  responsibility,  each  Field  Secretary 
may  also  be  available  for  service  in  other  parts  of  the  entire  field  when- 
ever, in  the  wisdom  of  the  Committee,  the  interests  of  the  whole  work 
may  make  such  service  desirable. 

In  addition  to  the  work  mentioned,  I  have  co-operated  with  the  State 
Committee  of  Colorado,  by  visitation  and  attendance  at  State  Conven- 
tion ;  and  have  aided  in  the  college,  railroad  and  financial  work  of  the 
International  Committee  as  I  have  had  opportunity.  Have  also  sustained 
relations  of  correspondence,  conference  and  co-operation  with  Mr.  Ander- 
son and  Mr.  Gates,  the  other  field  secretaries  of  the  International  Com- 
mittee, and  with  Mr.  Morse,  the  General  Secretary,  in  maintaining  the 
unity  of  our  work  of  general  field  supervision  in  North  America,  and  in 
planning  for  the  ultimate  adequate  supervision  of  the  entire  field. 

BIENNIAL  REPORT  OF  CECIL  L.  GATES, 

Field  Secretary. 

The  years  1893  and  1894  will  long  be  remembered  by  Association  men 
in  fche  West  and  Southwest  as  the  years  in  which  the  Association  work  of 
that  section  passed  through  trials  and  difficulties  that  might  well  have 
wrecked  a  more  strongly  organized  service.  But  in  the  face  of  these  unto- 
ward conditions,  improvements  in  the  work  have  been  planned  and 
established,  and  few  losses  have  been  sustained. 

At  the  opening  of  1893  I  was  engaged  in  the  development  of  the  work 
in  Colorado.  My  labors  there  were  continued  until  successful  Associa- 
tions were  established  at  every  available  point.  The  depression  in  the 
silver  industry  has  resulted  in  the  temporary  suspension  of  some  of  them, 
but  those  outside  of  mining  towns  are  still  doing  a  strong  work,  and  a 
high  standard  of  Association  service  obtains  throughout  the  State. 

Several  visits  were  made  in  1893  to  Salt  Lake  City,  where  an  aggressive 
work  was  established  and  is  still  maintained. 

In  June  of  the  same  year  a  visit  was  made  to  the  City  of  Mexico,  to 
secure  definite  information  regarding  the  work  there,  and  the  possibili- 
ties of  its  future  development  and  sustentation.  Several  days  were  spent 
in  that  city  and  in  San  Luis  Potosi,  counseling  with  the  board  of 
directors  and  others  interested. 

Considerable  time  has  been  devoted  to  the  visitation  of  railroad  points 
in  Kansas,  Nebraska,  Idaho,  Wyoming  and  Colorado,  where  railroad  de- 
partment work  has  been  established  or  is  possible  in  the  future.  Interviews 
were  held  with  prominent  officials  of  the  Northern  Pacific,  Southern  Pacific, 
Union  Pacific,  Denver  and  Rio  Grande,  Mexican  National  and  other  rail- 
roads, with  reference  to  the  establishment  or  maintenance  and  improve- 
ment of  railroad  departments  of  the  Association.  Careful  attention  has 
been  given  also  to  the  working  out  of  plans  for  rendering  the  local  Asso- 
ciations more  helpful  to  railroad  men. 

At  the  request  of  the  State  Committee  of  Kansas  a  systematic  visita- 
tion of  the  Associations  of  that  State  was  made,  previous  to  the  annual 
convention  of  1893.  This  visitation  has  been  followed  by  a  considerable 
amount  of  work  at  points  where  assistance  has  been  particularly  desired, 
and  by  frequent  counsel  with  members  of  the  State  force,  and  with  many 
of  the  general  secretaries  and  boards  of  directors. 


ASSOCIATION  BUILDING,  WATERBURY,  CONN. 

DEDICATED  OCTOBER  2,  1893. 
Dimensions,  60  x  130  feet.        Cost,  $70,000.         Population,  35,000. 


17 

In  December,  1893,  the  State  Committee  of  Missouri,  owing  to  the 
resignation  of  its  State  Secretary,  was  called  upon  to  face  a  serious  problem 
in  its  work.  The  immediate  visitation  of  a  number  of  Associations,  with 
a  view  to  their  extrication  from  financial  and  other  difficulties,  was  de- 
manded. Under  a  special  arrangement  with  the  International  Committee, 
I  have  given  fourteen  weeks  of  service,  at  various  intervals,  to  the  Mis- 
souri work.  Attention  has  been  given  to  nearly  every  detail  of  Associa- 
tion service,  and  a  close  connection  has  been  maintained  with  nearly  all 
the  Associations. 

Conditions  similar  to  those  surrounding  the  Missouri  State  work  were 
found  to  exist  in  Arkansas,  and  I  was  asked  to  assume  a  close  relation  to 
that  field.  Since  April,  1894,  careful  attention  has  been  given  to  the 
various  problems  in  the  work  in  that  State.  The  Associations  have  been 
visited  and  aid  has  been  given  in  nearly  all  departments  of  the  work. 

Extensive  correspondence  has  been  carried  on  with  points  in  Louisiana, 
Indian  Territory  and  Texas,  and  visits  have  been  made  at  various  times 
to  plan  and  counsel  with  the  secretaries  of  local  Associations,  and  also  in 
connection  with  State  work. 


BIENNIAL  EEPOKT  OF  H.  P.  ANDEBSEN, 

Field  Secretary. 

During  the  past  two  years  my  work  has  been  confined  to  the  Southern 
States  east  of  the  Mississippi  river.  To  these  States  I  have  maintained 
a  close  relationship,  having  my  residence  and  headquarters  in  Atlanta. 

I. — For  the  first  two  months  I  acted  as  State  Secretary  of  Georgia,  and 
prepared  for  and  aided  in  conducting  the  Georgia  State  Convention.  I 
aided  in  uniting  the  Georgia  and  South  Carolina  State  Committees  in  the 
employment  of  W.  M.  Lewis  as  State  Secretary,  and  assisted  in  arranging 
the  schedule  of  his  time  of  service  in  the  two  States.  I  also  assisted  in 
arranging  for  a  State  Convention  in  Mississippi,  and  helped  to  effect  a 
union  of  the  Mississippi  State  Committee  with  that  of  Alabama  in  the 
employment  of  F.  L.  Willis  as  State  Secretary.  In  the  absence  of  a  State 
Secretary  in  Tennessee,  I  became  acting  State  Secretary,  giving  for  fifteen 
months  one-fourth  of  my  time  to  work  in  that  State,  and  arranged  for 
and  aided  in  conducting  the  two  State  Conventions.  I  also  attended  to 
as  much  of  the  details  of  the  organization  of  the  State  work  and  of  State 
supervision  in  Tennessee  as  was  feasible.  I  attended  22  meetings  of 
State  Committees  in  eight  States,  counseling  with  them  and  assisting  in 
outlining  the  policy  of  their  work. 

The  depression  led  to  a  need  of  special  financial  aid  to  State  Commit- 
tees. I  visited  various  cities  in  Kentucky,  Tennessee,  Alabama  and  North 
Carolina  for  this  purpose.  I  helped  to  arrange  for  and  attended  confer- 
ences of  Southern  State  Secretaries  at  Charlotte,  N.  C. ,  and  Atlanta,  Ga. 

II. — The  general  financial  depression  has  caused  great  demand  for  as- 
sistance in  the  financial  department  of  local  Associations,  which  has  been 
made  more  urgent  by  special  emergencies.  I  spent  five  weeks  in  Augusta, 
Ga.,  aiding  to  secure  the  $30,000  needed  to  save  the  property  there.  I 
spent  nearly  two  months  in  Memphis,  Tenn. ,  where  a  disastrous  fire  had 
caused  the  loss  of  the  Association  property  and  the  death  of  the  general 
secretary.  I  organized  and  assisted  in  a  canvass  to  raise  $5,500,  aided  in 


18 

securing  a  new  secretary  and  in  fitting  up  attractive  rooms.  At  Greens- 
boro and  Henderson,  N.  C. ;  Montgomery,  Ala.,  and  at  Clarksville,  Chat- 
tanooga and  Bristol,  Tenn. ,  assistance  was  rendered  by  personal  solicita- 
tion when  the  life  of  those  Associations  was  threatened.  Help  was  also 
given  on  financial  lines  to  the  Associations  in  Athens,  Atlanta  and  Rome. 
Ga.;  Nashville,  Tenn.;  Wilmington,  Charlotte  and  Asheville,  N.  C.,  and 
Birmingham  and  Mobile,  Ala.. 

in. — I  aided  State  Secretaries  and  boards  of  directors  in  securing  15 
general  secretaries  and  physical  directors,  and  have  counselled  with  a 
number  of  young  men  about  entering  the  secretarial  work. 

IV. — Incidentally  I  have  co-operated  with  the  College  Secretaries  of 
the  Committee,  visiting  a  number  of  institutions  and  counselling  as  to 
methods,  especially  emphasizing  Bible  Study.  I  attended  the  College 
Students'  Summer  School  at  Lake  Geneva  last  Summer,  and  acted  as 
treasurer  of  its  executive  committee. 

V. — Much  time  has  been  devoted  to  attending  conventions  and  confer- 
ences. In  addition  to  representing  the  Committee  at  13  State  Conventions 
in  eight  States,  I  attended  one  district  conference  in  Kentucky,  two  in 
Tennessee  and  one  in  North  Carolina.  I  attended  two  general  secretaries* 
conferences  in  Kentucky  and  one  in  Georgia;  the  International  Confer- 
ences of  General  Secretaries  in  Louisville  and  Cedar  Eapids,  and  the  In- 
ternational Convention  in  Indianapolis. 

BIENNIAL    REPORT    OF    S.    A.    TAGGART, 

Secretary. 

My  services  during  the  period  of  time  covered  by  this  report  have  been 
divided  between  the  effort  of  enlisting  Associations  in  the  special  Exten- 
sion Work  and  more  varied  features  of  service  in  behalf  of  the  Com- 
mittee. The  latter  has  consisted  in  attendance  upon  State  and  district 
conventions  and  secretaries'  conferences,  conferences  with  State  Com- 
mittees, boards  of  directors  and  general  secretaries,  the  public  pre- 
sentation of  the  importance  and  requirements  of  the  local  Associations, 
building  projects,  solicitation  of  funds,  and  the  holding  of  evangelistic 
meetings  for  young  men. 

I. — At  the  following  places  where  I  have  visited  the  Extension  Work 
has  been  presented  at  meetings  of  members  of  Associations  or  of  boards 
of  directors,  and  sometimes  both  :  Brooklyn  (Central),  Cincinnati,  Cleve- 
land, Canton,  East  Liverpool  and  Springfield,  O.  ;  Springfield,  Spring- 
field (Armory  Hill),  Mass.;  Stamford,  Conn. ;  Clinton,  la. ;  Grand  Forks, 
N.  D. ;  San  Diego,  Cal. ;  Dallas,  Tex. ;  St.  Louis  ;  Saginaw,  Mich. ;  Evans- 
ville,  Terre  Haute,  Crawfordsville,  South  Bend,  Earlham  College,  and 
Fort  Wayne,  Ind. ;  Pittsburgh  (Central),  Pittsburgh  (East  Liberty),  Pitts- 
burgh (Railroad),  Philadelphia  (N.  E.),  Philadelphia  (West),  Oil  City, 
McKeesport,  Bethlehem,  Lancaster,  Harrisburg,  Sharpsburgh,  Coates- 
ville,  Danville,  and  Washington,  Pa.;  Dover,  Paterson,  Morristown, 
Trenton  and  Trenton  (R.  R.),  N.  J. 

I  also  visited  the  following  places  in  order  to  strengthen  the  oversight  of 
the  Extension  Work  by  consultation  with  the  committees  in  charge,  or  by 
endeavoring  to  search  out  suitable  chairmen  for  committees  :  Dayton, 
Cincinnati  and  Toledo,  O. ;  Indianapolis,  Ind. ;  Dallas,  Tex. ;  Los  Angeles, 


19 

Cal.;  St.  Louis;  New  York  (23d  Street),  Buffalo,  N.  Y.;  Baltimore;  Min- 
neapolis ;  Chicago  (West  Side)  :  Wheeling,  W.  Va. ;  Philadelphia  (Cen- 
tral), Philadelphia  (S.  W.),  Germantown,  Scranton  (R.R.),  Wilkes  Barre, 
Carlisle,  York,  Lancaster  and  Germantown,  Pa. 

In  addition  to  the  foregoing,  personal  conferences  have  been  held  upon 
the  Extension  Work  with  general  secretaries  and  other  representatives  of 
Associations,  at  Detroit,  Grand  Rapids,  Kalamazoo,  Covington,  Louisville, 
Newport  (Ky.),  Washington,  Cedar  Rapids,  Dubuque,  Chicago, 
Sterling  (HI.),  Peoria,  Lima,  Youngstown  and  Erie,  Altoona,  Johnstown, 
Pittston,  Chester,  Williamsport  and  Scranton  (Pa.). 

The  subject  has  been  presented  also  at  the  various  State  and  district 
conventions  and  secretaries'  conferences  that  I  have  attended. 

II.— The  difficulties  in  the  way  of  prosecuting  the  Extension  Work 
have  been  much  greater  during  the  past  two  years,  owing  largely  to  the- 
stringency  of  the  times.  What  has  been  accomplished  has  been  chiefly 
educational  and  preparatory,  I  trust,  to  much  more  substantial  results  in 
the  future. 

Past  experience  teaches  that  the  success  of  such  a  movement  cannot  be 
measured  by  the  interest  shown  in  it  by  the  members  of  Associations. 
It  does  depend,  however,  upon  the  willing  and  competent  responsibility 
that  can  be  secured  to  manage  it.  The  lack  in  this  respect  is,  I  might 
say,  the  sole  reason  for  seeming  failure,  and  the  supply  of  this  lack  will 
be  the  key  to  success  in  the  future.  All  other  difficulties  can  be  over- 
come, in  course  of  time,  under  the  wise  direction  of  the  right 
management. 

IH. — The  promotion  of  the  Extension  Work  has  frequently  been  forced 
to  become  incidental  to  varied  features  of  service  I  have  rendered. 

I  have  represented  the  Committee  at  the  State  Conventions  of  Arkansas,. 
Minnesota,  and  Pennsylvania ;  the  district  conventions  at  Rochester  and 
Williamsburg,  Pa.,  and  Batavia,  N.  Y. 

Conferences  have  been  held  with  representatives  of  the  State  Com- 
mittees of  California,  North  Dakota,  Texas,  and  Minnesota.  Conferences 
of  secretaries  in  Cedar  Rapids,  la.,  and  New  York  City  have  been 
attended.  The  exercises  connected  with  the  opening  of  new  buildings 
at  Johnstown  and  McKeesport,  Pa.,  were  participated  in. 

The  financial  needs  of  the  Committee  have  been  presented  by  personal 
interviews  in  Pittsburgh,  New  York  City,  Philadelphia,  Scranton, 
Wilkes  Barre,  Harrisburg,  Lancaster,  Germantown,  Altoona,  Coatesville, 
Franklin,  Titusville,  Washington,  Chester  and  Berwick,  Pa.,  and 
Wheeling,  W.  Va. 

I  have  assisted  in  contemplated  building  projects  at  Lancaster  and 
Hazleton,  Pa.  It  has  been  my  privilege  in  many  places  to  hold  evan- 
gelistic meetings  for  young  men  on  the  Lord's  Day. 

At  Devil's  Lake,  N.  D.,  I  presented  the  mission  of  the  Association  at 
the  Chautauqua  Assembly,  convened  there,  and  later  at  Grand  Forks  in 
the  same  State. 

IY. — The  correspondence  embraced  in  the  Extension  Work  has  covered 
all  parts  of  the  country.  In  much  of  this  there  has  been  the  expression 
of  brotherly  interest  and  the  expressed  desire  to  prosecute  such  a  move- 
ment in  the  future.
