BIENNIAL  EEPOET  OF  ROBERT  WEIDENSALL, 

Secretary. 

During  the  past  two  years  I  have  attended  the  International  Con- 
vention at  Indianapolis,  May  1893,  and  the  International  Secretaries' 
Conferences  of  1893,  1894,  and  State  Conventions  and  Secretaries'  Con- 
ferences in  Illinois,  Nebraska,  Maryland  and  Minnesota  ;  the  Western 
Secretarial  Institute,  promoting  an  important  change  in  its  constitution. 

Last  Summer  I  attended  the  Jubilee  Conference  in  London,  the 
Secretaries'  Conference  at  Margate,  and  visited  the  Associations  in  many 
places  in  Great  Britain,  in  Paris,  Berlin,  Geneva,  Turin  and  many  of  the 
chief  cities  of  eight  countries  in  Europe. 

In  promoting  county  work  I  have  visited  Rochester,  Minn.,  Edgefield 
County,  S.  C.,  Jefferson  County,  W.  Va.,  and  am  arranging  to  visit  in 
the  near  future  counties  in  Minnesota  and  Illinois.  In  all  this  county 
work  I  receive  the  hearty  co-operation  of  the  State  Secretaries .  It  is  a 
department  of  the  work  as  yet  only  just  beginning,  but  destined  to  a 
great  future. 

With  Messrs.  Hague,  Ober  and  Lougee  I  co-operated  in  securing 
financial  help  for  the  Associations  in  Minneapolis,  Sioux  City,  Iowa,  and 
Lincoln  and  Hastings,  Neb. 

In  the  last  two  years  I  have  spent  more  or  less  time  at  more  than  100 
cities  and  towns — many  of  these  in  the  British  Isles  and  on  the  continent 
of  Europe  ;  visited  more  than  50  Associations ;  made  public  addresses 
and  otherwise  rendered  special  services  to  the  following  among  other 
Associations:  Omaha,  North  Platte  (Neb.),  Charleston,  Washington,  Bal- 
timore and  Chicago. 

BIENNIAL  REPORT  OF  GEORGE  B.  HODGE, 

Secretary  Educational  Department. 
My  work  may  be  briefly  noticed  under  the  following  heads  : 

1.  Study. — The  pioneer  character  of  the  department  has  necessitated 
much  study  of  practical  work  for  young  men.     This  has  included  the 
visitation  of  the  best  Association  educational  work,  and  also  that  of  other 
institutions,  with  the  object  of  selecting  the  best  methods,  adapting  them 
to  the  Associations  and  recommending  their  adoption. 

2.  Office  and  Publications. — Much  time  has  been  given  to  office  work — in 
correspondence  and  conference,  collecting  and  classifying  information, 
making  numbers  of  charts,  preparing  and  publishing  "  Educational  Class 
Work,"  "Annual  Report  of  1894,"  "Outlines  and  Suggestions,"  "Class 
Record  Book,"  a  variety  of  blanks,  etc. 

3.  Gatherings. — Five  international  and  ten  State  conferences  and  conven- 
tions have  been  attended  and  participated  in,  striving  to  awaken  interest 
and  cultivate  the  growth  of  the  work. 

4.  Visitation. — In  16  States  over  100  visits  to  60  Associations  have  been 
made  in  the  interests  of  the  work,  and  help  and  encouragement  given. 

5.  Exhibits. — Much  of  the  growth  of  interest  is  due  to  the  exhibits  held: 
International,  at  Indianapolis  and  the  World's  Fair;  State,  in  New  York, 
Ohio,  Connecticut,  Illinois,  New  Jersey  and  Minnesota;  and  local,  at  25 


21 

or  more  places.  The  portable  exhibit,  inaugurated  in  May,  1894 — the 
frames  and  cases  for  which  were  made  by  the  industrial  class  of  the 
Springfield,  Ohio,  Association,  and  the  class  work  material  secured  from 
several  leading  Associations — has  visited  43  Associations  and  been  exam- 
ined by  25,000  people.  The  department  is  under  special  obligation  to  the 
individual  students  making  this  very  useful  exhibit  possible  by  the  loan 
of  their  work. 

6.  Conferences.  — I  have  had  many  conferences  with  committees  and  boards 
and  over  one  thousand  consultations  with  individuals.  During  the  two 
years  about  one-third  of  the  time  has  been  spent  in  the  office  and  the  re- 
maining two-thirds  in  the  field,  and  40,000  miles  traveled. 

NOTE. — The  complete  report  for  1893  is  found  in  the  "Annual  Report  of 
the  Educational  Department  for  1894,"  and  a  similar  report  for  1894  will 
be  published  in  the  forthcoming  "Annual  Eeport  of  the  Educational  De- 
partment for  1895,"  which  will  be  ready  for  distribution  in  August. 

BIENNIAL  EEPOET  OF  LUTHER  GULICK,  M.  D., 

Physical  Department. 

My  work  for  the  International  Committe'e  during  the  past  two  years 
maybe  conveniently  divided  into  (1)  the  carrying  out  of  plans  started  in 
former  years,  and  (2)  the  study  and  working  out  of  new  lines  of  effort. 

Under  the  first  head,  correspondence  has  been  carried  on  with  men 
contemplating  the  work  of  the  physical  directorship,  courses  of  reading 
have  been  recommended,  libraries  corresponded  with  regarding  the  best 
books  on  physical  education,  suggestions  given  about  the  physical 
department  in  Association  buildings  to  be  erected,  and  in  regard  to 
the  equipping  of  gymnasiums  and  athletic  grounds.  The  preliminary 
anthropometric  tables  have  been  completed,  and  placed  in  a  tentative 
way  before  the  public.  They  are  already  proving  of  widespread  value 
and  interest.  After  a  year  or  two  of  trial,  as  is  always  given  to  such 
cases,  they  will  become  to  a  regular  part  of  the  physical  department  publi- 
cations of  the  International  Committee.  State  Committees  have  been 
corresponded  with  in  regard  to  the  work  of  their  physical  department 
committees.  The  Pentathlon  and  the  Pentathlon  official  records  have 
been  kept  before  the  physical  directors. 

The  new  work  that  has  been  done  this  year  has  been  the  study  of  the 
problem  of  Association  co-operation  in  the  physical  work.  The  result 
will  be  submitted  to  the  Springfield  Convention.  The  problem  is  an 
exceedingly  large  one,  and  its  correct  solution  would  give  the  Associa- 
tions a  prestige  and  leadership  in  this  department  which  would  greatly 
aid  them  in  their  endeavors  to  attract  young  men. 

There  are  young  men  in  large  and  rapidly  growing  numbers  who  are 
interested  in  the  various  branches  of  sport,  and  who  can  be  won  and  held 
to  the  Association  by  this  means;  and,  particularly,  because  other 
existing  organizations  are  either  unable  or  do  not  desire  to  really  take 
hold  of  these  sports  in  a  way  to  be  of  service  and  interest  to  them.  These 
young  men  are  largely  found  in  the  cities,  and  spend  the  working  hours  of 
the  day  in  self-support.  These  factors  make  the  problem  both  important 
and  difficult.  First,  it  is  difficult  to  secure  grounds  of  sufficient  size  foi 
most  athletic  games  within  city  limits,  and  it  is  hardly  feasible  to  go  out 


22 

side,  as  the  time  and  light  are  both  limited  in  the  evening.  Then  these 
young  men  are  usually  of  moderate  means,  and  their  sports  must  not  be 
too  expensive.  They  must  also  be  those  that  have  only  a  minimum  of 
danger,  as  the  average  young  business  man  or  clerk  can  less  afford  to  be 
laid  off  from  work  on  account  of  a  sprained  ankle  than  can  the  average 
student. 

Then,  again,  the  atmosphere  which  surrounds  much  of  sport  is  directly 
antagonistic  to  the  spirit  of  the  Young  Men's  Christian  Association.  I 
refer  to  the  intense  rivalry  which  leads  to  undue  specialization  and  ex- 
cessive effort,  and  to  the  placing  of  an  undue  value  on  victory. 

The  Associations  must  have  to  do  only  with  sport  which  is  beneficial  to 
the  contestants,  and,  further,  if  we  cannot  create  and  maintain  a  spirit  of 
manliness,  honesty  and  courtesy  which  shall  frown  down  and  utterly 
prevent  all  cheating,  unfair  ruling,  and  considering  victory  as  of  first 
importance,  it  were  better  that  we  refrained  from  athletic  sport  altogether. 

A  movement  of  this  kind  can  only  be  accomplished  by  a  union  of  those 
who  believe  in  it. 

BIENNIAL  REPORT  OF  JOHN  R.  MOTT, 

College  Secretary. 

During  the  years  1893  and  1894  my  work  has  taken  me  into  nearly 
every  section  of  the  United  States  and  Canada,  as  well  as  into  three 
European  countries,  and  has  necessitated  over  55,000  miles  of  travel. 

I.  VISITATION. — Notwithstanding  the  fact  that  the  executive  work  of 
the  college  department  continues  to  take  an  increasing  amount  of  my 
time,  it  has  still  been  possible  for  me  to  visit  84  colleges  and  11  city 
Associations  in  25  States  and  two  Provinces.     This  does  not  include 
visitations  in  European  lands. 

II.  ORGANIZATION. — Associations  were  organized  at  14  institutions,  at 
four  of  which  I  had  the  co-operation  of  my  colleagues.     The  most  im- 
portant institution  to  enter  the  intercollegiate  movement  during  the  two 
years  has  been  Columbia  College.     This  constituted  about  the  last  great 
institution  on  the  continent  that  had  not  taken  this  step. 

in.  CONVENTIONS.— Fully  40  conventions  and  conferences  have  been 
attended.  The  list  includes  three  Summer  schools,  two  deputation 
conferences,  eight  presidential  conferences,  two  college  conferences, 
three  professional  school  training  conferences,  nine  State  Conventions, 
one  International  Convention,  one  World's  Conference,  seven  conferences 
of  secretaries,  and  a  few  special  gatherings,  such  as  the  Second  Interna- 
tional Convention  of  the  Student  Volunteer  Movement,  the  Convention  of 
the  Brotherhood  of  St.  Andrew,  and  the  Keswick  (England)  Conference 
for  the  Deepening  of  the  Spiritual  Life. 

IV.  MATTERS  RECEIVING  SPECIAL  ATTENTION. — 1.  General  Executive  Work. 
—  As  the  intercollegiate  movement  increases  in  extent,  and  as  each  depart- 
ment of  its  work  takes  on  a  higher  and  more  complex  development,  it  is 
necessary  for  me  to  give  more  time  to  working  through  other  men,  in 
order  to  preserve  the  unity  and  to  insure  the  steady  and  solid  progress  of 
the  work.  Therefore,  an  increasing  amount  of  time  is  spent  each  year  in 
conducting  the  various  kinds  of  training  conferences  and  in  outlining 


23 

advanced  policies  with  international,   State  and  local  committees  and 
leaders. 

±  Publication  Work.— An  exhaustive  pamphlet  on  "The  Missionary 
Department  of  the  College  Association  "  has  been  prepared  and  printed. 
An  extended  report,  showing  the  "  Progress  of  the  Intercollegiate  Move- 
ment "  during  the  college  year  1892-93,  was  written,  printed  and  intro- 
duced. The  department  on  the  "Monthly  Meeting "  in  The StudentVolun- 
teer  has  been  edited  from  month  to  month  through  the  larger  part  of  the 
two  years.  In  conjunction  with  my  colleagues,  a  few  printed  circular 
letters  were  prepared  and  sent  to  all  the  college  Associations. 

3.  Work  in  State  Universities.—  Within  the  two  years  a  thorough  visita- 
tion of  nearly  all  of  the  State  universities  was  made.     These  institutions 
are  growing  in  attendance,  wealth  and  influence.    They  have  within  them 
over  20,000  young  men.     The  Association  is  the  only  religious  agency 
which  can  cultivate  this  exceedingly  important  field.      The  difficulties 
and  problems  in  this  field  are  perhaps  greater  than  in  any  other,  save  the 
professional  schools  of  our  large  cities.     A  careful  study  of  the  conditions 
and  problems  of  the  field  was  made,  and,  in  each  case,  a  policy  was  sug- 
gested to  the  Association  for  the  better  prosecution  of  its  work. 

4.  Professional  Student  Field. — For  the  first  time  in  the  history  of  the 
intercollegiate  movement  an  effort  has  been  put  forth  to  grapple  with  the 
needs  and  problems  of  this  entire  field.     Together  with  Mr.  Brockman  it 
has  been  possible  to  visit  practically  all  the  cities  having  in  them  large 
numbers  of  professional  students.     The  work  has  been  successfully  or- 
ganized in  several  cities  where  little  or  nothing  was  being  done  for  this 
class.     In  the  cities  where  the  work  was  already  organized,  training  con- 
ferences were  conducted,  in  which  the  leaders  of  the  Associations  in  the 
various  schools  were  carefully  instructed  in  the  principles  and  methods 
of  the  College  Associations.     The  possibilities  of  this  field  are  equalled 
only  by  its  difficulties.    We  hope  that  the  next  five  years  may  witness  a 
steady  progress. 

5.  Special  Agents. — Percy  C.  Leslie  undertook,  early  in  1894,  the  office 
correspondence  and  work  of  the  college  department,  and  was  succeeded 
in  September  of  that  year  by  Clayton  S.  Cooper.     Their  important  work 
has  been  very  efficiently  attended  to. 

Logan  Herbert  Boots  closed  his  engagement  as  a  College  Secretary  in 
September,  1893,  but  since  that  time  has  represented  the  committee  ac- 
ceptably at  the  New  England  State  Conventions,  and  has  visited  several 
College  Associations. 

E.  Lawrence  Hunt  visited  the  Pacific  Coast  for  several  months  during 
the  college  year  1893-94,  giving  chief  attention  to  the  leading  institutions, 
organizing  three  Associations  and  participating  in  a  college  conference. 

C.  C.  Michener,  of  the  Iowa  State  force,  made  a  similar  visit  for  the 
Committee  to  the  colleges  of  the  Pacific  Coast  early  in  the  present  college 
year,  rendering  very  efficient  service. 

W.  H.  Sallmon,  president  and  now  general  secretary  of  the  Yale  Asso- 
ciation, spent  several  weeks  in  each  of  the  last  two  college  years  visiting 
the  colleges  of  the  Dominion  of  Canada.  He  also  taught  most  acceptably 
one  of  the  Bible  classes  at  the  Northfield  Summer  School. 


24 

Gilbert  A.  Beaver  and  Kev.  Harlan  P.  Beach  have  rendered  invaluable 
co-operation  at  the  Northfield  Summer  Schools  and  in  the  College  De- 
partment. 

J.  L.  Marshall,  Jr.,  has  spent  a  few  weeks  in  each  of  the  last  two  col- 
lege years  in  useful  visitation  on  behalf  of  the  Committee. 

5.  Student  Volunteer  Movement.  —As  the  representative  of  the  Associations 
on  the  executive  committee  of  this  Movement,  and  as  its  chairman,  I 
have  continued  to  give  special  attention  to  its  interests.     It  is  gratifying 
to  report  that  the  Movement  accomplished  more  during  the  last  two  years 
than  in  any  other  period  of  its  history.     It  is  rendering  a  service  of 
incalculable  value    to  the   Associations,   to  the  mission  boards  of   all 
denominations,  and  to  the  great  cause  of  world-wide  evangelization. 
Several  new  pamphlets  have  been  issued.     The  circulation  of  The  Student 
Volunteer  has  greatly  increased.      The  educational  department  of  the 
Movement  has  been  created.     The  possibilities  of  this  one  step  alone  are 
simply  boundless.     The  secretarial  force  of  the  Movement  has  increased 
from  two  to  seven,  making  possible  a  much  more  thorough  cultivation  of 
the  field.     The  second  international  convention  was  held  at  Detroit  in 
March,  1894,  and  was  not  only  the  largest  student  convention  ever  held  in 
the  world,  but  also  the  largest  and  most  significant  missionary  gathering 
ever  held.     Record  should  be  made  of  the  practical  and  spiritual  help 
rendered  the  Associations  in  our  colleges  on  other  lines  as  well  as  that  of 
missions  by  the  secretaries  of  the  Movement,  Messrs.  Lyon,  Sharman, 
Pitkin,  Eddy  and  Luce. 

6.  Work  in  European  Universities. — In  response  to  an  invitation  from 
the  Student  Volunteer  Missionary  Union  of  Great  Britain,  I  spent  several 
weeks  in  May,  June  and  July,  1894,  in  studying  and  promoting  the  re- 
ligious life  and  work  of  the  British  colleges.    It  was  my  privilege  to  visit 
practically  all  of  the  great  universities  of  England,  Scotland,  Ireland  and 
Wales.    Much  was  learned  that  has  been  helpful  to  me  in  the  American 
work ;  and,  on  the  other  hand,  the  lessons  from  the  experiences  of  the 
college  Associations  of  America  proved  to  be  stimulating  and  helpful  to 
the  British  workers.     A  remarkable  student  conference  was  held  at  Kes*- 
wick,   which  resulted  in  the  final  organization  of  an  inter-university 
Christian  movement  corresponding  to  our  own.    Able  secretaries  were  ap- 
pointed, and  remarkable  results  have  followed.     Some  assistance  was 
also  rendered  to  the  student  work  on  the  continent,  particularly  in  Paris. 
Our  faith  claims  a  marvellous  development  in  the  realm  of  organized  and 
aggressive  Christian  work  among  the  students  of  Europe  during  the  next 
few  years.     There  is  no  more  significant  sign  on  the  horizon  of  the  stu- 
dent world. 


BIENNIAL  EEPOET  OF  F.   S.   BEOCKMAN, 

College  Secretary. 

The  following  is  a  summary  of  my  work  during  the  last  two  years  : 

Visitation. — My  work  has  been  largely  among  the  colleges  of  the  South 

and  Southwest,  but  the  demands  of  other  sections  have  prevented  my 

giving  my  entire  time  to  this  field.     One  hundred  and  ninety  visits  have 

been  made  to  142  institutions  in  22  States.    These  visits  have  been  mainly 


ASSOCIATION    BUILDING,   GRAND   RAPIDS,    MICH. 

OCCUPIED  NOVEMBER  20,  1892. 
Dimensions,  88x88  feet.  Cost,  $92,000.  Population,  85,000. 


25 

for  the  purpose  of  strengthening  existing  organizations.  In  20  institu- 
tions hitherto  unorganized,  however,  Associations  were  established. 
Among  these  20  colleges  are  several  prominent  institutions  whose  influ- 
ence will  be  felt  in  the  intercollegiate  movement.  Invitations  have  been 
accepted  in  nine  instances  from  theological  seminaries.  In  no  case,  how- 
ever, did  the  visit  seriously  interfere  with  my  college  visitation.  Aid  has 
also  been  given  to  seven  city  Associations. 

Conferences,  Conventions  and  Summer  Schools. — A  large  portidn  of  my  time 
has  been  consumed  in  attendance  upon  different  Association  gatherings. 
I  was  present  at  two  sessions  of  each  of  the  following  :  Lake  Geneva 
Summer  School,  Northfleld  Summer  School,  the  International  Secretaries' 
Conference,  the  Conference  of  the  Secretaries  of  the  International  Com- 
mittee, and  the  Tennessee,  Arkansas  and  Mississippi  State  Conventions. 
I  have  attended  one  session  of  each  of  the  following:  The  International 
Convention  at  Indianapolis,  a  conference  of  Southern  State  Secretaries, 
a  Southern  deputation  conference,  conferences  of  College  Association 
presidents  in  Kentucky,  Texas  and  Virginia,  district  conferences  in  Mis- 
souri and  Tennessee,  and  the  Virginia,  Georgia,  Kentucky  and  North 
Carolina  State  Conventions.  I  also  attended* the  International  Conven- 
tion of  the  Student  Volunteer  Movement  at  Detroit.  Together  with  Mr. 
Luce,  secretary  of  this  Movement,  I  conducted  a  missionary  training 
conference  at  Nashville,  at  which  all  the  colleges  of  Middle  Tennessee 
were  represented.  The  opportunity  offered  at  these  gatherings  for  coming 
in  touch  with  the  leaders  of  hundreds  of  institutions  from  all  over  the 
country,  and  of  thus  most  effectually  promoting  the  best  interests  of  the 
Association  movement,  has  fully  justified  the  large  amount  of  time  given 
to  this  particular  work. 

Office  Work. — Ninety-eight  days  have  been  given  to  correspondence, 
editorial  work,  and  conferences  with  Mr.  Mott  and  other  secretaries. 

Evangelistic  Effort. — Invitations  have  been  accepted  from  a  few  of  the 
leading  State  universities  of  the  South  to  assist  in  spiritual  awakenings. 
While  it  is  impossible,  with  all  of  the  executive  work  which  is  absolutely 
necessary,  to  give  a  large  proportion  of  time  to  this  kind  of  effort,  the  re- 
sults have  been  most  gratifying,  and  I  am  persuaded  that  more  assistance 
should  be  given  by  the  Committee  to  the  colleges  for  evangelistic  work. 
This  applies  especially  to  the  State  institutions  for  which  no  one  church 
or  other  Christian  agency  feels  responsible. 

Southern  Summer  School. — Some  time  and  effort  has  been  spent  during 
the  past  Winter  in  laying  plans  and  in  raising  a  guarantee  fund  for  the 
Summer  School  for  Southern  students  to  be  held  at  Knoxville,  Tenn. 
This  gathering  will  hold  the  same  relation  to  the  Southern  colleges  that 
Lake  Geneva  and  Northfield  do  to  the  West  and  East.  There  is  every 
prospect  of  a  large  and  representative  meeting  this  year. 


BIENNIAL  KEPOET  OF  CLAEENCE  J.  HICKS, 

Secretary  of  the  Railroad  Department. 

During  the  past  two  years  I  have  been,  as  heretofore,  chiefly  occupied 
with  the  administration  of  the  Eailroad  Department.     Much  time  has 


26 

been  spent  in  and  about  New  York  City,  both  in  office  work  and  in  deal- 
ing personally  with  railroad  officials.  This  has  brought  me  into  close 
touch  with  the  other  departments  of  the  Committee's  work  centering  at 
the  office,  and  has  enabled  me  to  render  some  service  in  financial  and 
other  lines. 

The  continued  depression  in  railroad  business  has  made  it  impossible 
to  secure  corporate  appropriations  for  any  large  extension  of  the  Eailroad 
Department,  and  the  stress  has  been  to  retain  appropriations  already 
secured.  The  continuance  of  these  appropriations,  with  but  few  excep- 
tions, by  officials  and  receivers  who  have  been  forced  to  cut  down  ex- 
penses to  the  lowest  possible  figure,  is  unmistakable  evidence  of  the  fact 
that  this  work  has  acquired  a  position  of  permanence  in  connection  with 
railroad  management. 

Since  June  1,  1893,  Mr.  Hamilton,  whose  work  is  reported  separately, 
has  aided  in  the  work  of  this  department.  "He  is  now  located  with  head- 
quarters in  Chicago,  and  has  been  intimately  connected  with  the  railroad 
work  in  that  section,  as  well  as  on  the  Chesapeake  &  Ohio.  C.  W.  Curran 
aided  in  the  Kailroad  Department  several  months  and  then  accepted  a  call 
to  the  Railroad  Association  at  Richmond,  Va.  E.  R.  Hicks  rendered  tem- 
porary service  for  three  months,  especially  in  connection  with  railroad 
work  in  the  South. 

R.  E.  Michaels,  under  direction  of  the  Committee,  and  along  the  line  of 
the  Chesapeake  &  Ohio  Railroad,  rendered  very  efficient  service  for  weeks 
in  the  Summer  of  1894  in  holding  evangelistic  meetings  for  railroad 
men.  In  the  midst  of  his  blessed  work  he  was  called  from  earthly 
service  to  heavenly  reward. 

Seven  Associations  have  been  added  to  the  list  since  the  last  report. 
(1.)  Gladstone,  Va.,  where  the  Chesapeake  &  Ohio  Railway  Company 
has  erected  a  small  but  very  complete  building,  and  has  leased  the  same 
in  perpetuity  to  the  International  Committee  at  a  nominal  rental. 
(2.)  Clifton  Forge,  Va.,  where  a  $13,000  building  has  been  erected, 
largely  at  the  expense  of  the  same  company.  The  directors  of  this 
company  contributed  $2,000  for  a  library,  which  has  been  carefully 
selected  under  direction  of  the  Committee,  and  placed  in  this  building 
for  the  free  use  of  Association  members  along  the  line  of  this  road.  The 
catalogue  of  this  library  has  been  placed  on  the  list  of  the  Committee's 
publications,  as  a  model  for  other  Railroad  Associations.  (3. )  Watertown, 
N.  Y.,  where  a  building  has  been  equipped  and  a  secretary  placed 
on  the  pay-roll  of  the  Rome,  Watertown  &  Ogdensburg  Railway  Co. 
(4.)  Depew,  on  the  New  York  Central,  organized  as  a  department  of  the 
Buffalo  Association.  (5.)  Long  Island  City,  where  a  library  association 
that  had  not  been  a  success  was,  by  unaminous  request  of  those 
interested,  organized  as  a  Railroad  Department  of  the  Brooklyn  Associ- 
ation. (6.)  Truro,  N.  S.,  where,  during  a  visit  from  C.  W.  Curran,  an 
independent  railroad  men's  organization  was  changed  into  a  Railroad 
Department.  (7.)  Huntington,  Pa.,  a  division  point  on  the  Pennsylvania 
Railroad. 

At  Middletown,  N.  Y.,  a  large  pledged  membership  of  employees  of 
the  New  York,  Ontario  &  Western  Railroad  has  been  secured,  and 
the  railroad  company  has  purchased  a  site  and  is  'now  getting  out 


27 

plans  for  a  $5,000  building,  to  be  erected  by  the  company  for  the  use  of 
the  men  centering  at  that  point. 

March  29th  to  April  1st,  1894,  the  Seventh  International  Railroad  Con- 
ference, attended  by  over  300  delegates,  was  held  in  the  Railroad  Men's 
Building,  New  York  City.  The  generous  donor  of  this  building,  Mr. 
Cornelius  Vanderbilt,  has  recently  enlarged  it  by  an  addition  that 
doubles  its  capacity. 

The  Pennsylvania  Railroad  Department  at  Philadelphia  has  taken 
possession  of  its  new  building,  costing  over  $50,000,  and  its  work  has 
grown  so  rapidly  that  the  building  is  already  too  small. 

During  October,  1894,  at  the  request  of  the  president  and  vice- 
president  of  the  Southern  Railway  Company,  I  made  a  thorough  study 
of  the  19  division  points  on  that  system,  in  company  with  E.  R.  Hicks, 
and  we  submitted  a  report  showing  that  the  privileges  of  the  Association 
were  needed  at  15  places.  This  report  has  received  very  favorable  con- 
sideration, and  much  of  the  time  of  one  secretary  of  the  Committee  will 
probably  be  required  during  1895  to  establish  and  supervise  Railroad 
Associations  on  that  line.  H.  O.  Williams,  for  several  years  State 
Secretary  of  Virginia,  has  accepted  a  call  to*  the  Railroad  Department, 
and  will  have  special  charge  of  this  work  in  the  South,  as  soon  as  he  can 
be  spared  from  his  present  position. 

During  February,  1895,  I  took  a  trip  over  the  Union  Pacific  in  company 
with  Secretary  C.  L.  Gates,  going  as  far  west  as  Pocatello,  visiting  the 
Railroad  Associations  and  studying  the  unoccupied  fields.  This  trip  was 
made  specially  in  connection  with  the  administration  of  the  "Sidney 
Dillon  Fund"  of  $25,000  that  has  recently  been  given  to  the  Committee 
by  the  heirs  of  Sidney  Dillon,  the  income  to  be  expended  in  promoting 
this  work  among  the  employees  of  the  Union  Pacific. 

A  large  amount  of  time  has  been  given  to  the  St.  Louis  Railroad  De- 
partment. A  lot  adjoining  the  new  station  has  been  secured  from  the 
Terminal  Company  on  a  perpetual  lease  at  a  nominal  rental.  A  majority 
of  the  roads  using  that  station  have  already  agreed  to  bear  their  propor- 
tion of  the  expense  of  erecting  thereon  and  maintaining  a  Railroad  Asso- 
ciation building,  to  cost  not  less  than  $50,000.  This  undertaking  involves 
securing  the  co-operation  of  about  20  different  corporations,  and  will  still 
take  much  time. 

I  have  attended  the  State  Conventions  of  the  Pacific  Northwest,  New 
York,  Georgia,  Ohio,  and  the  Maritime  Provinces,  and  the  Secretaries' 
Conference  at  Cedar  Rapids.  Have  also  attended  the  dinner  meetings  at 
New  York,  Brooklyn,  Cleveland,  Scranton,  New  Haven  and  Hartford. 

The  Committee  has  a  long  list  of  division  points  where  Associations 
have  been  asked  for,  and  where  some  progress  has  been  made  toward 
getting  them  established,  but  at  many  of  these  places  no  appropriations 
can  be  secured  jintil  railroad  earnings  begin  to  show  the  looked  for 
increase. 

REPORT  OF  E.  L.  HAMILTON, 

Secretary  Railroad  Department. 

I  began  work  for  the  Committee  on  June  1,  1893,  and  since  then  my 
time  has  been  chiefly  given  to  the  Railroad  Associations  in  the  middle, 


28 

western  and  southern  States.  Have  made  158  visits  to  54  Associations, 
and  16  visits  to  six  unorganized  points  in  15  States.  Special  attention  has 
been  given  to  the  Chesapeake  &  Ohio  Railway  system,  visiting  each  of 
the  organized  points  several  times  and  assisting  in  organizing  new  Assso- 
ciations  at  Clifton  Forge  and  Gladstone,  Va.  Arranged  for  the  series  of 
special  evangelistic  meetings  conducted  by  the  late  R.  E.  Michaels, 
secretary  of  the  railroad  work  at  Richmond,  Va. ,  who  spent  from  three 
days  to  two  weeks  with  each  of  the  Associations  on  the  Chesapeake  & 
Ohio  Road.  His  efforts  resulted  in  about  50  professed  conversions.  Con- 
siderable time  was  also  given  to  the  pamphlet,  "Safety  in  Travel," 
recently  published  by  the  passenger  department  of  the  Chesapeake  & 
Ohio,  illustrating  the  buildings  and  work  of  the  Railroad  Associations  on 
that  line.  The  pamphlet  has  been  thoroughly  circulated  by  the  Com- 
mittee and  has  been  reviewed  by  and  received  editorial  notice  in  most  of 
the  leading  papers  of  the  country,  both  religious  and  secular. 

I  attended  the  Indiana  State  Conventions  for  1893  and  1894  ;  also  those 
of  Nebraska,  West  Virginia,  Kentucky  and  Virginia.  Assisted  Mr.  Hicks 
in  working  up  an  interest  among  the  Associations  in  the  Railroad 
Conference  held  in  New  York  City,  March  28-April  1,  1894,  and  also 
in  preparing  the  report  of  the  Conference  for  publication.  Carefully 
revised  the  plans  drawn  by  the  Chesapeake  &  Ohio  Railway  for  a  new 
Association  building  at  Russell,  Ky.,  and  have  the  president's  promise 
that  it  will  be  built  during  the  Summer  of  1895.  At  Brightwood,  Ind., 
just  on  the  outskirts  of  Indianapolis,  a  building  owned  by  the  Cleveland, 
Columbus,  Cincinnati  &  St.  Louis  Railway  Company  is  being  remodeled 
and  refurnished  at  the  company's  expense  and  a  Railroad  Department 
will  soon  be  organized  there.  A  first-class  restaurant  and  commodious 
sleeping  apartments  will  be  provided  in  the  building.  Have  attended 
several  anniversaries  and  committee  conferences,  met  with  boards  of 
directors  and  committees  of  management,  interviewed  many  railroad 
officials,  and  delivered  65  addresses  on  religious  topics  and  Association 
work;  50,183  miles  were  traveled  during  the  nineteen  months  covered  by 
this  report.  Thorough  organization  and  systematic  work  on  business 
principles  have  been  among  the  objective  points  in  all  my  effort. 


BIENNIAL  REPORT  OF  CLAUS  OLANDT,  JR., 

Secretary  of  the  German  Department. 

The  five  years  preceding  1893  each  witnessed  the  dedication  of  a 
building  for  work  among  German-speaking  young  men.  During  1893  a 
property  was  secured  in  Brooklyn  ;  in  1894,  at  Quincy,  111.,  valued  at 
$22,000;  and  in  1895  the  building  at  Buffalo,  valued  at  $50,000,  is  to  be 
dedicated. 

During  1893  nearly  all  of  my  time  was  devoted  to  the  German  work. 
Much  effort  was  given  in  assisting  to  establish  the  German  Branch  in 
Brooklyn,  and  in  securing  money  toward  the  purchase  of  its  valuable 
property.  In  Buffalo  also  considerable  attention  was  given  to  the 
building  fund.  At  Quincy,  111.,  time  was  devoted  to  the  plans  for  the  new 
building  as  well  as  to  the  building  fund.  At  Philadelphia  solicitation 
was  undertaken  for  the  current  expenses  and  for  the  building  fund. 


29 

A  number  of  weeks  were  spent  with  the  New  York  German  Branch, 
assisting  in  various  ways.  At  Chicago  several  weeks  were  devoted  to 
the  current  expenses.  A  visit  or  two  was  made  to  Rochester,  N.  Y., 
preparatory  to  organizing  a  German  Branch.  The  Indianapolis  Conven- 
tion was  attended  and  various  candidates  for  secretaryship  were  visited. 
More  subscriptions  were  given  toward  the  international  work  by  German 
friends  than  ever  before. 

In  1894  a  month  was  lost  through  illness,  and  but  a  part  of  the  year 
was  devoted  to  the  German  work.  A  new  Branch  was  organized  at 
Rochester  with  over  60  members,  and  with  fine  quarters  in  the  city 
Association  building. 

A  very  successful  conference  of  German-speaking  friends  from  different 
parts  of  the  country  was  held  in  New  York  during  August.  A  report  has 
been  printed  in  German,  with  illustrations.  Secretary  Elsaesser  of 
Stuttgart,  Germany,  paid  this  country  a  short  visit  during  the  Summer; 
wherever  he  came  in  contact  with  our  German  Branches  his  visits 
proved  very  helpful. 

It  was  my  privilege  to  attend  the  World's  Conference  at  London  and 
Secretaries'  Conference  at  Margate,  also  to  spend  a  few  days  in  Paris 
visiting  the  French,  the  German  and  the  Anglo-American  Associations  ; 
I  also  spent  about  two  weeks  at  Berlin  with  Association  friends,  attend- 
ing conferences,  making  addresses  and  talking  with  individuals  about 
various  phases  of  the  work. 

At  London  I  met  a  number  of  prominent  and  earnest  German 
Christians  who  were  very  much  interested  in  our  American  work  ;  as  a 
result,  Lieutenant  Colonel  von  Knobelsdorf  came  over  during  October, 
and  spent  a  week  each  with  eight  of  our  German  Branches.  Though  the 
visit  was  entirely  too  short,  much  good  resulted,  and  our  heartfelt  thanks 
are  due  him  for  this  free  gift  of  his  time.  We  have  the  prospect  of  a 
visit  from  two  German  gentlemen  the  present  year  ;  one,  the  court 
preacher,  Stoecker ;  the  other,  the  young  Pastor  Krummacher  of  Pots- 
dam, the  son  of  the  author  and  court  preacher. 

Considerable  time  has  been  devoted  to  the  work  in  the  Southwest— in 
Texas  and  Arkansas.  Several  months  were  spent  in  New  England,  especi- 
ally in  New  Hampshire  and  Vermont,  before  and  after  the  Keene 
Convention.  At  all  of  the  conferences  and  conventions  it  was  my 
privilege  to  attend  there  were  manifestations  of  the  power  of  the  Holy 
Spirit. 

During  1893,  as  well  as  1894,  some  time  was  given  to  soliciting  funds 
for  the  International  Committee.  Though  both  of  these  years  have  seen 
many  enterprises  suffer  shipwreck,  yet  we  can  say  with  gratitude  to  God 
that  no  German  Branch  has  been  compelled  to  close  its  doors.  In  many 
ways  the  German  work  is  in  a  better  condition  than  it  has  ever  been 
before. 


BIENNIAL  REPORT  OF  W.  A.  HUNTON, 

Secretary  Colored  Men's  Department 

My  statement  of  work  performed  during  the  period  covered  by  this 
report  may  be  made  under  seven  heads. 


30 

Conferences. — I  attended  in  all  nine  conferences  and  conventions, 
namely,  four  conferences  of  representatives  of  Colored  Associations  held, 
respectively,  at  Norfolk,  Va. ;  Nashville,  Tenn. ;  Atlanta,  Ga. ;  and  Peters- 
burg, Va. ;  also  two  conferences  of  members  and  secretaries  of  the  Inter- 
national Committee  at  New  York,  the  International  Secretaries'  Con- 
ference at  Louisville,  the  International  Convention  at  Indianapolis,  and 
the  World's  Conference  at  London. 

City  Work.—  I  made  91  visits  to  26  cities  and  towns  in  12  different  States 
in  connection  with  local  Association  work.  I  addressed  gospel  meetings, 
organized  Bible  classes,  attended  meetings  of  directors  and  committee- 
men,  had  consultations  with  local  secretaries  and  other  officers,  and  de- 
voted 112  days  to  the  solicitation  of  funds  for  local  work.  Associations 
were  organized  in  the  following  cities:  New  Haven,  Conn. ;  Camden,  N.  J. ; 
Wilmington,  Del.;  Pittsburgh,  Pa.;  Baltimore,  Memphis  and  Little 
Rock.  Investigations  were  made  and  work  done,  occupying  from  two 
days  to  three  weeks,  in  eight  other  cities  and  towns  where  Associations 
have  not  been  permanently  organized. 

College  Work. — Sixty-five  visits  were  made  to  28  schools  of  higher  learn- 
ing in  11  States,  from  one  to  three  days  being  spent  at  each  school.  Six 
College  Associations  were  organized.  This  work  among  students  con- 
tinues to  increase  in  interest  and  value.  Many  of  the  most  promising 
young  men  of  the  race  that  were  active  workers  in  some  normal  school  or 
college  have  become  efficient  members  of  city  Associations. 

Correspondence.  — The  Associations  of  the  Colored  Men's  Department 
are  scattered  over  such  a  large  area  that  it  is  impossible  for  me  to  visit 
many  of  them  oftener  than  once  a  year.  But  I  have  endeavored  to  keep 
in  touch  with  their  work  by  frequent  correspondence. 

Publications.—!,  prepared  for  publication  "The  Colored  Men's  Depart- 
ment of  the  Young  Men's  Christian  Association,"  which  contains  an 
historical  outline  of  the  work  among  colored  men,  and  a  report  of  five 
conferences  with  several  of  the  best  papers  read  at  these  meetings. 

Summary. — I  made  156  visits  to  26  cities  and  28  schools  located  in  20 
different  States  ;  conducted  four  conferences  of  representatives  of  Colored 
Associations,  and  attended  five  other  conferences  and  conventions  ; 
devoted  112  days  to  financial  solicitation  ;  organized  13  Associations  ; 
prepared  for  publication  "The  Colored  Men's  Department, "  and  kept  up 
a  large  correspondence. 

Needt. — Two  peculiar  needs  of  this  department  at  this  time  are(l),  a  closer 
supervision  through  the  agency  of  the  International  Committee,  which  is 
essential  to  the  proper  development  and  extension  of  the  work,  and 
which  can  be  had  only  by  an  increase  in  the  secretarial  force  in  charge  of 
this  department;  and  (2)  more  liberal  financial  support  for  the  local  work, 
which  will  make  possible  the  employment  of  competent  secretarial  leader- 
ship, a  very  particular  and  immediate  need. 


REPORT  OF  CHARLES  A.  EASTMAN, 

Secretary  Indian  Department. 

I  entered  the  work  June  1,  1894,  and  by  September  10  had  visited  all  of 
the  Associations  on  the  Sioux  Reservations  in  North  and  South  Dakota 


31 

and  Nebraska.  This  tour  was  necessarily  rapid  and  the  visits  brief,  as  it 
seemed  best  to  get  a  comprehensive  view  of  the  whole  field  of  the  Reserva- 
tion work  and  the  exact  condition  of  the  Associations  before  the  annual 
meeting  of  the  Associations  at  the  Indian  Missionary  Conference  in  Sep- 
tember. 

I  was  present  at  this  Conference  at  Cherry  Creek,  South  Dakota,  Sep- 
tember 13-16,  which  was  well  attended  by  representative  members  of  the 
Sioux  Associations. 

In  October  I  visited  the  Associations  on  the  reservations  in  North  Da- 
kota and  in  Manitoba.  In  Manitoba  I  found  a  good  field  for  future  As- 
sociation work  among  the  Crees  and  Sotos. 

In  November  and  December  I  again  visited  the  Associations  on  the 
reservations  in  South  Dakota,  including  Standing  Bock,  Cheyenne  River, 
Lower  Brule,  Crow  Creek  and  Flandreau.  Fifteen  Associations  were 
visited  on  this  trip  and  a  longer  time  spent  at  each  place.  My  work  was 
mostly  that  of  instructing,  interesting  and  explaining  the  more  important 
features  of  the  Association  work.  I  also  made  systematic  effort  to  induce 
every  Association  to  take  up  regular  study  of  the  Bible,  and  gave  special 
attention  to  the  training  of  leaders. 

In  January  and  February  I  made  a  six  days'  visit  to  the  Association  at 
the  Carlisle  Indian  Training  School  in  Pennsylvania,  met  the  Inter- 
national Committee  in  New  York  City,  visited  the  Associations  on  the  Sis- 
seton  Reservation  and  attended  the  Minnesota  State  Convention. 

In  March  and  the  first  part  of  April  I  visited  the  Associations  on  the 
Yankton  and  Santee  Reservations,  at  the  Haskell  Institute,  Lawrence, 
Kansas,  and  the  Indian  Schools  at  Telequah  and  Muskoge,  in  the 
Indian  Territory,  and  attended  the  Texas  State  Convention  at  Austin. 

As  the  result  of  the  study  of  the  field  and  work  of  the  Indian  Asso- 
ciations for  the  past  ten  months,  I  would  say  : 

1.  The  Associations,  though  willing  and  enthusiastic,  are  very  limited 
in  experience. 

2.  Everywhere  the  Indian  young  men  are  anxious  to  take  hold,  but  the 
great  drawback  is  the  lack  of  competent  leaders. 

3.  There  is  great  need  of  simple  and  practical  classes  for  Bible  study; 
to  deepen  and  broaden  the  religious  lives  of  the  young  men  and  to  fit 
them  for  intelligent  Christian  service. 

4.  I  have  been  profoundly  impressed  with  the  good  work  done  by  a 
number  of  these  Associations  under  discouraging  circumstances,  and  my 
faith  in  the  possibilities  of  the  work  has  been  greatly  strengthened. 

5.  The  Associations  on  the  Reservation  can  supplement  the  Associations 
in  the  various  Indian  Training  Schools,  and  in  this  way  greatly  help  to 
solve  the  problem  of  ';the  returned  Indian  student,"  and  how  he  can 
make  use  on  the  Reservation  of  what  he  has  gained  at  school. 

6.  As  steps  toward  the  better  development  of  the  work,  I  would  recom- 
mend (a)  an  annual  Indian  Association  Summer  School,  for  training  in 
Bible  study  and  methods  of  Christian  Association  work;  and  (b)  that  sev- 
eral carefully  selected  young  men  be  trained  in  the  Association  Training 
Schools  at  Chicago  and  Springfield,  for  leadership  and  organization  of  the 
Associations  on  the  different  Reservations . 


32 

BIENNIAL  REPORT  OF  LUTHER  D.  WISHARD, 

Secretary  of  the  Foreign  Department. 

The  foreign  department  of  the  Committee  involves  not  only  the  work  of 
its  secretaries  in  foreign  mission  lands,  but  also  a  steadily  accumulating 
work  in  this  country,  consisting  of  work  at  the  office,  visitation  of  Associ- 
ations, attendance  at  conventions  and  addresses  in  churches  and  before 
various  religious  bodies  for  the  purpose  of  promoting  prayerful  interest  in 
and  financial  support  of  the  foreign  work. 

The  work  in  foreign  lands  is  reported  by  the  field  secretaries.  It  may, 
however,  be  well  to  gather  into  a  few  paragraphs  the  salient  facts  of  the 
foreign  movement  for  1893  and  1894. 

1.  JAPAN.— The  Tokyo  building  was  furnished  and  dedicated  in  May, 
1894.     The  Summer  School  held  in  August,  1893,  was  attended  by  about 
600  persons,  a  larger  number  than  has  ever  been  present  at  similar  Asso- 
ciation gatherings  in  America  or  Europe.    The  Associations  have  mani- 
fested a  spirit  of  the  liveliest  patriotism  during  the  war  by  appealing  for 
supplies,  and  encouraging  the  young  men  of  the  country  to  make  any 
needed  sacrifices  for  the  government.     The  building  in  Tokyo  affords 
Christians  of  all  denominations  a  rallying  place  from  which  to  inaugurate 
evangelistic  work  at  home  and  a  foreign  mission  to  the  Koreans.     The 
Associations  throughout  the  empire  are  growing  in  numbers  and  effi- 
ciency.    Preliminary  steps  have  been  taken  toward  the  formation  of  a 
national  organization. 

2.  INDIA. — The  organization  of  the  national  union  has  been  perfected 
by  the  adoption  of  a  constitution.     A  promising  Association  has  been 
formed  in  Calcutta,  whose  work  will  be  chiefly  among  young  Englishmen 
and  Eurasians.     Money  was  subscribed  in  Great  Britain  last  Summer,  in 
response  to  the  personal  appeal  of  Mr.  McConaughy,  for  the  purchase  of 
the  site  for  a  building  in  Madras.     The  lot  has  since  been  secured.     The 
force  of  secretaries  has  been  increased  by  the  addition  of  J.  Campbell 
White  for  the  students'  work  in  Calcutta,  and  Raymond  J.  Davis  for  the 
general  secretaryship  of  the  Associations  of  students  and  business  men 
in  Madras.     A.  P.   Stockwell  has  become  the  general  secretaryship  of 
of  the  city  Association  in  Calcutta. 

3.  BRAZIL. — Mr.  Clark  has  effected  the  organization  of  an  Association 
in  Rio  de  Janeiro  which  survived  the  stormy  days  of  the  revolution,  and 
is  acquiring  a  strong  hold  upon  the  sympathies  and  confidence  of  the 
young  men  of  the  capital.     The  inquiries  which  Mr.  Clark  receives  from 
various  parts  of  South  America  indicate  that  other  cities  are  likely  to  fol- 
low the  example  of  Rio  de  Janeiro  by  organizing  Associations. 

4.  OTHER  COUNTRIES. — The  Associations  in  China  and  Ceylon  have 
maintained  their  work  so  faithfully  without  secretaries  as  to  fully  confirm 
the  wisdom  of  the  missionaries  in  those  countries  in  asking  the  American 
Committee  to  send  secretaries  to  organize  and  direct  Association  move- 
ments there.     The  Committee  has  appointed  D.  Willard  Lyon,  a  graduate 
of  the  University  of  Wooster,  to  pioneer  the  movement  in  China.     Mr. 
Lyon  is  peculiarly  qualified  for  this  important  service,  not  only  by  his 
birth  and  early  training  in  China,  but  by  his  extended  experience  as  a 
leader  in  the  Student  Volunteer  Movement  in  this  country.    It  is  expected 


that  he  will  sail  for  his  field  in  August.  Mr.  Louis  Hieb,  a  graduate  of 
Dickinson  College,  Carlisle,  Pa. ,  formerly  connected  with  the  Association 
in  Camden  and  more  recently  with  student  Association  work  in  Pennsyl- 
vania, has  been  chosen  to  direct  the  movement  in  Ceylon. 

Students'  Associations  are  now  organized  in  Chili,  Japan,  China,  India, 
Ceylon,  Burmah,  South  Africa,  West  Central  Africa,  Persia,  Kurdistan, 
Asia  Minor,  Syria,  Turkey  in  Europe  and  Bulgaria.  Associations  of 
young  business  men  exist  in  Mexico,  .Argentine  Republic,  Brazil,  British 
Guiana,  Uruguay,  Japan,  China,  India,  Ceylon,  the  Caucasus,  Asia 
Minor,  Syria,  Turkey  in  Europe,  Egypt,  South  Africa,  Madagascar  and 
Hawaii.  % 

Through  the  work  of  the  home  secretary  of  the  foreign  department  it  is 
believed  that  the  interest  of  the  American  Associations  in  the  foreign 
work  has  been  slowly  but  steadily  increased.  The  secretary's  time  has 
been  largely  devoted  to  financial  solicitation,  and  he  is  able  to  report  that 
the  foreign  budgets  of  the  Committee  for  1893  and  1894  were  fully  met. 
By  public  addresses  in  churches  and  various  religious  gatherings  the 
principles  of  the  foreign  work  have  been  discussed  and  a  steadily  increas- 
ing constituency  of  financial  contributors  has  been  secured.  The  calls 
for  the  extension  of  the  work  were  never  more  urgent  than  now,  and  if 
the  Associations  and  their  friends  will  respond  to  these  calls  by  furnish- 
ing men  and  money,  with  which  to  support  them,  there  is  little  doubt 
that  the  Young  Men's  Christian  Associations  may  become  one  of  the 
Church's  most  valuable  agencies  in  its  foreign  missionary  enterprises. 


BIENNIAL  EEPOET  OF  JOHN  T.  SWIFT, 

Secretary  for  Japan. 

An  interval  of  ten  months  separates  the  writing  of  this  report  from  any 
direct  participation  on  my  part  in  the  affairs  of  the  Associations  in  Japan. 
This  brief  period  has  sufficed  to  change  completely  the  international 
status  of  the  Japanese  empire,  and  to  revolutionize  the  opinions  of  the 
whole  civilized  world  respecting  the  relative  importance  and  peculiar 
destinies  of  the  nations  of  eastern  Asia. 

A  consideration  of  the  national  characteristics  by  which  such  a  change 
has  been  effected  cannot  but  deepen  our  convictions  that  work  amongst 
the  young  men  of  Japan  means,  in  a  very  intense  and  practical  way,  work 
for  the  young  men  of  all  the  great  nations  of  awakened  Asia. 

Returning  now  to  a  brief  review  of  the  situation  as  it  was  during  the 
sixteen  months  previous  to  May,  1894,  the  points  of  encouragement  were  : 
(1)  The  evidences  of  improvement  on  the  part  of  the  Associations  in  respect 
of  the  regularity  and  definiteness  of  their  work.  This  was  doubtless 
brought  about  in  large  part  by  the  visits  of  Mr.  Niwaand  Mr.  Miller,  and 
also  by  the  circulation  of  "Kirisutokyo  Sei  Neu "  (Christian  Young 
Man),  a  monthly  magazine  of  about  46  octavo  pages,  published  by  the 
Tokyo  Association  as  the  organ  of  the  Associations  throughout  the 
empire.  (2)  The  financial  independence  of  the  Associations,  which  were 
all  self-supporting  with  the  exception  of  the  one  in  Tokyo,  where  the 
national  character  of  many  of  the  enterprises  undertaken  renders  the 


34 

local  support  inadequate.  (3)  The  fact  that  the  results  of  the  work  itself 
were  in  almost  every  particular  the  fruits  of  the  labors  of  our  Japanese 
brethren,  whose  earnest  and  devoted  lives  have  been  applied  to  the  spread- 
ing of  the  gospel  message  amongst  their  fellow  men. 

Justice  requires  that  the  prolonged  and  assiduous  work  of  my  associate, 
Mr.  Miller,  upon  the  Japanese  language  should  receive  more  extended 
notice  than  he  is  likely  to  give  to  it.  Any  mere  statement  of  the  time 
which  he  has  devoted  to  the  mastery  of  its  threefold  intricacies  gives  but 
a  very  slight  conception  of  the  severe  and  unremitting  labor  that  he  has 
bestowed  upon  it  for  the  past  four  years.  It  should  be  gratifying  to  his 
American  friends  to  know  that  he  has  already  attained  such  recognized 
ability  in  its  use  as  will  greatly  enhance  the  value  of  his  service. 

My  own  time  previous  to  May,  1894,  was  of  necessity  entirely  spent  in 
Tokyo.  I  was  in  quite  constant  conference  with  the  officers  and  members 
of  the  Tokyo  Association  and  with  visiting  workers  from  other  localities. 
There  was  a  large  amount  of  clerical  work  demanding  my  attention,  and  I 
was  able  to  devote  some  time  to  the  study  of  the  language.  It  was  also 
my  privilege  to  do  some  personal  work  amongst  a  considerable  number  of 
young  men  with  whom  I  could  converse  in  English. 

The  completion  of  the  building  for  the  Tokyo  Association  also  gave  rise 
to  a  large  number  of  details  requiring  my  attention.  The  care  bestowed 
upon  its  plans  and  construction  by  the  architect  and  building  committee 
during  the  long  period  of  nearly  five  years  was  amply  justified  last  June 
when  it  endured,  without  sustaining  a  crack,  the  most  destructive  earth- 
quake that  Tokyo  has  experienced  in  many  years.  The  whole  structure 
consists  of  two  connected  fireproof  buildings  of  pressed  brick  with  white 
sandstone  trimmings,  each  occupying  a  ground  space  about  50  feet 
square.  The  rear  building  contains  the  Association  Hall,  capable  of  seat- 
ing about  1,000  people  ;  the  other,  occupying  the  front  of  the  lot,  is  three 
stories  in  height,  and  contains  a  central  social  hall,  two  parlors,  a  library, 
and  a  secretary's  office,  and  also  five  well  lighted  class  rooms,  a  committee 
room,  a  kitchen  and  some  space  for  physical  work.  The  whole  is  heated 
by  steam  and  lighted  by  electricity.  The  building  is  located  at  the  very 
heart  of  the  city,  in  the  quarter  most  resorted  to  by  young  men.  Its 
influence  is  manifest,  even  in  this  season  of  war  excitement,  in  the  more 
than  doubling  of  the  membership  and  of  the  attendance  upon  the  various 
classes,  but  especially  in  the  greatly  increased  attendance  upon  the 
evangelistic  meetings  for  young  men.  Nor  are  its  good  offices  confined 
to  strictly  Association  affairs  ;  it  is  the  largest  and  most  central  building 
belonging  to  the  protestant  evangelical  churches,  and  is  constantly 
used  by  them.  The  dedication  occurred  on  May  5,  1894,  and  drew  to- 
gether a  large  and  widely  representative  assembly. 

Leaving  Japan  on  May  llth  I  returned  to  the  United  States.  It  wus 
my  expectation  and  desire  to  be  at  my  post  again  in  the  following 
October  and  my  return  passage  was  engaged  accordingly,  but  the  urgent 
advice  of  several  physicians,  separately  consulted  was  that  I  should 
absent  myself  for  a  longer  period.  The  wisdom  of  their  counsel  has  since 
been  apparent.  For  the  entirely  sympathetic  action  of  the  Committee  iu 
this  respect  I  am  very  grateful. 


35 


BIENNIAL  BEPOBT  OF  B.   S.  MILLEE,  JR, 

Secretary  in  Japan. 

My  work  during  the  years  1893  and  1894  naturally  divides  itself  into  two 
parts,  that  done  in  Tokyo  and  that  done  in  the  other  cities  of  the  empire. 
The  year  1893  was  largely  devoted  to  the  latter  ;  1894  more  consecutively 
to  the  former. 

1.  In  1893  I  made  four  visits  to  the  Kobe  Association,  and  two  each  to 
the  Associations  of  Osaka,  Kyoto,  and  Nagoya,  spending  from  one  week 
to  one  month  at  each  visit.    In  1894  I  made  two  more  visits  to  Nagoya. 
The  main  object  of  my  work  in  Kobe  and  Nagoya  was  to  reorganize  the 
Associations  and  prepare  the  way  lor  the  call  of  general  secretaries  on  the 
basis  of  entire  or  partial  self-support.     Arrangements  were  made  at  Kobe 
for  the  call  of  a  secretary,  and  negotiations  for  a  man  begun,  when  they 
were  suddenly  stopped  and  the  Association  suspended  operations  for  a 
year.     Perhaps  the  best  that  can  be  said  for  the  work  there  at  present  is 
that  the  ground  has  been  cleared  of  encumbrances  and  the  way  opened 
for  reorganization  in  the  future. 

In  Nagoya  a  secretary  (Mr.  Masaki)  was  secured,  his  salary  pledged  in 
the  city,  and  his  work  begun.  He  proved  a  faithful  and  devoted  official, 
standing  at  his  post  until  driven  from  it  by  a  fatal  disease,  and  even  in 
the  weakness  of  his  last  days  writing  and  dictating  earnest  letters  in  be- 
half of  the  work.  The  work  itself  has  not  been  all  that  was  expected, 
owing  to  the  fact  that  the  principles  and  methods  of  Association  work 
were  not  fully  understood  either  by  the  workers  or  the  constituency  of 
the  Association,  and  still  more  to  the  fact  that  many  of  the  most  active 
young  men  have  left  Nagoya  for  other  cities,  leaving  Mr.  Masaki  almost 
single  handed.  In  the  beginning  of  the  work  in  that  city  it  was  my  privi- 
lege to  assist  in  a  blessed  revival  season  which  resulted  in  a  number  of 
conversions  among  the  students  and  other  young  men  of  the  city. 

A  general  secretary  was  placed  in  Osaka,  who  has  since  gone  to  the  war 
in  some  official  capacity.  In  Kyoto  my  time  was  spent  in  conferences 
with  the  Associations  of  the  Higher  Middle  School  and  the  Medical 
College.  I  have  spent  a  week  at  each  of  the  Summer  Schools  of  1893  and 
1894,  at  Suma  and  Hakone,  respectively. 

2.  In  1894,  especially  and  necessarily  since  Mr.  Swift's  departure  for 
America,  I  have  been  in  Tokyo,  where  I  have  had  the  supervision  of  the 
completion,  furnishing,  and  care  of  the  new  building,  together  with  an 
active  part  in  the  settling  of  many  questions  which  have  arisen  as  to  its 
use,  and  in  planning  for  the  enlarged  work  called  for  by  the  new  equip- 
ment.    The  results  of  the  work  in  the  new  building — as  can  be  seen  from 
President  Miyoshi's  report — are  very  gratifying,  and  are,  in  my  judgment, 
the  result  of  the  cumulative  wisdom  and  experience  of   the   board  of 
officers  as  a  whole,  and  of  the  growing  confidence  of  the  Christian  public 
of  Japan  in  the  work  and  mission  of  the  Association. 

Very  interesting  and  mutually  profitable  has  been  my  connection  with 
the  promising  set  of  young  men  calling  themselves  the  "  Northfield  Bible 
Class"  and  the  ; '  Northfield  Club. "  The  membership  consists  of  young 
men  who  have  studied  abroad,  and  who  are  most  probably  to  be  among 
the  leaders  of  New  Japan.  The  heart  of  the  club  has  been  a  class  meet- 


36 

ing  weekly  for  the  study  of  the  Bible  and  for  social  intercourse  combined, 
in  the  spirit  imbibed  at  the  Northfield  student  conferences. 

I  have  taught  continuously  during  this  interval  several  hours  per  week 
at  the  Tokyo  City  Association,  both  in  the  evening  classes  and  in  a  Bible 
class.  Two  or  three  hours  a  day  have  been  given  to  further  necessary 
study  of  the  Japanese  language. 


KEPORT  OF  DAVID  McCONAUGHY,  JR., 

Secretary  for  India. 

During  1893  I  was  continuously  in  Madras,  devoting  myself  almost 
wholly  to  the  local  work.  With  the  Associations  throughout  the  country 
I  have  kept  up  correspondence  and  looked  after  the  clerical  work  at  the 
headquarters  of  the  National  Council. 

Robert  McCann,  who  was  sent  out  in  November,  1892,  by  the  English 
National  Council  to  work  in  the  Bombay  district  and  was  elected  a  secre- 
tary of  the  National  Union,  extended  his  work  during  18  93  far  beyond 
the  bounds  of  that  district  and  was  very  helpful  to  the  Association  move- 
ment in  India  generally. 

At  the  invitation  of  our  committee,  B.  P.  Wilder  went  to  Calcutta  in 
June,  and,  until  the  arrival  of  the  permanent  secretary,  J.  Campbell 
White,  continued  to  work  with  the  Provisional  Committee  which  I  had 
formed  at  the  beginning  of  the  year.  Mr.  Wilder  did  such  effective  work 
among  the  non-Christian  students  that  the  principals  of  the  three  mission 
colleges  united  in  an  urgent  request  for  the  continuance  of  his  services. 

There  are  now  82  Associations,  with  an  aggregate  membership  of  3,400, 
in  this  country  Five  Associations  own  buildings,  and  as  many  more  have 
building  funds,  amounting  to  about  10,000  rupees. 

In  Madras  there  has  been  substantial  progress.  The  paid  up  member- 
ship on  December  31,  1893,  was  393—128  were  active  and  265  associate; 
260  are  Indians,  95  Eurasians  and  38  Europeans. 

The  receipts  during  the  year  1893  amounted  to  4,671  rupees,  and  the  ex- 
penditures to  4,636  rupees.  One  thousand  seven  hundred  and  eighteen 
rupees  were  contributed  by  the  members,  and  1,829  by  local  friends. 
The  general  attendance  in  the  rooms,  on  both  sides  of  the  city,  aggregated 
74,715. 

Educational  classes  have  been  conducted  in  bookkeeping,  commercial 
correspondence,  banking  and  phonography.  The  library  contains  1,036 
volumes. 

"The  Young  Men  of  India  "  has  now  widened  its  sphere,  so  as  to  in- 
clude the  Calcutta  Association,  whither  its  editorial  headquarters  have 
been  transferred. 

In  the  spiritual  work  there  has  been  not  only  healthy  growth  but 
marked  advance  in  several  new  directions.  With  one  single  exception 
the  attendance  at  all  the  religious  meetings  has  increased. 

At  Blacktown  the  Bible  and  Bible  Training  Classes  have  been  well 
maintained.  The  devotional  meeting  has  gained  both  in  numbers  and  in 
spiritual  power.  Chiefly  in  connection  with  open  air  preaching  2,500 
tracts  have  been  distributed. 


'67 


At  Vepery  similar  work  has  been  maintained. 

During  the  Week  of  Prayer  for  young  men  in  November,  the  evangel- 
istic meetings  at  Blacktown  developed  a  deep  interest,  which  bore  fruit 
in  a  number  of  definite  decisions  to  enter  the  service  of  Christ. 

During  1893  at  least  ten  of  our  associate  members  have  confessed  Jesus 
as  their  Lord  and  entered  actively  into  His  service. 

[The  foregoing  is  Mr.  McConaughy's  report  for  1893.  His  report  for 
1894  has  failed  to  reach  us.  The  work  in  his  field  was  well  maintained 
during  1894  and  substantial  progress  made.  He  attended  the  Jubilee 
Conference  in  London,  June  1-7,  and  during  his  stay  in  England  was 
successful  in  securing  money  sufficient  to  make  possible  the  purchase 
of  a  site  for  the  contemplated  and  much  needed  building  for  the  Associa- 
tion at  Madras.  Such  a  purchase  has  since  been  made,  and  it  is  hoped 
that  the  money  for  the  building  will  soon  be  furnished  by  the  friends  of 
the  work  in  America  and  elsewhere.  Mr.  McConaughy  returns  home  for 
a  much  needed  vacation  and  for  conference  with  the  Committee.  He  is 
expected  to  be  in  attendance  upon  the  Springfield  Convention.] 


EEPOKT  OF  J.  CAMPBELL  WHITE, 

Secretary  in  India. 

Though  the  field  was  ripe  for  organization  and  many  of  the  preliminary 
steps  had  been  taken  toward  that  end,  nothing  definite  was  finally  decided 
until  my  arrival  in  Calcutta,  in  December,  1893.  It  seemed  best  for 
many  reasons  to  spend  the  first  few  months  in  a  careful  study  of  the  field 
and  its  needs,  taking  time  to  become  acquainted  with  the  people  and  their 
ways  of  thinking.  During  this  time  the  question  was  fully  discussed  of 
where  il  was  best  to  begin  operations,  whether  among  the  20,000  Euro- 
peans and  Eurasians  at  the  south  end  of  the  city,  or  the  50,000  English 
speaking  Bengalis  at  the  north  end.  It  was  clear  from  the  first,  from 
geographical  reasons  alone  that  it  would  not  be  possible  to  reach  both 
classes  together. 

In  order  to  appreciate  the  pressure  that  was  brought  to  bear  for  begin- 
ning the  work  in  the  European  end  of  the  city,  two  things  must  be  kept  in 
mind:  (1)  The  effect  of  the  lives  of  the  Europeans  upon  the  natives.  In 
all  great  ports  in  heathen  lands  the  godlessness  of  the  lives  of  so-called 
"Christians"  (merely  because  they  come  from  a  Christian  country) 
is  one  of  the  greatest  barriers  to  effective  work  with  the  natives. 
The  missionaries  therefore  feel  that  it  is  really  working  for  the  natives  to 
raise  the  standard  of  living  among  the  Europeans.  By  this  means  Euro- 
peans, instead  of  being  a  hindrance,  may  be  of  incalculable  help  to  Chris- 
tian effort  among  the  natives,  as  is  proved  by  the  splendid  work  some  of 
them  do  in  addition  to  their  official  or  business  duties.  (2)  The  other 
fact  to  be  kept  in  mind  is,  that  any  work  among  the  natives  which 
depends  largely  for  its  support  on  European  residents,  must  win  first  of 
all  their  active  sympathy.  The  college  sub-committee  of  the  board  of 
directors — all  of  them  missionaries  directly  interested  in  student  work — 
agreed  unanimously  that  the  place  to  begin  was  with  the  Europeans. 

-Results  have  more  than  justified  the  wisdom  of  the  decision.     A  strong 


38 

central  Association  lias  been  formed  and  gotten  into  working  order.  The 
membership  has  become  nearly  800  during  the  first  year.  Young  men 
of  all  classes  have  been  interested  and  drawn  into  the  work.  The  gospel 
meetings  have  attracted  a  class  of  young  men.that  are  seldom  seen  at  a 
church  service.  All  churches  have  joined  most  heartily  in  the  work  of 
the  Association,  and  are  ready  to  stand  by  it  in  its  difficult,  yet  very 
hopeful,  mission. 

When  Eev.  John  McNeill  was  here  recently,  conducting  a  series  of 
successful  evangelistic  meetings,  the  young  men  from  the  Association 
were  among  the  leaders  in  the  movement.  Mr.  McNeill  himself  took  a 
very  deep  interest  in  our  work,  and  offered  to  inaugurate  a  canvass  for 
an  Association  building.  Already  16,000  rupees  have  been  subscribed 
toward  the  fund,  and  the  canvass  is  only  well  begun.  When  this  build- 
ing, with  its  hall  for  all  interdenominational  meetings  and  united  mis- 
sions, has  been  secured,  it  may  become  one  of  the  greatest  centers  of 
aggressive  Christianity  in  Calcutta  and  in  India. 

The  work  has  become  sufficiently  strong  now,  with  help  that  has  been 
obtained  in  England,  to  assume  the  support  of  its  own  secretary. 
A.  P.  Stockwell  has  just  reached  here  from  America  to  act  in  that 
capacity.  I  am  thus  able,  at  the  end  of  a  little  over  a  year's  work,  to  give 
my  attention  almost  wholly  to  the  native  student  class  under  vastly  more 
favorable  conditions  than  would  have  been  possible  had  I  given  my 
whole  attention  to  it  from  the  time  of  my  arrival  in  India. 


BIENNIAL  EEPOET  OF  MYEON  A.  CLAEK, 

Secretary  for  Brazil. 

The  years  1893  and  1894  were  spent  almost  exclusively  in  Eio  de 
Janeiro.  I  moved  there  in  April  of  the  first  named  year,  having  failed  to 
accomplish  anything  definite  in  Sao  Paulo.  During  a  visit  to  Eio  in  1892 
addresses  had  been  made  to  prepare  the  way  for  an  organization.  Soon 
after  my  removal  preliminary  meetings  were  held,  and  on  July  4th 
our  first  Brazilian  Association  was  definitely  organized,  with  seventy-one 
charter  members  and  a  constitution  on  our  American  plan,  and  contain- 
ing the  Paris  basis  and  the  Portland  test.  Eooms  centrally  located 
were  secured  and  on  August  8th  formally  opened.  Committees  were 
organized,  meetings  planned,  a  canvass  for  funds  for  current  expenses 
made,  when  right  in  the  midst  of  this  auspicious  opening  came  the  cele- 
brated Custodio  de  Mello  revolution  of  the  6th  of  September.  Firing  into 
the  city  soon  became  common,  and  on  October  5th  our  rooms  were  badly 
damaged  by  a  bursting  shell.  The  constant  danger  from  the  bombard- 
ments and  the  rigor  of  recruiting  service  kept  young  men  at  home,  and 
our  rooms  were  nearly  abandoned.  With  difficulty  we  kept  up  what  lines 
of  work  we  had  begun,  sometimes  night  after  night  passing  without  any 
young  men  frequenting  the  rooms.  The  directory  was  determined,  how- 
ever, not  to  close  the  rooms,  and  we  held  to  our  post.  The  Week  of 
Prayer  was  observed  in  November,  though  with  discouraging  attendance. 
Also  about  this  time  our  Sunday  afternoon  gospel  meetings  were  inaugu- 
rated, which  have  been  kept  up  ever  since  with  but  slight  interruption  in 
February  and  March  of  last  year.  Thus  we  entered  1894  with  a  dark  out- 


39 

look.  The  yellow  fever  now  begun  its  ravages,  and  for  six  months  was 
epidemic,  carrying  off  4,664  persons,  the  daily  death  rate  reaching  102  on 
March  6th.  I  was  taken  down  with  the  fever  in  March  and  Mrs.  Clark  in 
May,  but  by  God's  mercy  and  thanks  to  careful  treatment  we  escaped 
with  our  lives.  The  naval  revolt  was  crushed  in  March,  though  its  effects 
were  still  felt  for  some  months,  and  in  May  prospects  began  to  brighten. 
Throughout  the  rest  of  the  year  constant  progress  was  made  and  many 
encouraging  meetings  were  held.  The  Jubilee  was  observed  by  a  big 
meeting  on  June  8th,  attended  by  some  ninety  young  men.  Historical 
speeches  were  made  and  refreshments  served,  the  daily  press  giving  a  de- 
scription of  the  meeting,  a  courtesy  not  often  extended.  The  Week  of 
Prayer  was  again  observed  in  1894,  four  of  the  five  evangelical  churches 
holding  special  services  for  young  men  and  during  the  sermon  mention 
being  made  of  our  work.  Evening  classes  in  Portuguese,  English 
and  sacred  music  were  maintained  through  a  great  part  of  the 
year ;  Sunday  gospel  meeting  was  attended  by  an  average  of  45  young 
men,  the  attendance  reaching  92  one  day  ;  weekly  prayer  meeting  had  an 
average  attendance  of  12  ;  eight  monthly  receptions  averaged  56.  The 
total  membership,  which  on  December  31,  1893,  was  66,  on  January  1, 
1895,  had  reached  98.  The  number  of  volumes  in  the  library  at  the  end 
of  1894  was  150,  and  the  number  of  papers  on  file  in  the  reading  room  21. 
As  a  result  of  the  religious  work  of  the  Association  at  least  two  men  have 
publicly  professed  their  faith  in  Jesus,  and  joined  an  evangelical  church, 
and  some  three  or  four  more  have  become  regular  attendants  at  the 
churches. 

On  the  20th  of  November,  1894,  I  left  Eio  with  my  family  for  a  six 
weeks'  rest  at  Sao  Paulo,  and  thus  had  occasion  to  review  the  situation 
in  that  city.  Possibly  a  modified  form  of  Association  may  be  organized 
there  during  the  coming  year.  In  Campos  an  Association  was  organ- 
ized June  25th,  its  constitution  being  almost  an  exact  counterpart 
of  that  of  Eio.  In  that  city  there  are  two  evangelical  churches, 
though  one  is  practically  abandoned.  The  other  church  is  flourishing, 
and  the  Association  was  organized  through  the  instrumentality  of  one  of 
its  members  who  had  lived  in  Eio  and  had  seen  the  workings  of  our 
Association.  From  correspondence  with  the  secretary,  I  learn  that  it  is 
doing  a  good  evangelistic  work,  and  should  be  counted  in  our  brotherhood.v 

In  Juiz  de  Fora  exists  a  missionary  school  of  higher  education,  with 
whose  director  some  correspondence  was  had  toward  the  close  of  1894, 
looking  toward  a  visit  and  a  possible  organization  of  our  first  College 
Association.  A  cordial  invitation  was  received  from  the  English  Associa- 
tion at  Buenos  Ayres  to  visit  them  during  the  year,  but  it  was  not  possible 
to  do  so  ;  in  the  future  a  visit  to  the  two  chief  cities  of  the  Eiver  Plate 
may  be  profitable  to  the  cause. 

Let  me  repeat  in  closing  the  never-ceasing  request  that  prayer  be  con- 
stantly made  by  the  home  brethren  for  their  representatives  among  the 
"  young  men  of  all  lands." 


BIENNIAL  REPORTS  OF  CORRESPONDING  MEMBERS. 

FOR  1893  AND  1894. 


GREAT  BRITAIN. 

The  event  of  the  year  has  been  the  celebration  in  London  of  the  Jubilee 
of  the  formation  of  the  Young  Men's  Christian  Association. 
The  chief  items  of  this  great  function  were  : 

1.  Special  services  in  (a)  St.  Paul's  Cathedral ;  preacher,  the  Right 
Rev.  the  Lord  Bishop  of  Ripon.     (b)  Westminster  Abbey  ;  preacher,  the 
Right  Rev.  the  Lord  Bishop  of  London. 

2.  A  reception  of  the  delegates  by  the  Lord  Mayor  and  Corporation  of 
the  City  of  London,  in  the  historic  Guildhall,  at  which  the  presentation 
of  the  freedom  of  the  city  was  made  to  Sir  George  Williams. 

3.  The  Jubilee  meeting,  on  the  evening  of  June  6th,  in  the  Albert  Hall. 

4.  An  excursion  to  Windsor  Castle  at  the  invitation  of  her  majesty 
Queen  Victoria.     The  Association,  as  a  body,  has  been  much  honored  by 
the  gracious  act  of  the  Queen  in  conferring  the  honor  of  knighthood  upon 
Mr.  Williams. 

The  Jubilee  Conference  was  attended  by  nearly  2,000  delegates.  Much 
interest  was  displayed  in  the  proceedings  by  the  churches,  no  less  than 
1,400  sermons  being  preached  in  connection  with  the  celebration. 

Very  satisfactory  progress  is  shown  in  the  increase  of  both  Associations 
and  membership.  Associations,  auxiliaries  and  corresponding  centers, 
893  (316  in  1883);  membership,  87,464  (45,955  in  1883);  value  of  buildings 
owned  by  Association,  £379,695  (£153,637  in  1883);  income  of  Association, 
£69,003  (£30,259  in  1883). 

Important  and  encouraging  statements  were  presented  to  the  National 
Council  of  its  work  in  India,  at  the  Mediterranean  stations,  and  in  Egypt 
and  Palestine. 

After  much  consideration  R.  D.  Pringle  has  been  appointed  to  the  gen- 
eral secretaryship  of  the  Bombay  Association,  in  order  to  carry  on  the 
work  so  ably  sustained  by  friends  in  that  city,  and  which  has  been  most 
efficiently  helped  by  Robert  McCann,  who  concluded  his  mission  to  India 
as  traveling  secretary  for  the  Bombay  presidency  at  the  end  of  May. 
Under  his  direction  the  boundaries  of  the  Bombay  district  union  were 
enlarged,  the  finances  of  the  district  were  placed  upon  a  better  footing, 
one  building  was  acquired  and  three  building  projects  advanced,  and  a 
vigorous  work  was  prosecuted  amongst  non-Christian  native  educated 
young  men.  Everywhere  he  worked  in  the  closest  sympathy  with  the 
missionaries,  and  at  many  places  there  have  been  distinct  indications  of 
the  Holy  Spirit's  blessing  on  his  labors. 

During  the  year  the  National  Council  recommended  an  alteration  of 
the  rules  of  international  alliance,  whereby  the  United  Kingdom  should 
become  entitled  to  two  representatives  in  the  Central  International  Com- 
mittee at  Geneva,  Scotland  being  allowed  to  nominate  one  of  such  repre- 
sentatives. 

Much  activity  has  been  evinced  by  the  different  Associations  in  dealing
