with  the  evils  of  intemperance,  betting  and  gambling,  and  impurity. 
Weekly  budgets  of  Association  intelligence  have  been  inserted  in  the 
principal  religious  journals  with  marked  benefit. 

A  noticeable  feature  of  the  year's  work  has  been  the  amalgamation 
of  the  three  central  London  Associations — Exeter  Hall,  Aldersgate  Street 
and  Cornhill — under  the  direction  of  one  committee  It  is  believed  that 
this  departure  will  influence  the  whole  London  work  in  bringing  about 
greater  co-operation  of  effort  on  the  part  of  the  seventy  Associations  in 
the  metropolis. 

Throughout  the  country  there  has  been  a  great  increase  of  spiritual 
work.  Especially  has  this  characteristic  feature  been  noticeable  in  the 
multiplication  of  special  missions  for  young  men.  In  order  to  promote 
this  desirable  side  of  the  work  it  has  been  decided  to  appoint  a  young 
men's  evangelist  for  this  line  of  effort  among  the  Associations. 

E.  J.  KENNEDY,  Cor.  Mem. 


GERMANY. 

.  The  Association  cause  in  Germany  is  still  advancing.  Since  my  last 
report,  in  1893,  the  number  of  Associations  has  increased  from  1,005  to 
1,180,  and  there  are  now  46  buildings  for  the  exclusive  use  of  the  work. 

For  years  past  special  effort  has  been  made  to  reach  the  500,000  young 
men  in  the  army.  .Results  have  as  yet  been  small,  but  encouraging.  The 
National  Committee  issues  an  annual  list  of  "Association  members  under 
arms  "  for  the  benefit  of  these  young  men  themselves,  and  for  the  Asso- 
ciations in  various  towns.  The  last  list  shows  1,263  such  names  in  202 
garrisons. 

The  importance  of  the  White  Cross  work  is  being  more  and  more  felt. 
In  the  last  two  years  about  2,000  young  men  have  joined. 

The  students'  movement  has  made  a  great  step  in  advance  in  the  for- 
mation of  a  Christian  Students'  Union  for  Germany,  with  headquarters 
at  Berlin,  Count  Pueckler  being  its  president.  A  traveling  secretary 
(former  student)  has  been  called,  and  annual  summer  conferences  have 
been  held  with  much  blessing.  Another  College  Secretary  has  been 
engaged  to  take  charge  of  the  growing  work  among  the  "gymnasts" 
(young  men  in  high  schools  preparing  for  the  university  course)  in  the 
larger  towns. 

Three  more  great  centers  of  our  country  have  been  provided  with 
Young  Men's  Christian  Associations  proper  (Christlicher  Verein  Junger 
Manner),  in  addition  to  already  existing  Juenglings-Vereine,  viz., 
Leipsic,  Dresden  and  Breslau.  In  each  of  them  a  vigorous  aggressive 
work  has  been  established,  with  competent  secretaries  to  carry  it  on. 

A  very  practical  addition  to  Association  literature  has  been  issued  in 
the  shape  of  a  monthly  paper,  giving  detailed  outlines  not  only  for  weekly 
Bible  classes,  but  also  for  literary  discussions  and  lectures  on  topics  of 
general  interest.  It  has  proved  of  special  value  to  Associations  in  smaller 
places. 

The  third  National  Conference,  held  at  Eisenach,  at  the  foot  of  the 
Wartburg,  in  October,  1893,  was  one  of  great  blessing  ;  it  was  especially 
gratifying  to  have  such  an  experienced  Association  worker  as  the  assist- 
ant State  Secretary  for  Ohio,  L.  L  Doggett,  in  our  midst. 


42 

The  deepened  interest  in  the  "international  cause"  manifested  itself 
in  the  large  delegation  to  the  Jubilee  Conference  in  London  last  June  ; 
320  Association  delegates  from  Germany  having  been  in  attendance. 

Our  hearts  are  full  of  gratitude  to  God  for  the  many  proofs  of  his 
guidance  and  care,  and  we  look  forward,  with  confidence  and  hope  for 
still  greater  blessings  in  the  future. 

CHBISTIAN  PHLLDIUS,  Cor.  Mem. 


HAWAII. 

Since  June,  1893,  the  Association  in  Honolulu  has  had  as  general 
secretary  D.  W.  Corbett,  a  graduate  of  the  Springfield  Training  School. 
He  is  a  power  for  good  in  this  community  and  the  Association  has  made 
considerable  progress  since  his  advent  among  us. 

The  Y.  M.  C.  A.  Review,  an  illustrated  monthly,  continues  in  its 
useful  career.  Over  100  students  were  enrolled  last  year  in  the  educational 
classes.  The  aggregate  attendance  at  the  religious  services  held  in 
Association  Hall  during  the  past  two  years  was  27,000.  The  meetings  on 
Sunday  evenings  are  remarkable  for  uniformity  of  attendance  and  in 
sustained  interest  The  expenses  of  the  Association  for  the  past  two  years 
were  $8,100.  About  $700  worth  of  books  have  been  added  to  the  circu- 
lating library.  The  reading  room  is  well  supplied  with  reading  matter 
and  the  average  daily  attendance  of  readers  is  150. 

The  main  feature  of  the  present  year  is  the  building  of  an  addition  to 
the  hall  to  cost  $16,000.  Most  of  the  money  for  this  is  pledged,  and  we 
hope  to  have  it  finished  by  July,  free  of  debt.  This  addition  will  contain 
a  well  appointed  gymnasium,  baths,  and  rooms  for  educational  work. 

The  general  secretary  has  visited  many  of  the  Associations  of  native 
Hawaiians  outside  of  Honolulu.  As  these  are  more  of  the  character  of 
Christian  Endeavor  Societies,  they  are  not  reported  further. 

At  the  leper  colony  on  the  island  of  Molokai,  a  hall  has  been  built  by 
the  generosity  of  a  friend.  The  Association  among  the  lepers  has  enrolled 
90  members,  and  is  supervised  by  John  Waiamau,  the  salaried  general 
secretary,  formerly  a  member  at  Honolulu 

The  present  membership  of  the  Honolulu  Association  is  274.  The 
standing  committees  are  faithful  to  the  duties  assigned  them.  That  on 
temperance  is  formulating  some  views  to  present  to  the  first  session  of  the 
legislature  of  the  new  Republic  of  Hawaii,  which  it  is  hoped  will  receive 
favorable  attention. 

A.  F.  JUDD,  Cor.  Mem. 

JAPAN. 

The  work  of  the  Associations  of  this  country  for  the  past  year  has  been 
affected  by  two  prominent  events  :  First,  the  completion  and  opening  of 
the  new  building  of  the  Tokyo  Association,  the  generous  gift  of  our 
friends  in  America,  and  second,  the  breaking  out  of  the  war  between  this 
country  and  China.  The  first  event  has  given  the  work  of  the  Association 
an  impetus  which  will  be  observed  in  the  results  recorded  below ;  the 
second  has  given  a  characteristic  turn  to  the  activities  of  many  Associa- 
tions during  the  year. 

I. — The  new  building  of  the  Tokyo  Association,  which  has  been  of  such 


43 

inestimable  value  to  its  work  in  many  ways,  was  dedicated  on  May  5, 
1894.  It  is  worthy  of  remark  in  passing  that  that  day,  the  fifth  day  of 
the  fifth  month,  is  the  great  annual  festival  of  Japan  in  honor  of  the 
boys,  as  March  3d  is  the  corresponding  holiday  in  honor  of  the  girls  of  the 
country.  It  therefore  seemed  most  appropriate  that  on  that  day  our  new 
building  should  be  dedicated  to  the  highest  interests  of  the  boys  and 
young  men  of  the  nation.  The  building  is  one  of  the  most  beautiful  in 
the  city,  and  the  interior  is  planned  for  the  work  of  the  Association  after 
a  careful  study  of  many  models.  The  one  thing  which  we  were  pre- 
vented from  having,  by  the  nature  of  the  land  and  of  the  country,  is  a 
well  equipped  gymnasium  ;  but  this  lack  is  in  part  made  good  by  a  room 
fitted  up  for  fencing  and  light  gymnastics,  and  by  out-of-door  sports. 

The  possession  of  such  a  building  has  given  our  work  an  impetus  in 
many  ways.  This  is  noticeably  true  of  our  evening  classes.  The  build- 
ing itself  inspires  the  young  men  of  the  city  with  confidence  in  the  in- 
tegrity of  the  institution  and  of  the  work  done  there.  Moreover,  we  have 
this  year  had  the  advantage  of  the  services  of  a  very  efficient  principal, 
Mr.  Murakami,  of  the  Imperial  University,  who  has  done  much  to  sys- 
tematize the  work  of  the  school  and  make  it  thorough  and  popular.  The 
force  of  foreign  teachers  has  been  kept  comparatively  large  (four  in  num- 
ber), and  we  can  unhesitatingly  claim  to  have  one  of  the  best  night 
schools  in  the  city.  The  classes  opened  in  September  with  60  students  as 
against  30  last  year,  and  closed  in  December  with  134  actual  attendants 
as  against  55  last  year.  The  number  of  students  registered  during  the 
year  would  reach  a  much  higher  figure.  A  literary  society  has  held  reg- 
ular monthly  meetings  during  the  year. 

The  religious  work  has  been  organized  into  a  department,  with  K. 
Matsumura  as  evangelist.  There  are  probably  no  such  audiences  of 
young  men  elsewhere  in  Japan  as  gather  every  Sunday  in  our  Association 
hall.  Mr.  Matsumura  manifests  a  warm  personal  regard  for  the  spiritual 
welfare  of  the  young  men  who  gather  around  him,  by  holding  regular 
inquiry  meetings  for  their  benefit  and  by  personal  work.  The  total  attend- 
ance at  these  Sunday  meetings  for  the  year  was  4,968.  There  has  been  a 
slight  increase  in  the  attendance  at  the  Bible  classes.  We  have  been  in- 
debted again  this  year  to  Eev.  George  W.  Taft  for  a  course  in  the  Life  of 
Christ. 

The  membership  of  the  Association  has  increased  from  124  last  year  to 
207  this  year.  Of  this  number  136  are  active  members.  It  has  seemed 
best  to  us  to  guard  against  a  too  sudden  increase  in  membership  until  the 
nature  of  the  institution  and  its  work  were  better  understood.  The  library 
has  been  increased  by  about  300  volumes,  and  the  reading  room  has  been 
visited  by  2,746  persons  during  the  year,  and  the  number  of  other  visitors 
to  the  rooms  has  been  679.  The  Christian  Young  Man  has  increased 
in  quality,  influence  and  circulation.  Nearly  500  copies  are  issued  per 
month,  many  of  which  are  subscribed  for  by  other  Associations  of  the 
empire.  A  course  of  popular  lectures  was  begun  in  the  Fall,  and  is  being 
successfully  carried  out.  The  average  attendance  has  been  300. 

The  boarding  house  and  relief  work  of  the  Association  have  continued 
much  as  before.  The  former  has  passed  through  a  critical  and  experi- 
mental stage  of  self-government,  but  is  now  more  directly  than  ever  under 


44 

the  control  of  the  board  of  directors.  The  average  number  of  boarders 
has  been  18.  Two  boarding  houses  besides  our  own  have  become  known 
to  us  where  there  are  groups  of  Christian  men,  and  to  which  we  think 
young  men  can  be  referred  with  safety. 

II. — It  remains  to  notice  the  work  of  a  number  of  other  societies  which, 
while  independent  organizations,  have  an  intimate  relation  to  the  work  of 
the  Tokyo  Association.  Foremost  of  these  is  the  "  Doshi  Kwai,"  organ- 
ized by  Christians  in  view  of  the  war.  The  headquarters  of  this  society 
have  been  at  the  rooms  of  the  Association,  and  a  large  number  of  the 
members  of  its  executive  committee  are  members  or  officers  of  the  Associ- 
ation. Its  object  was,  in  the  first  place,  to  stir  up  the  patriotism  of  the 
Christians  and  to  unite  their  efforts  as  citizens  in  behalf  of  their  country, 
at  the  same  time  to  take  advantage  of  the  seriousness  of  the  times  to 
preach  "the  Kingdom  of  Eighteousness "  to  their  fellow  countrymen. 
The  leading  Christians  of  many  denominations  were  sent  over  the  empire 
on  this  mission.  As  the  war  progressed  the  work  of  the  "  Doshi  Kwai  " 
took  a  more  practical  turn,  in  the  sending  of  money  and  nurses  to  the  as- 
sistance of  the  Bed  Cross  Society.  Over  800  yen  were  collected  last  year 
for  the  above  purposes. 

The  Christian  Business  Men's  Club  numbers  50  members  ;  it  is  organ- 
ized for  the  mutual  assistance  of  the  members  in  carrying  on  their  busi- 
ness on  Christian  principles.  It  has  monthly  meetings  for  discussion  and 
for  practical  talks  from  experienced  business  men. 

III. — The  hitherto  recognized  and  reported  centers  of  Association  work 
outside  of  Tokyo,  in  cities,  have  been  Kobe,  Osaka  and  Nagoya.  We  re- 
gret to  say  that  the  Kobe  Association  has  suspended  its  work  during  the 
year  from  lack  of  a  general  secretary.  In  Osaka  the  work  was  well  di- 
rected by  Secretary  Inouye  until  the  breaking  out  of  the  war,  when  he 
went  to  Korea  as  an  officer.  The  Nagoya  Association  has  struggled  for 
existence  on  a  basis  of  self-support,  and  has  been  much  weakened  by  the 
loss  of  many  of  its  strongest  members. 

Outside  of  these  larger  cities  must  now  be  taken  into  account  a  large 
number  of  Associations  which  have  been  formed  in  smaller  places,  bear- 
ing the  name  and  in  many  respects  doing  the  work  of  Young  Men's  Chris- 
tian Associations.  Such  we  believe  to  be  the  Associations  in  Sendai, 
Sapporo,  Otaru,  Hiroshima,  Okayama,  Gifu,  Hirosaki,  Tsuruga,  Shizu- 
oka,  which  have  been  admitted  to  the  National  Union  ;  and  Jomu,  Waka- 
matsu,  Wakayama,  Yokohama,  Nagasaki,  Hikone  and  other  places,  which 
have  not  yet  united  with  the  Union. 

The  number  of  Associations  in  the  National  Union  is  now  35  ;  the  num- 
ber of  other  Associations  known  to  exist  is  25.  Their  work  is  largely  de- 
termined by  local  conditions,  but  a  general  feature  is  the  evangelistic 
meeting,  usually  by  and  for  young  men.  These  Associations,  especially 
those  in  the  Union,  receive  the  magazine  of  the  Tokyo  Association  each 
month,  send  reports  of  their  work  to  the  same,  receive  occasional  visits 
from  Tokyo  workers,  and  are  brought  together  once  a  year  at  the  annual 
meeting  of  the  Union,  held  in  connection  with  the  summer  school. 

IV. — There  are  15  College  Associations  in  the  Union;  two  others  are 
known  to  exist.  The  main  points  of  interest  in  their  work  for  the  year 
past  may  be  summarized  as  follows  : 


45 

The  Association  in  the  Imperial  University  has  received  a  number  of 
strong  members  from  other  schools ;  it  has  held  regular  meetings,  but 
done  little  active  work.  The  Association  of  the  Higher  Commercial 
College,  Tokyo,  has  held  its  meetings  at  the  building  of  the  city  Associa- 
tion. 

The  Kyoto  Higher  Middle  College  Association  was  nearly  destroyed  by 
a  change  in  the  educational  policy  of  the  empire,  which  abolished  the 
school  as  such  and  changed  it  to  a  technical  and  professional  school. 
The  members  of  the  Association  were  scattered  among  other  schools,  but 
five  remained  and  continued  to  carry  on  the  work  in  their  new  building 
with  considerable  spirit. 

The  Associations  of  the  Sapporo  Agricultural  College  in  the  north  and 
of  the  Kwansei  Gakuin  in  the  west  have  been  conspicuous  for  their  work 
in  connection  with  the  outbreak  of  the  war.  The  latter  sent  representa- 
tives to  the  military  headquarters  at  Hiroshima  to  found  a  branch  Associ- 
ation and  co-operate  in  the  Christian  work  there  among  the  soldiers  in  the 
barracks  and  hospitals. 

The  College  Associations  had  their  annual  summer  school  gathering 
this  year  at  Hakone.  Excitement  over  the  prospect  of  war  reduced  the 
attendance  to  about  one  hundred.  The  school  was  serious  and  spiritual 
in  its  tone. 

We  cannot  close  this  report  without  expressing  our  deep  sense  of  loss  in 
being  deprived  for  the  greater  part  of  the  year  of  the  wise  counsels  and 
self-sacrificing  efforts  of  our  friend  and  secretary,  Mr.  Swift,  and  the  hope 
that  his  return  to  us  in  greatly  improved  health  may  be  hastened. 

TAIZO  MIYOSHI,  Cor.  Mem. 

CANADIAN  WEST. 

The  work  in  the  Canadian  West  has  been  decidedly  prosperous  not- 
withstanding the  financial  depression.  The  openings  for  the  engagement 
of  our  Provincial  Secretary  in  the  adjacent  States  the  past  year  allowed 
us  to  both  reduce  our  expenses  and  engage  part  of  the  time  of  Brandon's 
secretary,  thereby  helping  that  point  in  its  finances,  and  also  training 
another  man  for  Provincial  work.  We  have  thus  had  the  benefit  of  two 
good  men  instead  of  one,  and  the  work  has  advanced. 

We  have  added  Neepawa  to  our  town,  and  St.  John's  College  to  our 
college  list,  besides  having  a  well- worked  Intercollegiate  Association. 
We  now  have  106  points  at  which  we  are  in  touch  with  the  young  men 
through  corresponding  members  of  our  Provincial  Committee,  and  in  this 
sparsely  settled  land  we  try  to  secure  a  number  of  young  men  in  each 
little  place  to  do  personal  work  without  much  definite  organization  or  ex- 
pense. This  method  we  find  succeeds.  We  now  have  Springfield  gradu- 
ates as  secretaries  in  our  three  city  Associations,  and  we  feel  that  the 
work  is  in  far  better  hands  than  ever  before. 

We  are  always  grateful  for  the  definite  help  we  have  had  on  account  of 
the  supervision  of  the  International  Committee,  and  we  approve  heartily 
of  the  new  plan  for  supervising  the  work  in  these  western  districts. 

ROBT.  D.  RICHARDSON,  Cor.  Mem. 

NEW  BEUNSWICK. 
At  different  points  in  the  Province  the  outlook  for  the  coming  vear  is 


46 

more  encouraging  than  for  some  time.  Influential  business  men  are 
becoming  more  impressed  with  the  importance  of  the  special  efforts  on 
behalf  of  the  young  men  and  boys  of  our  land. 

In  St.  John3  the  past  year  has  been  very  successful,  especially  the 
educational  work.  Under  the  supervision  of  our  new  secretary,  Geo.  E. 
Williams,  much  activity  has  been  manifested  and  a  large  number  of  new 
members  enrolled.  The  boys'  branch  is  doing  good  work,  but  is  not  the 
success  it  would  be  with  proper  rooms.  The  great  need  of  St.  John  is  a 
new  building. 

Moncton  is  carrying  a  heavy  financial  load.  Effort  was  made  with  a 
degree  of  success  to  reduce  the  debt  on  the  building  during,  the  past 
Summer,  Messrs.  Olandt  and  Curran  of  the  International  Gommittee 
rendering  valued  assistance.  Reports  from  Chatham  are  encouraging. 
The  growth  in  membership  has  been  large.  The  rooms  are  open  all  the 
time  and  well  patronized.  A  general  secretary  is  employed,  an  active 
boys'  branch  is  in  operation,  and  there  is  a  successful  educational  work. 
St.  Stephen  reports  progress  in  every  direction.  The  Association  has 
organized  a  branch  in  Milltown,  two  miles  distant,  and  is  reaching  a  large 
number  of  young  men  and  boys. 

Sackville,  although  a  comparatively  new  organization,  is  doing  good 
work.  The  College  Association  at  Sackville  (Mt.  Allison)  is  in  a  flourish- 
ing condition.  A  pleasantly  furnished  room  has  been  assigned  by  the 
faculty,  carpet  and  furniture  having  been  donated  by  the  ladies  of 
Sackville.  The  College  Association  at  Fredericton  is  also  doing  a  good 
work.  The  Intercollegiate  Conference  met  there  last  November  and  much 
benefit  was  received.  A  boys'  camp  was  held  at  Campobello  Island  last 
season,  attended  by  55  ^boys.  It  proved  not  only  a  season  of  recreation 
but  of  education  as  well. 

The  Maritime  Convention  held  at  St.  Stephen  was  well  attended  and 
proved  a  source  of  refreshing  to  the  local  Associations  and  a  blessing 
to  the  community  generally.  C.  J.  Hicks  represented  the  International 
Committee.  We  desire  to  express  our  gratitude  to  the  Committee  for 
sending  these  representatives.  The  brethren  coming  to  us  from  year 
to  year  have  proved  a  great  source  of  strength  and  inspiration. 

W.  S.  MOBBISON,  Cor.  Mem. 

NOVA  SCGTIA. 

Notwithst  anding  the  pressure  of  the  times  progress  has  been  made. 
The  work  has  been  taking  more  definite  shape  as  a  work  for  young  men 
only.  Amherst  has  improved  facilities — a  gymnasium  and  separate  rooms 
for  boys.  Halifax  has  had  a  change  of  secretary,  and  a  railroad  branch 
has  been  added.  New  Glasgow  has  changed  rooms.  A  lot  has  also  been 
bought,  and  $2,200  has  been  subscribed  toward  a  prospective  building 
to  cost  $8,500.  Pictou  has  remodeled  the  interior  of  its  fine  building 
and  added  gymnasium  and  bath  room.  An  increased  membership  and 
other  definite  results  have  followed.  The  Pictou  Academy  has  done  good 
work  among  the  students. 

Westville  had  a  secretary  for  eight  months,  but  is  temporarily  without 
one.  A  district  conference  was  lately  held  there,  and  the  work  has  been 
greatly  strengthened.  Spring  Hill  has  been  without  a  secretary  for  a 


47 

year,  but  has  continued  its  religious  and  boys'  work.  A  lot  has  been 
purchased,  $2,000  and  more  or  less  material  has  been  secured,  and  the 
Association  will  soon  begin  building. 

Stillwater  was  inactive  for  a  time,  but  was  lately  reorganized  ;  has 
rented  rooms  which  are  open  evenings  and  is  doing  a  practical  work  for 
young  men.  Truro  has  steadily  advanced  in  Bible  study  and  in  work  for 
the  young  men  and  boys.  Yarmouth  has  engaged  a  new  secretary,  and 
maintains  the  largest  young  men's  meeting  in  the  Province. 

Sydney  and  Port  Morien,  Cape  Breton,  have  each  added  to  their  mem- 
bership. The  latter  has  a  most  active  corps  of  workers.  Dalhousie 
College  Association  has  emphasized  Bible  study  among  the  students,  and 
done  much  to  encourage  personal  work.  Acadia  College  Association  is 
also  still  progressive. 

Associations  have  been  organized  at  Shubenacadie  and  Kentville,  both 
with  good  prospects  of  success. 

In  common  with  our  sister  Provinces  we  enjoyed  the  helpful  words  of 
international  representatives  George  A.  Hall,  T.  K.  Cree  and  C.  J.  Hicks, 
who  attended  the  Maritime  Conventions,  and  W.  H.  Sallmon,  who  was 
present  at  the  college  conference,  Wolfville,  $".  S. 

J.  C.  MACKINTOSH,  Cor.  Mem. 


ONTAKIO. 

The  past  two  years  have  been  marked  by  a  steady  progress,  not  so 
much  in  the  number  of  new  organizations  as  in  -the  character  of  the  work 
accomplished.  General  secretaries  have  been  placed  at  several  points 
where  they  were  much  needed  ;  Bible  study  has  been  a  more  prominent 
feature  than  formerly,  and  definite,  personal  effort  for  the  souls  of  young 
men  has  been  emphasized  as  the  main  object  of  the  work. 

The  work  among  college  students  has  been  much  enlarged,  so  that 
Associations  now  exist  in  most  of  the  colleges  in  Ontario,  and  many  of 
them  are  doing  a  good  service. 

Representatives  of  the  International  Committee  have  repeatedly  been 
of  great  help  on  most  important  occasions.  The  recent  convention  at 
Bellville  is  considered  the  best  held  for  ten  years.  The  Provincial  Com- 
mittee has  secured  during  the  past  year  a  large  number  of  new  subscribers 
to  its  work.  JOHN  J,  GAETSHOBB,  Cor.  Mem. 


PEINCE  EDWARD  ISLAND. 

The  number  of  Associations  in  the  Island  is  two — Charlottetown  and 
Summerside.  The  former  has  just  wiped  out,  after  a  determined 
struggle,  a  heavy  floating  debt  which  had  been  gradually  accumulating 
for  some  years,  and  has  started  afresh  with  "pay  as  you  go  "  for  its  motto. 
It  was  felt  necessary  to  dismiss  the  general  secretary,  and  at  present  there 
is  none,  Much  interest  is  being  taken  in  the  work,  and  a  prosperous  Bible 
class  has  been  organized.  The  Summerside  Association  is  doing  a  good 
work,  and  the  interest  is  being  well  maintained. 

J.  D.  SEAMAN,  Cor.  Mem. 


48 

QUEBEC. 

The  Association  in  Sherbrooke  has  made  clear  advance  in  its  devotional 
work,  and  reports  seventeen  conversions  during  the  week  of  prayer.  The 
educational  work  has  been  successfully  begun. 

There  has  been  a  slight  increase  in  the  membership  of  the  Quebec 
Association.  The  junior  work  has  received  some  prominence,  and  there 
is  increased  interest  in  Bible  study.  The  matter  of  securing  a  gymnasium 
is  progressing. 

The  educational  department  of  the  Montreal  Association  is  being 
developed,  and  within  the  past  few  weeks  a  lot,  about  60  feet  square,  ad- 
joining the  Association  building,  was  acquired  by  Warden  King,  a  member 
of  the  board  of  directors,  at  the  cost  of  $10,000,  and  donated  to  the 
Association.  A  building  is  to  be  erected  thereon  for  the  extension  of  the 
educational  work. 

Secretary  Hodge  of  the  International  Committee  recently  gave  an 
illustrated  talk  on  work  along  this  line  to  a  large  number  of  prominent 
citizens  with  evident  effect. 

CHARLES  GUSHING,  Cor.  Mem. 


MEXICO. 

The  record  of  1893  in  itself  was  not  encouraging.  Scarcely  had  the 
well  matured  plans  of  George  N.  Taylor  begun  to  bear  fruit  when  he  was 
stricken  down  and  called  to  his  sure  reward.  The  blow  at  first  seemed 
almost  irretrievable,  and  there  followed  months  of  waiting  until  a 
new  secretary  could  be  supplied,  during  which  the  best  we  could 
do  was  to  maintain  an  organization  with  dwindling  membership  and 
accumulating  debt.  I.  E.  Munger,  of  Iowa,  joined  us  as  secretary  so 
late  in  the  year  that  the  financial  question  necessarily  absorbed  his  whole 
attention.  We  wish  to  bear  testimony  to  his  ability  and  earnestness  and 
to  the  substantial  help  afforded  through  him  by  the  International  Com- 
mittee. 

Mr.  Munger  resigned  January  1st,  1894.  After  mature  deliberation  the 
board  of  directors  extended  a  call  to  Edward  Page  Gaston  to  serve  as 
general  secretary.  Under  his  direction  the  membership  has  increased  dur- 
ing the  year  to  over  200,  about  half  being  young  Mexicans,  and  the 
debt  of  nearly  $1,000  has  been  entirely  paid,  leaving  the  Association  free 
from  encumbrance  for  the  first  time  in  its  history.  The  rooms  have  been 
visited  by  more  than  18,000  persons,  who  made  constant  use  of  the  read- 
ing and  chess  rooms,  gymnasium,  bowling  alleys  and  baths.  Educational 
and  Bible  classes  have  been  established,  many  young  men  assisted  in 
obtaining  employment,  and  special  work  undertaken  in  the  line  of  social 
purity. 

It  is  now  considered  that  the  organization  is  firmly  established  in 
Mexico,  and  we  are  encouraged  to  go  forward  in  the  line  of  natural  de- 
velopment, confident  that  the  blessing  of  our  Divine  Master  will  follow 
and  crown  all  genuine  labor  in  His  service. 

HENRY  P.  WEBB,  Cor.  Mem.

ASSOCIATION    BUILDING,    KINGSTON,   ONTARIO. 

DEDICATED  OCTOBER  10,  1892. 
Dimensions,  66  x  103  ieet.  Cost,  $22,000.  Population,   19,000.

ALABAMA. 

Since  our  last  report  we  have  entered  into  an  arrangement  with  Missis- 
sippi, whereby  one-third  the  time  of  our  State  Secretary  belongs  to  that 
State.  The  relationship  has  been  most  agreeably  managed  and  we  are  in 
excellent  condition.  There  are  19  Associations — thirteen  city  and  town 
and  six  college.  The  year  shows  a  gain  of  one  College  Association,  and 
a  loss  of  three  town  Associations.  Fpur  employ  general  secretaries — 
Mobile,  Montgomery,  Birmingham  and  Selma.  Montgomery  has  been 
reorganized  and  is  doing  splendidly  with  a  new  secretary  and  nearly  all 
old  obligations  met. 

Birmingham  Association  during  1894  paid  three-fourths  of  its  old 
debts.  Mobile  is  doing  good  work  and  is  preparing  to  enter  upon  a 
building  canvass.  Selma  is  doing  well.  In  fact  every  Association  in  the 
State  is  in  good  condition.  Especially  can  improvement  be  noted  in  the 
College  Associations  in  Bible  study  and  spritual  results.  As  a  result  of 
one  week's  visit  of  Mr.  Brockman  with  State  Secretary  Willis  to  two  State 
institutions  over  70  young  men  professed  conversion. 

We  have  held  three  district  conferences  which  proved  very  successful 
and  helpful  to  the  district,  and  financially  profitable  to  the  State  Com- 
mittee. 

We  have  been  very  much  encouraged  and  assisted  by  representatives  of 
the  International  Committee.  Mainly  through  the  work  of  Mr.  Andersen 
was  our  State  work  saved  from  financial  failure,  and  we  now  feel  hopeful 
of  closing  the  year  with  all  salaries  and  bills  paid. 

HABKY  HAWKINS,  Cor.  Mem. 

AEKANSAS. 

The  past  two  years  have  seen  little  improvement  in  the  Arkansas 
Associations.  Hot  Springs  and  Fort  Smith  are  fields  once  abandoned 
and  still  unreclaimed.  The  Association  at  Texarkana  gave  up  the  fight 
suddenly,  without  the  advice  of  the  State  Committee,  or  any  appeal 
whatever  for  its  assistance.  Little  Rock  and  Pine  Bluff  are  the  only 
remaining  Associations.  Both  are  well  organized  and  doing  fine  work. 
Little  Bock  has  lately  removed  to  new  rooms,  admitting  of  a  larger  work, 
and  Pine  Bluff  continues  to  make  the  most  of  its  splendid  quarters. 

Among  the  College  Associations,  Conway,  Quitman,  Arkadelphia, 
Fayetteville  and  Batesville  are  holding  their  own.  No  regular  State 
Secretary  has  been  employed  during  the  past  two  years,  but  the  State 
has  not  been  without  visitation.  In  this  connection  the  State  Committee 
desires  to  make  grateful  acknowledgment  to  the  International  Committee 
for  the  visits  of  Cecil  L.  Gates,  who  has  been  of  great  service,  especially 
to  Little  Bock,  and  for  the  help  given  the  College  Associations  by  F.  S. 
Brockman. 

BOBT.  E.  WAIT,  Cor.  Mem. 

CALIFORNIA. 

It  is  a  source  of  gratitude  that,  notwithstanding  the  two  years  of 
financial  depression,  not  one  of  the  Associations  in  California  has  been 
suspended,  though  all  have  been  obliged  to  reduce  their  expenses. 


50 

There  is  iiow,  however,  with  the  improved  business  outlook,  every  in- 
dication of  increased  activity  and  usefulness. 

Invaluable  services  have  been  rendered,  more  especially  in  the  college 
field,  by  the  International  Committee  through  E.  Lawrence  Hunt,  who 
was  with  us  in  1893,  and  C.  C.  Michener,  in  1894.  One  excellent  result 
of  these  visits  has  been  a  great  spiritual  uplift  to  the  college  work. 

The  State  Conventions  have  been  held  in  their  regular  order — in  Stock- 
ton, November  8-12,  1893,  and  in  Oakland,  September  11-16,  1894. 
We  were  obliged  to  dispense  with  the  services  of  Harry  Hillard,  College 
Secretary,  October  1,  1894.  John  L.  Speares  is  continued  as  State 
Secretary,  and  his  time  has  been  given  to  the  strengthening  and  upbuild- 
ing of  Associations  already  in  existence,  no  attempt  being  made  to  es- 
tablish new  organizations.  The  building  at  Santa  Cruz  has  been  saved 
through  his  efforts,  and  he  is  in  hopes  of  cancelling  the  mortgage  on  the 
San  Jose  property  within  the  next  few  months.  One  of  the  most  import- 
ant events  in  the  history  of  our  work  in  this  State  was  the  completion  and 
opening  of  the  new  building  of  the  San  Francisco  Association,  Septem- 
ber 9,  1894,  one  of  the  finest  and  most  complete  Association  buildings  in 
the  world.  Its  cost,  with  furnishing,  electric  light  plant,  etc.,  was 
$334,000..  It  is  an  ideal  structure,  and  the  work  in  it  is  fast  becoming  an 
ideal  work.  New  impetus  and  standing  have  been  given  to  the  Associa- 
tion cause  throughout  California,  and  we  may  say  the  entire  western  slope, 
by  the  erection  of  this  magnificent  building.  The  entire  property  is 
worth  not  far  from  half  a  million  dollars,  as  the  lot  was  purchased  for 
about  one-half  its  present  value  from  three  interested  gentlemen,  they 
also  making  a  cash  donation  of  $60,000  to  the  enterprise.  The  outlook 
is  brightening  generally,  and  we  shall  hope  in  the  next  two  years  to 
accomplish  a  better  work  in  California  than  has  heretofore  been  recorded. 

H.  J.  McCoy,  Cor.  Mem. 

COLOBADO. 

The  past  year  has  been  one  that  will  long  be  remembered  by  the  Colo- 
rado Associations.  They  have  been  tried  as  never  before  along  financial 
lines,  and,  like  the  sturdy  oak  that  bends  before  the  blasts,  they  are  only 
the  more  firmly  rooted  and  grounded. 

There  has  been  a  steady,  healthy  growth  in  every  city  and  College  As- 
sociation in  the  State,  and  in  the  case  of  Denver  Central  Department, 
Pueblo  and  Durango,  the  growth  has  been  remarkable.  Not  one  Associ- 
ation has  been  closed  during  the  year,  and  all  our  city  Associations  are 
manned  with  strong  and  experienced  secretaries.  A  good  work  was  done 
during  the  Summer  months  by  the  student  volunteers  among  some  of  the 
mining  camps,  and  along  all  lines  the  work  is  stronger  than  a  year  ago. 

WM.  F.  SLOCUM,  JB.,  Cor.  Mem. 

CONNECTICUT. 

The  financial  and  business  stress  has  seriously  affected  the  industries  of 
our  State,  thereby  checking  somewhat  our  progress.  We  have  endeav- 
ored, however,  to  maintain  the  high  standard  of  our  work  wherever  Asso- 
ciations existed,  and  the  courage  manifested  by  our  secretaries  speaks 


51 

well  for  the  men  and  the  cause  they  represent.  We  have  26  Associations, 
a  gain  of  two  since  our  last  report,  nearly  all  employing  salaried  officers, 
and  having  a  membership  of  7,327. 

Twelve  Associations  own  buildings  aggregating  in  value  $684,000,  and 
other  property  to  the  amount  of  $125,000.  Two  new  buildings  which 
were  in  process  of  construction  when  we  last  reported,  one  in  Hartford 
and  one  in  Waterbury,  have  been  completed,  and  prove  to  be  models  of 
convenience  and  aptitude  for  the  work.  The  Hartford  building — costing, 
with  its  furnishings,  $204,000— is  wonderfully  complete  in  all  its  appoint- 
ments and  a  monument  to  the  wisdom  and  munificence  of  the  citizens. 
Middletown  has  also  moved  into  a  new  $75,000  building,  not  yet  com- 
pleted, but  far  enough  advanced  to  be  habitable,  while  Wesleyan  Univer- 
sity, in  the  same  town,  is  pushing  the  canvass  for  funds  to  erect  a  build- 
ing at  a  cost  of  $30,000.  Norwich  has  only  $8,000  more  to  raise  to  begin 
the  erection  of  a  $55,000  building,  and  other  Associations  only  await  a  re- 
vival of  business  to  begin  the  effort  to  secure  buildings  of  their  own. 

The  educational  work  in  many  of  our  Associations  is  taking  high 
rank  and  proving  an  attractive  feature.  Classes  in  all  lines  of  intel- 
lectual and  practical  study  are  taught  by  •  careful  instructors  with 
grateful  results.  Exhibits  from  some  of  these  classes,  at  our  State 
Convention,  received  admiring  attention  and  commendation.  Bible 
study  may  be  said  to  be  of  growing  interest  among  our  Associations,  and 
systematic,  and  progressive  methods  are  being  carefully  considered. 

The  physical  department  undoubtedly  attracts  more  young  men  than 
any  other.  A  well  equipped  gymnasium  with  a  good  physical  instructor 
is  considered  an  essential  requisite  for  every  Association  in  the  State, 
while  football  and  baseball  teams  are  fast  becoming  necessary  features. 
The  social  element  has  been  carefully  fostered,  being  greatly  aided  by 
our  enthusiastic  ladies'  auxiliaries,  which  recently  for  the  first  time  held 
a  ladies'  auxilliary  conference,  forming  a  State  organization. 

Our  college  and  school  organizations,  four  in  number,  are  doing  grand 
work.  Intelligent  and  systematic  Bible  study  is  pursued,  and  in  one  of 
the  smallest  of  these  Associations  nine  young  men  are  studying  for  the 
Christian  ministry.  In  all  our  Associations  efforts  are  made  to  lead  our 
young  men  to  a  manly  confession  of  Jesus  Christ,  and  to  have  their  lives 
conform  to  His  teachings.  During  the  last  two  years  about  350  out  of 
our  Associations  have  united  with  Christian  churches. 

District  work  has  been  pushed  during  the  last  year  with  much  earnest- 
ness and  success.  J.  W  Cook,  who  had  served  as  State  Secretary  with 
great  acceptance,  felt  compelled  to  resign  his  position,  and  July  1st, 
1894,  E.  T.  Bates,  of  Holyoke,  Mass.,  came  tons  and  has  already  proved 
himself  a  zealous  and  efficient  officer.  Our  State  Convention,  recently 
held  at  Danbury,  was  well  attended,  enthusiastic,  full  of  interest,  and 
helpful.  C.  S.  Cooper,  College  Secretary  of  the  International  Committee, 
rendered  valuable  assistance  at  the  convention.  The  outlook  for  the 
future  is  hopeful  and  encouraging.  W.  B.  BURNHAM,  Cor.  Mem. 

FLORIDA. 

But  little  Association  work  is  being  done  in  this  State.  The  organiza- 
tion at  Titusville  is  the  only  one  known  to  be  at  present  in  operation. 

F.  A.  CURTIS,  Cor. 


52 

GEORGIA. 

Good  progress  has  characterized  the  work  in  Georgia  for  the  past  two 
years.  Better  work  has  been  done  with  better  results,  and  Association 
work  has  a  stronger  hold  upon  the  confidence  and  support  of  the  people 
than  ever  before.  Under  the  very  able  supervision  of  W.  M.  Lewis,  our 
State  Secretary  for  the  past  two  years,  and  with  the  co-operation  of  the 
State  Committee,  our  local  Associations  have  been  greatly  strengthened, 
and  are  doing  better  and  broader  work,  on  established  Association  lines. 

The  effort  has  been  to  more  firmly  establish  existing  Associations  rather 
than  to  increase  the  number.  Seven  new  Associations  have  been  organ- 
ized and  four  others  discontinued.  We  have  now  22  Associations,  with  a 
total  membership  of  3,450.  Six  Associations  own  their  buildings.  The 
total  value  of  buildings  and  furnishings  is  $220, 975,  with  a  debt  on  build- 
ings of  $29,000.  The  amount  expended  during  1894  for  current  expenses 
was  $20, 138. 64. 

Financially,  all  our  city  Associations  are  in  better  condition  than  for  a 
number  of  years  past.  The  Augusta  Association  has  paid  its  entire  debt, 
and  is  doing  a  strong  work.  The  Atlanta  Association,  with  its  branches, 
closes  the  year  practically  out  of  debt.  This  is  the  strongest  Association 
in  the  State,  owning  property  valued  at  $175,000,  upon  which  there  is  a 
debt  of  $15,000.  It  has  a  membership  of  900  and  is  doing  the  best  work 
in  its  history.  The  Atlanta  Railroad  Branch  has  within  the  year  removed 
into  new  quarters  well  adapted  to  its  needs. 

The  following  statistics  will  show  some  of  the  results  of  our  work :  In 
1893,  151  conversions  were  reported;  in  1894  the  number  was  319,  and  of 
this  number  209  united  with  churches.  The  total  attendance  at  meetings 
for  males  during  1894  was  45,007.  Attendance  at  lectures,  socials,  etc., 
13,006;  using  gymnasiums,  37,009;  using  bath  rooms,  47,697;  serving  on 
Association  committees,  44C.  Our  libraries  contain  2,285  volumes.  The 
State  Committee  has  uninterruptedly  taken  an  active  oversight  of  the 
work,  has  paid  off  an  old  debt, and  will  close  the  year  in  March  without  debt. 
Tlie  relations  between  the  State  Committee  and  the  local  Associations  are 
most  cordial,  and  State  Secretary  Lewis  meets  with  hearty  co-operation 
in  his  labors.  By  the  present  arrangement  Mr.  Lewis  divides  his  time 
between  Georgia  and  South  Carolina  in  the  proportions  of  two-thirds  to 
Georgia  and  one-third  to  South  Carolina.  With  the  growth  of  the  work 
in  this  State  it  will  before  long  demand  the  entire  services  of  the  State 
Secretary. 

The  State  Committee  would  express  its  appreciation  of  the  valuable 
assistance  received  from  the  International  Committee;  especially  in  the 
securing  of  general  secretaries  at  important  points  have  we  been  directed 
to  suitable  men.  H.  P.  Andersen  has  given  us  much  counsel  and  help, 
as  has  also  F.  S.  Brockman  in  the  college  work,  and  C.  J.  Hicks  in  the 
interest  in  our  railroad  department. 

J.  FRANK  BECK,  Cor.  Mem. 


ILLINOIS. 

The  two  years  since  my  last  report  have  been  marked  by  work  and 
blessing.    Financial  dangers  have  threatened,  but  not  overcome  at  any 


53 

point,  and  spiritual  blessings  have  been  many.  Owing  to  prevailing 
business  depression  the  work  has  been  largely  that  of  conservation  rather 
than  extension,  although  evidences  of  growth  are  apparent.  Statistics  in 
detail  will  be  found  in  the  tables  printed  in  the  State  and  International 
Year  Books.  The  Illinois  Associations  have  reported  nearly  4,000  pro- 
fessed conversions  during  the  two  years. 

Forty -two  secretarial  points  are  now  maintained,  doing  effective  work. 
Fourteen  Associations  own  their  buildings.  The  movements  for  build- 
ings at  Pana,  Elgin,  Champaign  (University  of  Illinois)  and  Galesburg 
are  each  steadily  nearing  success.  The  Chicago  Central  Department 
building  enterprise  seems  to  have  shown  that  the  financial  plans  were 
wise.  A  final  canvass  for  funds  remains  to  be  made,  but  success  is  cer- 
tain. The  Association  has  been  in  occupancy  over  a  year,  and  the  busi- 
ness portion  of  the  building  is  nearly  completed  and  rents  well.  The  de- 
velopment in  the  educational  work  in  Chicago  has  been  especially 
marked.  Nine  Chicago  branches  have  carried  on  an  efficient  and  grow- 
ing work. 

Four  Railroad  Associations  are  steadily  maintained.    At  one  railroad 

division  point  influences  for  peace  and  order  at  the  time  of  the  railroad 
strike  of  1894  were  directly  traceable  to  the  Association.  The  separation 
of  the  Chicago  terminals  of  the  railroad  systems  centering  there  intro- 
duces special  difficulties  in  the  way  of  a  work  which  shall  reach  men  of 
all  roads. 

Thirty-seven  College  Associations  are  now  in  existence,  several  of  them 
being  institutions  reached  since  my  last  report.  Campaigns  for  better 
Bible  study  and  for  the  purpose  of  reaching  new  students  have  been  vig- 
orously conducted  with  gratifying  results. 

Twenty-five  small  town  Associations  are  now  alive.  A.  T.  Stephens, 
formerly  serving  among  them,  left  the  State  Committee  to  take  a  secre- 
taryship at  Kankakee.  The  Committee  were  for  some  months  unable  to 
give  the  needed  attention  to  these  Associations,  and  several  were  discon- 
tinued. Notwithstanding  the  difficulty  in  maintaining  such  Associations 
and  the  fact  that  some  do  not  last  but  a  year  or  two,  the  results  obtained 
fully  justify  the  continuance  of  that  phase  of  Association  activity. 

The  plan  of  securing  corresponding  members  has  been  pursued. 
There  are  now  360  at  as  many  points  in  Illinois.  Letters  from  them  con- 
cerning young  men  going  to  other  places  and  the  educational  effect  of  the 
relation  of  such  members  to  the  State  Committee  has  proved  of  great 

value. 

The  division  of  the  State  into  districts  is  maintained.  Last  year  nine 
district  conventions  were  held,  each  one  having  marked  success  in  stimu- 
lating workers  and  in  direct  spiritual  results  in  the  towns  visited.  There 
has  been  an  increase  in  the  number  of  young  men's  Sundays  over  any 
previous  year.  Their  effect  has  been  educational  and  uplifting  upon  the 
communities  to  which  visits  were  made.  District  Conventions  are  now 
equalling  in  number  of  delegates  and  in  power  the  State  Conventions 
held  in  the  earlier  history  of  the  work. 

The  State  Conventions  of  1893,  held  at  Elgin,  and  1894,  held  at  Spring- 
field, the  State  capital,  were  notable  successes  as  to  strength  of  program 
and  number  of  delegates,  inspiration  to  work  throughout  the  State,  and 
helpfulness  to  local  Associations. 


54 

The  State  Executive  Committee,  notwithstanding  the  "  hard  times,"  has 
been  enabled  to  meet  its  expenses  and  to  reduce  its  debt  to  $3,000.  After 
eight  and  one-half  years  of  faithful,  efficient  service  as  office  secretary,,  W. 
F.  Levings  has  gone  into  business.  The  Committee  is  about  to  lose  the 
valuable  services  of  J.  V.  Read,  whose  assistance  along  financial  lines  has 
been  of  greatest  value  to  the  Committee  during  the  past  few  years.  One 
monumental  result  can  be  noted  from  the  fact  that  over  5,000  persons 
contributed  to  the  support  of  the  State  Committee's  work  in  1894. 
Messrs.  Brunei*,  Burt,  Bowman  and  two  new  men  will  be  with  us  in  1895, 
under  the  leadership  of  I.  E.  Brown. 

We  unite  in  the  feeling  that  greater  things  should  be  brought  to  pass 
for  our  Master  in  this  favored  and  central  State.  The  Summer  gatherings 
of  students  and  others  at  Lake  Geneva,  the  presence  of  Mr.  Ober  in 
Chicago,  representing  the  International  Committee,  the  sense  of  interest 
in  and  responsibility  for  the  Young  Men's  Era,  published  at  Chicago,  the 
growing  importance  and  value  of  the  Young  Men's  Christian  Association 
Training  School  at  Chicago,  and  other  like  privileges  and  opportunities, 
added  to  the  help  of  the  International  Committee  given  last  year  through 
Secretaries  Mott,  Hicks'  and  Hodge,  unite  to  stimulate  and  call  us  to 
better,  stronger  work  and  results  than  ever  before. 

ARTHUR  D.  WHEELER,  Cor.  Mem. 

INDIANA. 

In  November,  1894,  we  passed  our  quarter- centennial  of  organized  State 
work  in  Indiana.  Our  State  Convention  was  the  largest  and  strongest  of 
the  whole  25  ;  272  delegates  were  reported.  We  have  finished  the  most 
trying  year  of  our  history  without  the  loss  of  a  single  Association  and 
with  a  gain  of  three  College  Associations. 

There  are  now  5,600  members  in  our  30  Associations,  about  the  same  as 
two  years  ago,  though  the  high-water  mark,  which  was  considerably 
more  than  this,  was  reached  just  before  the  panic  of  1893.  One-half  of 
the  above  are  active  members  and  nearly  800  committeemen.  Current 
expenses  remain  about  the  same  as  two  years  ago,  $40,000  annually.  Our 
libraries  contain  6,500  volumes,  being  a  considerable  gain.  There  is  a 
material  gain  also  in  Bible  study,  both  in  the  number  of  classes  and  in 
the  attendance.  The  average  weekly  attendance  at  young  men's  gospel 
meetings  has  increased  from  992  to  1,258,  while  the  number  of  professed 
conversions  among  young  men  has  increased  from  255  to  nearly  500.  The 
average  daily  attendance  at  rooms  is  1,623,  against  1,218  two  years  ago. 

The  organization  of  the  State  work  itself  is  more  systematic  and  cohe- 
rent than  formerly.  We  now  have  six  standing  sub-committees,  those 
recently  added  being  on  college  work,  railroad  work,  State  athletics  and 
extension  work.  We  enter  1895  with  finances  in  better  shape  than  in  any 
former  year. 

From  the  International  Committee  we  have  received  occasional  valu- 
able co-operation,  especially  from  Secretaries  Hicks  and  Hamilton,  in 
connection  with  our  growing  railroad  work.  College  Secretary  Mott  was 
of  much  help  at  our  State  Convention,  as  were  also  Messrs.  Smith  and 
Shuey,  of  the  International  Committee. 

WALTER  C.  NUNEMACHER,  Car.  Mem. 


55 

IOWA. 

The  work  in  Iowa  has  made  substantial  progress.  In  spite  of  the  hard 
times  our  finances  are  in  good  condition.  The  State  Committee  expendi- 
tures have  been  $5,700  each  year,  and  no  bills  remain  unpaid.  The 
college  and  railroad  work  have  both  advanced.  Every  College  Association 
in  the  State  was  represented  at  the  convention  held  last  month. 

The  Dubuque  Association  has  moved  into  a  home  worth  $35,000.  H.  L. 
Stout  gave  them  the  residence  which  had  been  his  home  for  many  years, 
a  large,  substantial  brick  building  on  a  lot  102  x  118  ft.,  near  the  business 
center  of  the  city.  A  gymnasium  and  hall  adequate  to  their  needs  has 
been  added,  the  whole  making  a  splendid  equipment  for  their  growing 
work. 

Horace  S.  Eand,  of  Burlington,  offers  the  Association  a  lot  120x117,  in  a 
splendid  location  for  their  work,  on  condition  that  a  building  worth 
$30,000  shall  be  erected  upon  it.  It  is  hoped  that  before  another  year 
passes  the  reasonable  condition  will  be  met. 

At  Sioux  City  $46,000,  enough  to  save  their  building,  has  been  secured. 
H.  A.  Johns,  president  of  the  Association,  gave  two  months  of  his  entire 
time  to  this  work. 

Mr.  and  Mrs.  C.  B.  Soutter,  of  Cedar  Rapids,  have  added  to  their  gifts 
to  the  Association  an  artesian  well  at  an  expense  of  $5,000. 

The  railroad  department  at  Marshalltown  has  secured  $3,800  in  sub- 
scriptions toward  a  building. 

The  building  fund  at  Iowa  College  has  been  increased  to  $25,000.  At 
Central  University  the  laying  of  the  corner-stone  was  made  a  part  of  com- 
mencement exercises.  The  building  will  be  completed  this  Summer.  At 
Simpson  College  $7,000  was  subscribed  during  one  day.  Iowa  Wesley  an 
University  added  about  $3,000  to  its  building  fund,  making  the  amount 
$9,000. 

Great  advance  has  been  made  in  the  educational  department  of  the 
work.  Last  year  29  classes  were  reported,  with  an  enrollment  of  300 ; 
this  year  64  classes,  with  an  enrollment  of  over  600.  In  the  two  years 
1,861  young  men  have  professed  conversion. 

The  counsel  and  assistance  of  the  International  Committee  have  been 
greatly  appreciated. 

M.  H.  SMITH,  Cor.  Mem. 


KANSAS. 

The  years  1893-94  witnessed  marked  changes  in  the  Association  work  in 
our  State.  It  has  been  a  time  for  "holding  the  fort."  Early  in  1893 
several  of  the  small  town  Associations  succumbed  to  the  financial  strin- 
gency, but  for  the  past  eighteen  months  the  tide  has  been  slowly  turning, 
and  several  Associations  have  been  saved  by  the  prompt  action  of  the 
State  Secretaries.  During  1893  there  were  two  employees  of  the  State 
Committee,  while  during  most  of  1894  three  persons  have  been  employed — 
F.  E.  A.  Smith,  as  State  Secretary;  E.  M.  Aiken,  as  associate,  and  J.  C. 
Eexford,  as  office  secretary. 

There  are  at  present  32  Associations — eighteen  college,  twelve  city  and 
two  railroad,  and  employing  twenty-one  general  and  assistant  secretaries 
and  physical  directors.  One  hundred  small  towns  are  covered  by  cor- 


56 

responding  members.     Railroads  are  contributing  to  these  Associations  a 
total  of  $1,200  annually. 

In  October,  1893,  the  State  Convention  was  held  at  Fort  Scott,  and 
attended  by  164  delegates.  C.  L.  Gates  and  J.  E.  Mott  represented  the 
International  Committee,  and  State  Secretaries  Clarke  of  Michigan  and 
Bruner  of  Illinois  were  most  helpful.  Eev.  D.  Barns-Griffiths  conducted 
the  Bible  studies. 

The  annual  gathering  of  the  general  secretaries  was  held  at  Leaven- 
worth  in  February,  1894. 

The  annual  State  Bible  School  was  held  at  Forest  Park,  Ottawa,  June 
11-18,  1894,  with  an  attendance  of  nearly  200.  The  teachings  of  Prof.  E. 
E.  Lloyd,  Eev.  W.  C.  Veazie  and  others  were  very  profitable. 

With  only  three  exceptions,  the  Kansas  Associations  reported  less  in- 
debtedness January  1, 1895,  than  the  year  previous.  For  the  year  closing 
October  1,  1894,  the  State  Committee  expended  $3,519.  Kansas  is  in- 
debted to  the  International  Committee  for  efficient  services  of  six  of  its 
secretaries,  Messrs.  Gates,  Ober,  Mott,  Brockman,  Wishard  and  Hodge. 
Mr.  Mott  conducted  the  conference  for  College  Association  men  at  Law- 
rence, in  January,  1894,  and  in  May  of  the  same  year  Mr.  Brockman  made 
a  tour  of  most  of  the  College  Associations,  in  the  interest  of  the  Lake 
Geneva  Summer  School. 

Immediately  following  the  State  Convention  of  1894,  Mr.  Hodge  visited 
several  of  the  larger  city  Associations  with  his  educational  exhibit,  creat- 
ing a  deep  interest  in  this  department  of  Association  work. 

The  recent  State  Convention  at  Ottawa  was  largely  attended. 

H.  L.  EAYMOND,  Cor.  Mem. 

KENTUCKY. 

The  past  two  years  have  seen  a  marked  improvement  in  the  solidarity, 
growth  and  fruitfulness  of  the  work  in  Kentucky.  There  are  now  26 
Associations  in  the  State,  work  having  been  established  in  three  of  the 
largest  unorganized  cities  since  the  last  report.  The  number  of  secretaries 
has  increased  from  12  to  20. 

A  College  Secretary  has  been  employed  by  the  State  Committee  for  a 
third  of  his  time,  and  the  result  has  been  a  speedy  increase  in  the 
efficiency  of  the  college  work.  The  presidential  conference  has  also 
contributed  very  materially  to  the  growth  of  this  department. 

A  new  undertaking  is  the  maintenance  of  an  Association  tent  at  the 
annual  encampment  of  the  State  Guard.  The  work  has  been  a  marked 
success  and  fruitful  in  results. 

The  religious  work  of  the  Associations  is  receiving  more  thought  and 
attention  than  in  the  past.  One  Association  had  an  average  attendance 
of  700,  and  another  of  200,  at  the  weekly  meeting  for  men.  The  number 
of  professed  conversions  has  increased  each  year. 

Material  help  has  been  rendered  by  Secretaries  H.  P.  Andersen  and  F. 
S.  Brockman,  of  the  International  Committee. 

The  14th  State  Convention  was  held  at  Lexington,  February  21-24,  1895, 
with  an  attendance  of  250  delegates.  $3,800  was  raised  and  expended  last 
year  for  State  work,  and  $3,300  the  year  previous. 

The  outlook  for  the  present  year  is  full  of  promise .     There  are  more 


ASSOCIATION  BUILDING,  JOHNSTOWN,    PA. 

DEDICATED  JUNE  4,  1893. 
Dimensions,  41x132  feet.  Cost,  $30,000.  Population,  25,000. 


57 

cities  desiring  organization,  more  communities  becoming  acquainted  with 
Association  work,  more  possibilities  in  internal  growth  and  development 
than  ever  before. 

J.  A.  STUCKY,  Cor.  Mem. 

LOUISIANA. 

The  New  Orleans  Association  has  maintained  its  work  during  the 
past  two  years  in  good  condition  and  with  encouraging  results.  The 
erection  of  a  fine  building  has  been  commenced,  to  cost  with  the  lot  about 
$54,000,  and  to  be  completed  early  in  the  Autumn.  As  this  will  be  the 
first  Association  building  in  New  Orleans  much  interest  has  been  mani- 
fested in  the  undertaking.  A  number  of  College  Associations  in  the  State, 
notably  those  at  Baton  Rouge,  Jackson,  and  New  Orleans,  are  doing  good 
work,  which  has  been  stimulated  by  visits  from  Secretaries  Gates,  Brock- 
man  and  Hunton,  of  the  International  Committee,  I  regret  to  report  that 
the  Shreveport  Association  has  ceased  to  exist. 

No  general  State  work  has  been  carried  on  during  the  past  two  years. 

CHARLES  H.  SHUTE,  Cor.  Mem. 

MAINE. 

Maine  has  been  without  a  State  Secretary  since  September,  1893,  so 
that  some  of  the  weak  points  have  suffered  for  the  need  of  a  supervisory 
work.  The  Bath  Association  has  completed  and  is  now  occupying  a  new 
building  well  fitted  for  the  work.  The  State  Convention  of  1893  was  held 
with  the  Auburn  Association  and  was  a  very  successful  gathering.  Logan 
H.  Roots,  of  the  International  Committee  force,  did  good  work  among  the 
College  Associations  in  the  Fall  of  1893.  In  1894  no  State  Convention 
was  held. 

W.  S.  COREY,  Cor.  Mem. 

MARYLAND,  DELAWARE,  DISTRICT  OF  COLUMBIA  AND  WEST 

VIRGINIA. 

The  work  in  our  territory  during  the  past  two  years  has  made  some  sub- 
stantial progress.  Principally  on  account  of  the  financial  distress  six  Asso- 
ciations have  disbanded;  but  two  town  and  six  College  Associations  have 
been  organized,  a  gain  of  two.  The  intercollegiate  department  of  the 
Baltimore  Association  is  the  most  recent  addition,  in  the  organization  of 
which  the  services  of  International  Secretaries  Mott  and  Brockman  were 
conspicuous. 

The  number  of  paid  officers  has  been  increased  by  five,  making  a  total 
of  32,  and  at  present  every  secretarial  point  is  supplied. 

Two  buildings  which  were  both  in  process  of  erection  at  the  time  of 
the  last  report,  one  at  Cumberland  and  the  other  at  West  Branch,  Balti- 
more, Md.,  have  been  completed  and  are  now  occupied.  At  Charleston, 
West  Va.,  and  at  Annapolis,  Md.,  a  dwelling  and  a  business  block 
respectively,  have  been  bought  and  adapted  for  Association  purposes.  At 
the  Central  Branch,  East  Branch  and  German  Branch,  Baltimore,  and  at 
Washington,  D.  C.,  debts  on  buildings  have  either  been  paid  or  greatly 
reduced. 


58 

We  were  without  a  State  Secretary  for  three  and  one-half  months  until 
June,  1893.  Since  then  F.  W.  Lang  has  served,  giving  his  attention  prin- 
cipally to  aiding  existing  organizations  and  to  bettering  the  financial 
condition  of  the  State  work,  along  which  latter  line  much  yet  remains  to 
be  done.  In  June,  1894,  the  State  Committee's  office  was  removed  to 
Washington,  D.  C. ,  as  a  somewhat  more  central  location. 

The  deputation  work  of  the  Johns  Hopkins  University  Association  has 
been  kept  up  with  good  results.  The  last  State  Convention,  held  at  Cum- 
berland, Md. ,  January  17-20,  was  the  largest  and  most  representative  one 
yet  held,  every  section  of  the  field  and  a  large  majority  of  the  Associa- 
tions being  represented. 

Efficient  help  to  local  or  State  work  in  our  field  has  been  rendered  by 
ten  different  secretaries  of  the  International  Committee  during  the  past 
two  years. 

W.  H.  H.  SMITH,  Cor.  Mem. 


MASSACHUSETTS  AND  EHODE  ISLAND. 

The  work  in  these  States  is  being  pushed  vigorously  in  all  lines. 
Twenty-four  men  as  members  of  the  State  Committee  are  supporting 
heartily  the  tireless  labors  of  our  Sate  Secretary,  K.  M.  Armstrong,  and 
his  assistants.  Among  the  changes  to  be  noted  is  the  resignation  of 
Major  Russell  Sturgis  as  chairman  of  the  committee.  For  ten  years  he 
has  done  faithful  service  in  that  position.  His  successor  is  Oliver  H. 
Durrell. 

Religious  work  has  been  given  its  proper  pre-eminence,  and  the  num- 
ber of  professed  conversions  is  2,954  for  the  two  years.  Special  men's 
services,  Bible  classes,  district  conferences  and  deputation  days  are  some 
of  the  means  used.  The  employment  of  a  special  evangelist  for  work  in 
small  towns  during  the  Summer  months  was  an  experiment  that  proved 
successful. 

The  junior  department  work  is  emphasized.  Annual  conferences  are 
held,  boys'  camps — as  a  summer  recreation — are  increasing,  and  continued 
spiritual  results  in  connection  with  these  gatherings  are  noted  where  any 
faithful  effort  is  put  forth.  This  department  is  deemed  indispensable  to 
successful  work  for  young  men.  The  department  at  Salem,  Mass.,  is 
believed  to  be  the  oldest  in  the  world. 

District  work  has  yielded  splendid  returns.  Nine  district  conferences 
are  held  yearly  besides  deputation  days  and  intervisitation  of  committees. 

College  work  is  now  systematically  and,  we  believe,  successfully  in- 
augurated in  most  of  our  prominent  educational  institutions. 

Gymnasiums  are  increasing  in  number,  and,  being  in  charge  of  pro- 
nounced Christian  men,  are  yielding  spiritual  results.  Outdoor  athletics 
are  growing  in  favor  in  some  Associations. 

There  are  eighty-four  Associations,  with  a  membership  of  24,491;  eleven 
of  these  are  in  colleges  and  fitting  schools;  net  gain  in  two  years,  seven. 
Not  any  Association,  established  by  or  working  in  harmony  with  the 
State  organization,  has  ceased  to  exist.  Motto:  Build  slowly, — count 
cost — permanency. 

New  buildings  have  been  dedicated  at  Holyoke  and  Southbridge,  the 
cost  of  the  two  buildings  being  $230,000.  Buildings  are  nearly  completed 


59 

at  Fitchburg,  Springfield,  Melrose  and  Amesbury,  at  a  total  cost  of 
$290,000.  The  state  endowment  building  fund  amounts  to  $44,000,  of 
which  $11,250  are  paid  in.  The  State  Committee  and  secretaries,  local 
secretaries  and  physical  directors  hold  an  annual  meeting  for  devotional 
and  social  exercises,  with  good  results.  The  meetings  of  the  State  Com- 
mittee are  frequently  held,  by  invitation,  with  different  Associations, 
an  evening  gathering  for  the  furtherance  of  local  interests  being  usu- 
ally one  of  the  features. 

The  addition  of  a  large  number  of  corresponding  members  of  the 
State  Committee  is  proving  a  valuable  accession.  The  Tioo  States  is  a 
monthly  publication  issued  from  the  State  office.  It  has  proved  valuable 
as  a  medium  of  extending  Association  intelligence  and  conveying  useful 
suggestions.  We  have  also  received  special  favors  from  the  Boston 
papers. 

JAMES  A.  HALE,  Cor.  Mem. 

MICHIGAN. 

The  past  two  years  have  indicated  actual  progress  in  the  lines  of  gen- 
eral efficiency  among  the  Associations  in  Michigan.  Five  Associations 
have  been  discontinued  and  seven  new  ones  started,  leaving  now  thirty- 
four  in  all.  Many  new  rooms  have  been  occupied.  The  membership  has 
increased  676,  and  is  now  7,080.  The  number  of  contributors  is  1,473. 
The  district  work  plans  have  been  successfully  enlarged,  and  many  valu- 
able meetings  held  in  unorganized  towns. 

In  the  larger  Associations  the  educational  work  has  been  generally  taken 
up,  and  in  every  case  with  profit.  Limit  of  financial  ability  only  delays 
a  more  rapid  development  of  this  work.  In  the  hope  of  being  able  to  aid 
in  the  solution  of  the  social  questions  involving  labor  and  capital,  some 
Associations  are  inviting  papers  and  discussions  upon  social  problems 
for  their  Sunday  meetings. 

The  State  is  indebted  to  the  International  Committee  for  services  ren- 
dered by  C.  K.  Ober  ;  his  work  in  Grand  Eapids  was  especially  helpful. 
H.  M.  Clarke  is  continuing  to  do  valiant  Christian  work  in  a  wise  and 
helpful  way  in  his  capacity  as  State  Secretary. 

CLAY  H.  HOLLISTEK,  Cor.  Mem. 

MINNESOTA. 

More  Association  work  is  being  done  in  this  State  than  ever  before. 
William  Francis,  formerly  the  assistant  and,  later,  the  acting  State 
Secretary,  was  made  the  permanent  secretary  at  the  close  of  1893.  The 
State  work  in  1893  cost  $2,400,  and  in  1894,  $2,700. 

Section  work  exists  in  three  places,  and  in  three  counties  there  is  an 
organized  county  work,  employing  the  entire  time  of  three  secretaries, 
and  the  volunteer  services  of  about  225  young  men.  The  needs  of  the 
country  districts,  the  large  number  of  conversions,  and  the  rapid  devel- 
opment of  workers  that  follow  the  efforts  put  forth,  make  this  county 
work  one  of  much  interest  and  importance. 

In  the  holiday  vacation  of  1893,  75  picked  college  men  visited  16  towns 
and  conducted  evangelistic  meetings.  Among  the  results  were  450  pro- 


60 

fessed  conversions.  In  1894  the  same  number  of  men  visited  15  towns, 
and  300  conversions  were  reported.  The  awakening  and  harmonizing  of 
churches,  and  the  reflex  influence  on  the  colleges,  were  other  noticeable 
results.  In  a  total  of  50  towns  visited  by  student  vacation  bands  during 
the  past  few  years,  there  are  only  six  in  which  there  is  not  now  being 
carried  on  some  special  work  for  men  or  boys. 

Two  men,  at  the  expense  of  the  lumber  companies,  have  worked  among 
the  woodsmen,  preaching  and  singing  in  the  camps,  doing  personal  work, 
distributing  reading  matter,  and  selling  Testaments. 

Winona  has  secured  a  splendid  building  and  moved  it  on  to  a  choice  lot. 
The  plant  is  worth  at  least  $30,000,  and  was  largely  the  gift  of  the  Laird- 
Norton  Lumber  Co. 

There  are  now  52  centers  of  Association  influence  in  Minnesota.  Many  of 
the  Associations  are  getting  into  an  improved  financial  condition,  and  in 
many  the  religious  work  is  especially  strong.  Over  700  men  are  in  the 
Bible  and  training  classes.  The  State  Convention  at  Mankato,  in  1894, 
was  attended  by  232  delegates  and  corresponding  members. 

Very  valuable  aid  has  been  given  to  the  work  in  Minnesota  by  Secre- 
taries Wishard,  Taggart,  Mott,  Ober,  Hicks,  Hamilton,  Hodge  and 
Weidensall  of  the  International  Committee. 

B.  SNELL,  Cor.  Mem. 


MISSISSIPPI. 

Through  an  arrangement  brought  about  by  the  International  Com- 
mittee, Mississippi  has  united  with  Alabama  in  employing  a  State 
Secretary.  This  officer,  F.  L.  Willis,  has  devoted  one-third  of  his  time 
during  the  year  to  our  State.  He  has  made  49  visits  to  24  different  places, 
conducted  21  men's  meetings,  attended  56  other  meetings,  and  enlisted  50 
young  men  in  Bible  study. 

A  number  of  young  men's  prayer  meetings  have  been  organized,  and 
good  work  is  being  done  in  training  young  men  to  lead  meetings  and  take 
part  in  religious  exercises.  It  is  the  policy  of  the  State  Committee  to 
build  up  Associations  from  these  prayer  meetings.  Organization  is 
attempted  only  when  it  has  been  demonstrated  that  the  place  is  ready 
and  the  time  ripe  for  it. 

The  college  work  has  been  especially  blessed.  The  total  membership 
of  the  College  Associations  is  291,  and  the  number  enrolled  in  Bible 
classes  is  117.  The  total  number  of  professed  conversions  is  49. 

J.  B.  DOBYNS,  Cor.  Mem. 

MISSOUKI. 

Since  the  last  report  two  State  Conventions  have  been  held— at  Sedalia 
and  Columbia — the  latter  in  February  of  the  present  year,  in  accordance 
with  the  instructions  of  the  convention  held  three  years  ago,  that  as  soon 
as  practicable  the  State  Convention  be  transferred  from  the  Fall  to  the 
Spring. 

The  past  two  years  have  been  years  of  great  financial  difficulty,  and  at 
one  time  it  looked  as  though  several  of  the  Associations  in  our  smaller 
cities  would  be  compelled  to  disband.  But  chiefly  through  the  efforts  of 


61 

Secretary  C.  L.  Gates,  of  the  International  Committee,  the  workers  were 
rallied  at  these  critical  points,  important  reforms  in  their  methods  of 
work  adopted,  and  financial  canvasses  organized  and  prosecuted,  and  as 
a  result  the  Associations  referred  to,  with  but  one  exception,  are  in  a  bet- 
ter financial  condition  than  ever,  having  largely  reduced  their  indebted- 
ness and  provided  for  their  current  expenses.  The  single  exception  is 
Hannibal,  which  closed  its  doors  in  January,  1895.  No  words  can  express 
our  gratitude  to  the  International  Committee  for  the  services  of  Mr.  Gates, 
and  for  the  help  rendered  us  on  various  occasions  by  Messrs.  Hicks, 
Brockman  and  others  of  its  secretaries. 

When  H.  F.  Williams  resigned  the  editorship  of  the  Young  Men's  Era, 
in  the  Fall  of  1893,  he  accepted  the  State  Secretaryship  of  Missouri,  only 
to  resign  it  a  few  months  later,  much  to  our  regret,  on  account  of  ill 
health.  Since  that  time,  for  financial  reasons,  we  have  not  employed  a 
State  Secretary,  but  have  carried  on  the  work  by  the  aid  of  the  Inter- 
national Secretaries  and  other  workers  secured  through  the  International 
Committee,  and  by  the  voluntary  service  of  members  of  the  State  Com- 
mittee. 

The  St.  Louis  Association  purchased  a  new  site  in  July,  1893,  for 
$51,250,  and  last  Fall  contracted  for  a  building  to  cost  about  $150,000, 
which  is  now  in  course  of  erection. 

There  are  very  good  prospects  for  a  building  for  the  Union  Station 
Railroad  Branch  of  St.  Louis,  as  the  Terminal  Railroad  Company  has 
agreed  to  lease  the  Association  a  splendid  lot  at  a  nominal  rental,  and  the 
leading  railroad  corporations  have  expressed  their  willingness  to  con- 
tribute to  the  erection  of  a  building  to  cost  not  less  than  $50,000.  C.  J. 
Hicks,  Eailroad  Secretary  of  the  International  Committee,  has  had  much 
to  do  with  accomplishing  this  gratifying  result. 

The  chief  development  of  the  past  year  was  the  organization  of  Associ- 
ations in  five  of  the  medical  colleges  of  St.  Louis,  largely  through  the 
efforts  of  College  Secretaries  Mott  and  Brockman.  Four  of  these  Associ- 
ations were  represented  at  our  recent  State  Convention,  and  they  have  all 
had  a  successful  season's  work,  and  promise  much  usefulness  for  the 
future. 

The  Kansas  City  Association  lost  its  building  last  year  by  the  fore- 
closure of  its  mortgage,  but  is  still  occupying  it  at  a  reasonable  rental, 
and  the  outlook  for  the  work  there  is  better  than  for  years  past. 

The  State  Executive  Committee  was  recently  incorporated. 

E.  P.  Y.  BITTER,  Cor.  Mem. 


NEBRASKA. 

Nebraska  has  28  Associations  — 18  general,  10  college;  membership, 
4,975 ;  employed  officers,  19.  Our  last  State  Convention  was  held  at 
Beatrice,  with  an  attendance  of  190,  largely  college  students.  C.  K.  Ober, 
of  the  International  Committee,  and  C.  S.  Ward,  general  secretary,  Grand 
Rapids,  Michigan,  were  present.  A  Summer  conference  for  Bible  study, 
conducted  by  C.  M.  Copeland,  was  held  at  Fremont.  A  successful  dis- 
trict convention  was  held  at  Norfolk. 

Nebraska  has  now  no  regular  State  Secretary,  but  C.  M.  Copeland,  of 
Manitoba,  has  filled  that  position  temporarily  during  part  of  the  year.  A 


62 

large  amount  of  work  has  been  done  by  the  chairman  and  members  of  the 
State  Committee. 

By  special  effort  made  under  W.  E.  Lougee,  now  of  the  International 
Committee,  Hastings  raised  $3,700  to  pay  off  all  indebtedness.  The 
burning  of  the  mortgage,  accompanied  by  special  exercises,  was  a  unique 
and  satisfactory  affair. 

Harry  L.  Markell,  general  secretary  at  Fremont,  devoted  one-half  his 
time  during  the  latter  part  of  the  year  to  district  work  in  Fremont  dis- 
trict. A  number  of  Bible  classes  were  formed  in  small  towns,  three  new 
Associations  started,  and  a  foundation  laid  for  other  organizations. 

In  the  face  of  the  financial  discouragements  and  with  no  State  Secre- 
tary, our  Associations  have  not  only  held  their  own,  but  increased  in 
membership  and  strength. 

The  placing  of  a  resident  secretary  for  the  Northwest  in  Chicago,  in 
the  person  of  C.  K.  Ober,  has  been  of  great  value  to  the  Nebraska  work. 
Acknowledgment  should  also  be  made  of  the  efficient  service  rendered  by 
J.  B.  Mott  and  F.  S.  Brockman.  Eobert  Weidensall  also  brought  inspir- 
ation to  us  from  the  World's  Conference. 

C.  F.  HARRISON,  Cor,  Mem. 


NEW  HAMPSHIRE. 

There  have  been  many  changes  and  a  good  degree  of  progress  in  our 
State.  During  1893  New  Hampshire,  in  connection  with  Maine  and 
Vermont,  worked  under  the  direction  of  R.  H.  Shelton  as  State  Secretary, 
but  at  the  end  of  the  year  he  gave  up  the  position  on  account  of  feeble 
health.  For  the  year  1894  we  were  without  stated  supervision.  There 
are  seven  secretarial  points  in  the  State,  though  two  are  now  vacant. 
Manchester,  our  largest  city,  which  has  been  closed  to  the  work  until  the 
past  year,  now  has  a  well  organized  and  flourishing  Association,  with  a 
good  secretary.  The  Association  at  Keene  has  built,  furnished  and 
dedicated,  at  a  cost  of  $42,000,  a  fine  three-story  brick  building,  the  first 
in  the  State.  The  Concord  Association  has  moved  into  new  rooms,  giving 
it  very  fine  facilities. 

The  State  Convention  of  1893  was  held  at  Dover.  The  International 
Committee  was  represented  by  H.  M.  Moore,  Thomas  K.  Cree  and 
Logan  Herbert  Roots.  The  convention  was  in  every  way  a  success  and 
especially  helpful  to  the  local  Association.  New  Hampshire  and  Vermont 
held  a  joint  convention  in  December,  1894,  at  Keene.  It  was  a  large  and 
very  successful  meeting  and  resulted  in  uniting  the  two  States,  as  Massa- 
chusetts and  Rhode  Island  have  been  for  several  years.  The  International 
Committee  sent  to  our  aid  Glaus  Olandt,  Jr.,  who  planned  the  convention, 
and  it  was  largely  through  his  efforts  that  the  union  of  the  two  States  was 
brought  about.  At  this  convention  the  Committee  was  represented  by  H. 
M.  Moore,  Claus  Olandt,  Jr.  and  Cecil  L.  Gates.  The  work  in  this  State 
is  to-day  what  it  is  because  of  the  assistance  it  has  received,  and  is  still 
receiving,  from  the  International  Committee.  We  expect  before  the  year 
closes  to  have  a  secretary  for  the  combined  States;  but  we  shall  still  need 
the  Committee's  helpful  offices. 

H.  E.  FAY,  Cor.  Mem. 


68 

NEW  JEKSEY. 

The  past  two  years  has  been  a  period  of  development  rather  than  of 
extension.  Few  Associations  have  been  formed,  although  at  present  a 
score  of  towns  are  asking  for  organization.  The  majority  of  these  applic- 
ations will  be  deferred  until  adequate  financial  support  can  be  assured. 

The  existing  Associations — 36  local,  three  railroad  and  ten  college — 
are,  in  the  main,  strong  and  active. 

Notwithstanding  the  financial  stringency,  current  expenses  are  increas- 
ing and  the  full  force  of  salaried  officials,  46,  is  maintained  Men's  meet- 
ings show  an  increased  attendance,  with  more  inquirers  and  a  larger  pro- 
portion of  professed  converts  becoming  church  members.  In  the  college 
department,  seven  per  cent  of  those  attending  the  colleges  and  schools 
professed  conversions  in  the  past  year. 

Carnden,  Plainfield  and  Salem  have  occupied  their  new  buildings, 
valued  respectively  at  $35,000,  $60,000  and  $15,000. 

The  times  have  prevented  extension  of  the  railroad  work.  At  existing 
points,  however,  the  membership  is  increasing,  the  privileges  are  more 
generally  used,  and  there  are  many  men  showing  evidence  of  sound  con- 
version. Conferences  have  been  held  in  each. of  the  six  districts,  and 
many  young  men's  Sundays  conducted,  with  spiritual  fruit  in  all  cases. 

The  number  of  corresponding  members  has  been  extended,  and  good 
reports  of  their  work  received. 

The  recent  State  Convention  at  Plainfield  was  the  strongest  in  its  pro- 
gramme and  most  spiritual  in  its  tone  of  any  ever  held.  Its  local  effect 
has  been  marked. 

The  State  Committee  has  been  materially  strengthened  and  more 
aggressive  work  is  expected,  especially  in  the  lines  of  educational  work 
and  Bible  study. 

The  International  Committee  has  aided  at  many  local  points  and  at  the 
State  meetings. 

EDWAED  P.  HOLDEN,  Cor.  Mem. 


NEW  YOEK.
