The  work  in  the  State  has  been  most  encouraging  during  the  past  two 
years,  despite  the  financial  stringency. 

State  Conventions  were  held  at  Jamestown  in  1894,  and  Syracuse  in 
1895  ;  at  both  meetings  steady  advance  was  reported  in  every  depart- 
ment. 

At  present  there  are  156  Associations,  with  an  aggregate  membership, 
including  boys'  departments  and  sections,  of  38,938. 

There  are  51  buildings,  valued  at  $3,327,950,  as  against  45,  valued  at 
$3,004,250  in  1892.  New  buildings  have  been  acquired  by  the  Twenty- 
sixth  Ward  and  the  Prospect  Park  Branches  of  Brooklyn.  Brooklyn 
German  Branch  has  secured  a  lot  and  is  working  for  a  building.  West 
Troy  has  completed  a  building  valued  at  $23,500.  North  Tonawanda  and 
Geneva  have  completed  their  buildings.  The  Kailroad  Men's  Building 
in  New  York  City  has  been  enlarged  and  extended  by  the  expenditure  of 
$100,000  by  the  same  generous  friend  of  railroad  men  who  secured  the 
erection  of  the  main  building.  Elmira  has  raised  $75,000,  and  plans  are 
being  made  for  a  new  building.  Waterville  Association  has  been  pre- 


64 

sented  by  Mrs.  I.  D.  Brainard  with  a  property  which,  after  alteration, 
will  give  them  an  excellent  home.  Buffalo  German  Branch  has,  after  a 
hard  struggle,  about  secured  its  building.  The  New  York  City  Associa- 
tion, through  a  generous  friend,  has  received  the  promise  of  a  gift  of 
property  valued  at  $200,000,  to  be  used  as  an  endowment,  while  the  bequest 
of  the  late  W.  H.  Vanderbilt,  now  amounting  to  $140,000,  was  further  in- 
creased to  $165,000  by  a  gift  of  $25,000  from  Mr.  Cornelius  Vanderbilt, 
and  the  money  used  to  purchase  lots  for  a  West  Side  Branch.  Plans  for 
a  handsome  and  complete  building  are  being  prepared.  $120, 000  has  been 
so  far  secured  toward  the  building  fund.  The  Associations  at  Buffalo  and 
Albany  and  the  Railroad  Branch  at  Long  Island  City  have  been  crippled 
temporarily  by  fire,  but  work  has  continued  and  buildings  been  repaired 
and  remodeled  with  the  insurance  money  and  gifts  from  friends. 

In  1894,  after  17  years  of  very  faithful  and  efficient  service,  E.  P.  Platt 
retired  from  the  chairmanship  of  the  State  Executive  Committee,  to  the 
great  regret  of  his  associates,  and  was  succeeded  by  Dr.  Lucien  C. 
Warner. 

The  secretarial  force  of  the  State  is  211,  of  whom  26  are  physical 
directors  with  six  assistants,  and  six  librarians.  In  several  sections  of  the 
State  regular  meetings  for  the  secretaries  are  arranged,  and  a  systematic 
course  of  Bible  and  other  studies  carried  on.  District  work  has  been 
actively  maintained,  conventions  have  been  held  in  each  of  the  nine  dis- 
tricts, with  aggregate  attendance,  in  1894,  of  784.  These  conventions  not 
only  were  self-supporting,  but  provided  a  balance  for  State  work.  Effort 
has  been  made  to  reach  every  part  of  the  State,  and  in  unorganized  towns 
we  have  95  new  corresponding  members.  Twelve  "sections  "  have  been 
organized  in  towns  not  ready  for  regular  Associations,  and  have  proved 
successful. 

There  are  27  College  Associations  in  the  State,  four  being  in  State  nor- 
mal schools,  one  at  West  Point  Military  Academy,  five  in  preparatory 
schools,  13  in  colleges,  and  medical  and  technical  schools.  To  further  the 
introduction  into  the  College  Associations  of  graduates  from  preparatory 
schools,  213  names  of  such  candidates  were  secured  and  forwarded  to 
officers  of  College  Associations. 

Railroad  work  shows  marked  prosperity.  There  are  now  30  branches, 
and  the  railroads  appropriate  $33,500  towards  current  expenses ;  a  special 
committee  of  railroad  officials  has  charge  of  the  work. 

Sixty-eight  Associations  report  gymnasiums;  12  were  represented  by  32 
men  at  the  annual  pentathlon  contest. 

Educational  work  is  carried  on  by  63  Associations  (54  in  1892),  with  271 
classes  (212  in  1892),  and  5,242  different  members  (3,285  in  1892).  The 
educational  exhibit  is  a  feature  of  our  State  Conventions. 

Forty-three  Associations  report  982  young  men  enrolled  in  Bible  and 
training  classes,  as  against  499  for  last  year.  Seventy-five  Associations 
report  1,422  conversions  in  1894.  Work  among  non-English  speaking 
young  men  is  steadily  growing.  After  10  years  of  steady  work  52  As- 
sociations report  boys'  departments.  An  annual  boys'  conference  was 
held  in  three  sections  and  a  boys'  camp  held  for  five  weeks  instead  of 
two.  An  Association  at  the  State  military  camp  was  carried  on  as  usual, 
with  encouraging  results.  A  Women's  Auxiliary  annual  conference  was 


65 

held  at  the  same  time  and  place  as  the  State  Convention  in  each  year, 
with  increasing  interest. 

The  International  Committee  has  again  helped  us  most  efficiently,  as 
will  be  seen  from  the  following  extract  from  the  annual  report  to  our 
State  Convention  : 

*'  We  desire  to  express  our  appreciation^  the  valuable  assistance  we  have 
repeatedly  received  from  the  International  Committee.  Not  only  has 
advantage  been  taken  of  the  visits  of  their  agents  to  the  New  York  office 
for  counsel  and  advice,  but  special  assistance  has  been  given  at  our  local 
Associations  and  at  our  conventions." 

W.  H.  MIOSALES,  Cor.  Mem. 

NOETH  CAROLINA. 

The  financial  pressure  of  the  past  two  years,  though  less  severe  with  us 
than  in  some  other  States,  has  still  interfered  somewhat  with  the  efficiency 
of  the  work,  and  we  have  not  quite  held  our  own  in  the  number  of  organ- 
izations or  membership.  One  of  the  Committee's  secretaries  resigned 
early  in  1893,  and  we  felt  unable  to  secure  another.  We  have  thus  been 
able  to  pay  our  current  expenses  and  to  slightly  reduce  the  debt  that 
lay  upon  us  in  1893. 

Two  State  Conventions  have  been  held,  at  Winston  in  1893,  and  at  Wil- 
mington the  past  year.  All  the  secretarial  points  have  been  kept  in  vig- 
orous work,  and  at  the  close  of  the  last  year  there  was  but  slight  indebt- 
edness for  local  current  expenses.  The  conventions,  both  district  and 
State,  have  been  fairly  well  attended,  and  better  work  has  been  done  at 
these  meetings.  There  is  an  evident  growth,  particularly  respecting  the 
scope  and  proper  accomplishment  of  the  work  and  its  great  possibilities, 
which  promises  well  for  our  future.  The  spiritual  harvest,  especially  in 
the  large  towns,  has  been  fully  up  to  the  high-water  mark  of  former 
years.  The  college  work  is  managed  with  remarkable  skill  and  success. 
The  town  Associations  have  also  materially  broadened  their  work  and  are 
evidently  growing  in  public  favor. 

The  International  Committee,  through  its  representatives,  Messrs. 
Brockman  and  Andersen,  has  materially  furthered  the  work  of  the  State 
Committee,  and  the  latter  gentleman  last  Fall  made  a  special  and  success- 
ful effort  to  assist  the  Committee  in  its  financial  canvass. 

GEORGE  B.  HANNA,  Cor.  Mem. 

NORTH  DAKOTA. 

The  work  in  North  Dakota  has  advanced  during  the  past  year.  Our 
first  State  Convention  was  held  in  Grand  Forks,  June  1-3,  1894,  and  the 
attendance  and  interest  were  good.  We  had  then  four  Associations — 
Fargo,  Grand  Forks,  Larimore  and  the  State  University.  The  interest 
has  since  spread  over  the  State,  and  at  the  last  convention,  held  in  Fargo, 
February,  1895,  we  had  an  attendance  of  101  delegates.  We  had  em- 
ployed a  State  Secretary  for  a  little  over  two  months,  but  at  the  conven- 
tion it  was  decided  to  employ  one  for  at  least  five  months  this  year. 
Eight  hundred  dollars,  the  amount  asked  for,  was  all  pledged  at  the  con- 
vention. The  report  of  the  State  Secretary  showed  that  Associations  had 
been  organized  at  Devil's  Lake  and  Minot,  and  that  young  men's  meet- 


66 

ings  had  been  organized  in  several  other  places  during  the  year.     The 
outlook  for  the  future  is  bright. 

During  the  past  year  a  "  Y.  M.  C.  A.  Day  "  was  held  at  the  Chautauqua, 
Devil's  Lake,  and  at  the  Assembly,  Detroit  Lake,  Minn.,  both  under 
charge  of  Secretary  Van  Vranken,  of  Grand  Forks.  We  are  indebted  to 
the  International  Committee  for  very  many  favors  received,  including 
the  efficient  help  of  Secretaries  Ober,  Eastman  and  Taggart.  Mr.  Pit- 
kins'  visit  to  the  State  University  in  the  interest  of  the  student  volunteer 
movement  proved  a  great  blessing  to  that  institution.  The  Indian  work 
in  the  State,  as  reported  by  Mr.  Eastman,  is  prospering.  You  may  look 
for  "  advance  all  along  the  line  "  in  North  Dakota  this  year. 

T.  CARTER  GRIFFITH,   Cor.  Mem. 


OHIO. 

Notwithstanding  the  serious  business  depression  during  1894,  there  was 
raised  and  spent  for  current  expenses  of  the  Associations  in  this  State 
$134,652.  Seventy  Associations  have  been  in  active  operation  ;  16  of 
them  own  the  buildings  that  they  occupy,  which,  with  the  land,  are 
valued  at  a  total  of  more  than  $1,000,000.  Twelve  other  Associations 
have  building  funds  pledged,  and  are  steadily  at  work  trying  to  secure 
permanent  homes.  There  are  70  men  devoting  their  entire  time  to 
the  work  as  secretaries  and  physical  directors.  The  educational  work 
has  been  carried  on  upon  a  wider  scale  and  with  better  success  than 
ever  before. 

The  college  work  has  continued  with  increasing  interest  and  success. 
Delegations  from  this  department  were  present  at  the  Summer  Schools 
at  Northfield  and  at  Lake  Geneva,  and  at  the  student  volunteer  conven- 
tion at  Detroit. 

The  directly  spiritual  work  of  the  Associations  has  been  steadily 
advanced. 

One  of  the  four  new  buildings  occupied  for  the  first  time  in  1894  is 
the  handsome  structure  at  Otterbein  University,  being  the  first  Col- 
lege Association  building  in  Ohio.  The  State  Secretaries  have  been  very 
active,  and  have  rendered  the  most  efficient  service  throughout  the 
year. 

The  recent  State  Convention  at  Newark  was  largely  attended,  and 
has  left  a  permanent  impression  upon  the  churches  of  that  city,  as  well 
as  upon  the  delegates  in  attendance. 

H.  P.  LLOYD,  Cor.  Mem. 


OREGON,  WASHINGTON,  IDAHO  AND  BRITISH  COLUMBIA. 

Since  our  last  report  the  Association  work  in  the  Pacific  Northwest  has 
been  passing  through  its  most  critical  period.  The  financial  depression 
has  been  severely  felt  by  all  our  local  Associations,  as  well  as  by  the 
general  work.  However,  we  are  glad  to  report  that  through  the  self- 
sacrifices  of  our  friends  we  have  been  able  to  hold  nearly  all  of  the  points. 

A  very  serious  drawback  to  the  work  has  been  the  number  of  changes 
made  by  the  local  secretaries.  At  the  present  time  nearly  all  the  placea 
are  filled,  and  a  good  work  is  being  accomplished. 


67 

James  A.  Dummett,  who  is  now  in  the  fifth  year  of  his  service  as  our 
traveling  secretary,  has  stood  by  his  post  faithfully.  To  his  self-sacrific- 
ing labors  can  be  attributed  very  largely  the  holding  together  of  the  work 
during  the  recent  crisis.  At  both  of  our  annual  conventions  and  at  our 
college  conferences  the  International  Committee  rendered  valuable 
assistance. 

Our  college  work  is  in  a  very  encouraging  condition,  with  19  College 
Associations  in  Oregon  and  Washington,  and  the  prospect  good  for  the 
organization  of  another,  at  the  State  University  of  Idaho. 

On  the  whole,  we  believe  the  work  with  us  is  on  the  up-grade. 

GEORGE  F.  OBOHABD,  Cor.  Mem. 

PENNSYLVANIA. 

We  have  147  Associations  in  the  State,  a  gain  of  four  since  my  last 
report.  In  addition  to  these  there  are  21  district  sections,  which  are 
equivalent  to  th  Associations  organized  in  the  smaller  towns  formerly. 

Of  paid  officers,  including  general  secretaries,  assistants,  physical  di- 
rectors, librarians  and  State  Secretaries,  there  are  138,  a  net  gain  of  22  in 
the  past  two  years. 

One  hundred  and  twenty-nine  Associations  report  a  membership  of 
26,388,  of  which  13,510  are  active  ;  17  district  sections  report  membership 
of  891,  of  which  627  are  active;  120  Associations  report  4,185  members 
serving  on  committees. 

Thirty-one  Associations  own  buildings,  valued  at  $1, 881, 214  ;  41  Asso- 
ciations report  total  value,  above  indebtedness,  of  all  property  and 
funds,  except  furniture  and  libraries,  $1,680,764;  two  College  Associa- 
tions report  building  funds  of  $106,000  ;  92  Associations  report  value  of 
furniture  $134,635 ;  69  Associations  report  value  of  libraries  $64,700. 

During  the  year  we  have  received  from  the  International  Committee 
timely  counsel  and  help  through  Messrs.  Taggart  and  Cree  at  several  local 
points,  and  through  Mr.  Mott  in  connection  with  the  College  Presidents' 
Conference.  Mr.  Taggart  was  also  present  at  our  State  Convention,  where 
he  gave  valuable  assistance. 

C.  H.  ZEHNDEB,  Cor.  Mem. 

SOUTH  CAKOLINA. 

We  count  ourselves  fortunate  in  not  having  been  compelled  to  retrench 
during  the  two  extraordinary  years  which  this  report  covers.  While  the 
times  have  been  hard  upon  the  work  everywhere,  this  has  been  peculiarly 
true  with  the  small  Associations  of  which  our  State  organization  is  mainly 
composed. 

There  are  at  the  present  time  25  Associations  in  the  State,  16  town  and 
city  and  nine  college.  Our  two  secretarial  points  are  Charleston  and  Co- 
lumbia. At  Charleston  a  good  beginning  has  been  made  in  the  work  of 
clearing  the  debt  upon  the  building. 

The  work  in  the  colleges  has  been  in  many  respects  encouraging.  The 
success  of  the  county  organization  in  Edgefield  is  remarkable.  This 
work  has  now  been  maintained  for  six  years,  with  the  continuous  service 
of  the  same  county  secretary. 


68 

The  South  Carolina  State  Committee  has  for  the  last  two  years  joined 
with  that  of  Georgia  in  the  employment  of  a  State  Secretary,  who  has  di- 
vided his  time  between  the  two  States. 

We  acknowledge  help  received  from  the  International  Committee  at 
various  times.  Mr.  Weidensall's  assistance  in  Edgefield  County  has  been 
particularly  valuable  and  is  much  appreciated. 

ATHA  T.  JAMISON,  Cor.  Mem. 


SOUTH  DAKOTA. 

The  work  in  this  State  has  been  carried  on  along  the  usual  lines.  One 
new  Association  has  been  organized,  at  Huron,  while  the  work  at  Sioux 
Falls  has  steadily  advanced.  The  work  in  the  colleges  has  been  developed 
as  never  before,  and  strong  Associations  are  now  sustained  in  every 
college  save  one  in  the  State.  The  work  has  been  greatly  helped  and 
strengthened  by  the  visits  of  Secretaries  Ober,  Brockman  and  Boots,  of 
the  International  Committee. 

C.  S.  PALMER,  Cor.  Mem. 


TENNESSEE. 

Tennessee  has  13  city  and  20  College  Associations,  with  a  total  mem- 
bership of  3,370.  All  of  them  are  in  a  more  encouraging  condition  than 
a  year  ago. 

The  State  Convention  held  in  Sweetwater,  February  7-10,  1895,  was 
attended  by  121  delegates  and  seven  corresponding  members  from  25  As- 
sociations. H.  P.  Andersen  and  F.  S.  Brockman  represented  the  Inter- 
national Committee  and  rendered  valuable  assistance.  Two  district  con- 
ventions were  held  during  1894,  one  at  Cleveland,  and  the  other  at  Mossy 
Creek.  Both  were  well  attended  and  resulted  in  arousing  considerable 
interest  in  the  State  work. 

Immediately  following  the  Sweetwater  gathering  a  presidential  confer- 
ence was  conducted  by  Mr.  Brockman,  at  which  18  College  Association 
presidents  and  other  officers  received  thorough  instructions  as  to  their 
duties. 

At  the  close  of  the  State  Convention  in  Knoxville  in  1893,  the  resigna- 
tion of  our  State  Secretary  took  effect,  leaving  us  for  a  few  months  with- 
out this  valuable  aid.  Through  the  help  of  the  International  Committee, 
we  were  enabled  to  arrange  for  the  co-operation  of  H.  P.  Andersen 
during  the  interval  until  our  committee  was  again  able  to  employ  some  one 
for  the  full  year.  Mr.  Andersen's  work  has  proved  so  efficient  that  steps 
are  being  taken  to  again  place  a  State  Secretary  in  the  field. 

During  the  past  two  years  two  of  our  largest  Associations  have  met 
with  serious  loss  by  fire.  The  rooms  of  the  Memphis  Association,  that 
had  just  been  handsomely  furnished,  were  destroyed,  and  the  general  sec- 
retary, A.  K.  Perkins,  lost  his  life  while  endeavoring  to  make  his  escape. 
Later  the  Nashville  Association  building  was  completely  ruined. 

The  State  Committee,  through  the  acting  State  Secretary,  came  to  the 
rescue  of  the  Memphis  Association,  helping  it  to  secure  new  rooms  and 
another  secretary,  and  the  Association  is  now  doing  a  more  effective  work 
than  ever  before. 


69 

The  services  of  Mr.  Brockman  in  visitation  among  the  colleges  of  the 
State  have  been  most  valuable.  Arrangements  are  now  being  made  for 
holding  the  second  session  of  the  Summer  School  for  Southern  Colleges 
at  the  University  of  Tennessee,  Knoxville,  in  June. 

JAMES  H.  COWAN,   Cor.  Mem. 


TEXAS. 

Association  work  in  Texas  has  held  its  own  during  the  past  two  years, 
so  far  as  numerical  strength  is  concerned.  There  has  been  very  marked 
improvement,  however,  in  the  work  of  existing  organizations,  the  most  of 
our  Associations  being  on  a  better  foundation  to-day  than  ever  before. 
There  are  21  general  and  12  college  organizations — 33  in  all — with  a  total 
membership  of  5,300.  Dallas  made  a  special  effort  to  increase  its  member- 
ship, with  most  gratifying  results,  and  now  has  more  than  800  members. 
A  flourishing  Association  has  been  organized  at  Austin,  the  capital  of  the 
State,  with  a  general  secretary  and  physical  director,  and  a  membership 
of  about  400. 

There  are  15  general  secretaries,  seven  physical  directors  and  four 
other  paid  employees,  besides  the  State  force.  'A  successful  indoor  pen- 
tathlon was  conducted  at  Fort  Worth  last  April,  in  connection  with  our 
State  Convention.  Several  Associations  have  been  conducting  successful 
evening  educational  classes  in  various  branches,  with  encouraging 
results. 

Three  Associations  have  recently  moved  into  new  quarters  especially 
adapted  to  their  work.  Galveston  will  erect  a  new  building  this  year,  to 
cost  $47,500,  on  a  centrally  located  lot,  costing  $17,500.  This  is 
made  possible  by  a  bequest  of  the  late  Henry  Eosenberg.  The  building 
movement  is  receiving  considerable  attention  in  other  parts  of  the  State. 
A  very  successful  work  was  conducted  at  the  State  military  camp  at 
Austin  last  season.  It  was  greatly  appreciated  by  the  militia. 

The  International  Committee  has  rendered  us  valuable  assistance  at 
our  conventions  and  secretaries'  conferences,  and  in  the  State  -work, 
through  their  representatives,  C.  L.  Gates,  F.  S.  Brockman,  J.  E.  Mott 

and  C.  Olandt,  Jr. 

JUDSON  B.  PALMER,  Cor.  Mem. 


UTAH. 

The  panic  of  1893  and  1894  was  very  severe  on  the  work  of  the  Associa- 
tion in  Salt  Lake  City,  which  is  so  far  our  only  organization.  We  closed 
1893  with  quite  a  deficit,  but  with  renewed  zeal  and  devotion  we  carried 
on  the  work  through  1894  and  paid  part  of  our  deficit.  Our  work  is  in  a 
very  healthy  condition,  the  membership  having  increased  slightly  over 
1893.  The  spirit  of  union  and  fraternity  is  stronger  than  ever. 

Our  membership  is  composed  of  strong,  energetic  young  men,  for  the 
most  part  those  who  have  had  little  experience  in  Association  work.  We 
therefore  feel  that  we  should  be  in  close  touch  with  the  International 
Committee.  Suggestions  coming  from  the  Committee  have  been  of  great 
assistance  to  us.  Mr.  Gates  visited  us  two  or  three  times  in  1893,  and 
materially  assisted  our  board  in  outlining  the  work.  Mr.  Ober  visited  us 


70 

last  month  and  gave  us  new  hope  and  encouragement.  Scarcely  a  day 
has  passed  since  he  left  us  that  we  have  not  seen  good  results  from  the 
visit. 

All  branches  of  the  work  have  been  kept  open.  The  gymnasium  is  a 
very  attractive  feature,  but  the  greatest  amount  of  enthusiasm  has  pre- 
vaded  in  our  religious  work.  Many  churches  report  additions  to  their 
membership  through  our  work. 

FRANK  PIERCE,  Cor.  Mem. 


VERMONT. 

Notwithstanding  the  recent  severe  financial  depression  we  are  glad  to 
report  that  none  of  the  Associations  of  Vermont  have  suffered  severely  for 
lack  of  support. 

No  changes  have  been  made  in  general  secretaries  with  the  exception 
of  St.  Johnsbury,  Mr.  Lewis  having  resigned  to  become  the  College 
Secretary  for  Massachusetts  and  Ehode  Island.  F.  S.  Smith,  of  Water- 
bury,  Conn.,  was  secured  to  take  his  place.  A  new  Association  has  been 
formed  at  Montpelier,  with  very  bright  prospects.  A  profitable  State 
Convention  was  held  at  St.  Johnsbury  in  January,  1894,  and  in  December, 
1894,  a  joint  convention  for  New  Hampshire  and  Vermont  was  held  at 
Keene,  N.  H.,  at  which  it  was  unanimously  decided  to  unite  the 
Association  work  of  the  two  States,  and  also  employ  a  State  Secretary  as 
soon  as  a  suitable  man  could  be  secured. 

Not  having  had  a  State  Secretary  in  1894,  the  work  at  large  fell  upon 
the  members  of  the  State  Committee  until  about  October,  when  the 
International  Committee  sent  Glaus  Olandt,  Jr.,  to  our  relief.  His  labors, 
in  preparation  for  and  at  the  inter-State  meeting  proved  so  satisfactory 
that  we  were  led  to  covet  his  services  longer.  The  International  Com- 
mittee has  manifested  a  great  interest  in  our  State  work  and  has 
responded  to  calls  for  counsel  and  services. 

G.  F.  NORTH,  Cor.  Mem. 


VIRGINIA. 

Association  work  in  the  "Old  Dominion "  has  made  marked  advances, 
in  spite  of  the  financial  depression  which  has  been  felt  everywhere  for  the 
past  two  years.  The  results  secured,  in  every  instance,  have  been  by 
much  prayer,  larger  effort  and  the  most  rigid  economy.  Six  new  Associa- 
tions have  been  organized ;  a  number  of  small  town  organizations  that 
ceased  to  show  any  activity  have  been  dropped.  Two  secretarial  points — 
Danville  10,000  and  Winchester  5,000 — while  they  still  preserve  their  organ- 
ization, have  found  it  necessary  to  dispense  with  the  services  of  a  general 
secretary.  We  now  report  51  Associations — 22  local,  18  college,  ten 
railroad  and  one  army.  Three  district  conferences  were  held  in  1893,  and 
six  in  1894..  Two  conferences  of  presidents  of  College  Associations  and 
two  conferences  of  Association  employees  have  also  been  held. 

Five  new  buildings  have  been  secured  and  completed — Crewe,  for  rail- 
road men,  $4,000;  Roanoke,  railroad,  $800;  Gladstone,  railroad,  $4,500; 
Clifton  Forge,  railroad,  $14,000 ;  Hampton,  local,  $6,000 ;  Petersburg 
local,  still  unfinished,  $35,000.  Richmond  City  raised  $22,500  last  Sum- 


w 

B    I 


71 

mer  to  pay  the  entire  indebtedness  resting  on  the  building  and  work  at 
that  point.  Eoanoke  City  raised  $7,000  on  its  building  and  lot.  Four- 
teen Associations  own  buildings  valued  at  $225,500. 

Both  the  college  and  the  railroad  work  are  in  better  condition  to-day 
than  at  any  previous  time  in  our  history. 

The  present  situation  is  as  follows:  51  Associations  in  the  State,  19 
secretarial  points,  33  paid  agents,  14  buildings,  current  expenses  $30,000. 
The  railroads  gave  last  year  $8,480  to  the  work  at  ten  divisional  and 
terminal  points.  The  total  membership  reported  by  47  Associations  is 
6,656.  Thirty  Associations  reported  368  professed  conversions  for  1893, 
20  reporting  143  uniting  with  churches.  For  1894,  reports  from  34  Asso- 
ciations give  451  professed  conversions,  32  reporting  235  uniting  with 
churches. 

Tlae  day  and  week  of  prayer  was  generally  observed.  At  the  University 
of  Virginia  the  meetings  were  conducted  by  John  B.  Mott,  and  resulted  in 
reaching  for  Christ  between  80  and  90  of  the  students. 

The  eighteenth  annual  convention  was  held  at  Eoanoke,  February  14- 
18,  1894,  and  attended  by  308  delegates  ;  the  nineteenth  convention 
was  held  in  Staunton,  February  6-10,  1895,  and  attended  by  295  dele- 
gates. F.  S.  Brockman,  C.  J.  Hicks  and  H.  Thane  Miller  represented 
the  International  Committee  at  Boanoke ;  H.  Thane  Miller,  George  A. 
Hall  and  E.  L.  Hamilton  at  Staunton. 

H.  O.  Williams  has  continued  as  State  Secretary.  W.  B.  Haight  was 
in  charge  of  the  office  work  until  June  1,  1894.  His  successor  is  W.  B. 
Walker. 

Special  mention  should  be  made  of  the  valuble  services  rendered  dur- 
ing the  past  two  years  by  the  following  secretaries  of  the  International 
Committee— J.  B.  Mott,  F.  S.  Brockman,  E.  Lawrence  Hunt,  C.  J.  Hicks, 
E.  L.  Hamilton  and  W.  A.  Hunton.  Their  visits  are  always  welcome  and 
ever  helpful. 

JAMES  B.  GBEQOBY,  Cor.  Mem. 


WISCONSIN. 

Two  years  have  made  considerable  change  in  the  Wisconsin  Associations, 
which  now  number  35.  Not  all  these  are  strong,  and  three  or  four  are 
alive  only  in  name,  but  in  the  main  the  work  is  in  a  good  condition. 
During  this  time  there  has  been  a  change  in  the  State  Secretary  ;  F.  E. 
Anderson,  for  thirteen  years  general  secretary  at  Bacine,  having  accepted 
the  position  on  the  resignation  of  J .  B.  Pratt.  The  net  value  of  property 
now  held  by  the  Associations  (allowing  for  shrinkage)  is  about  $225,000. 
Nine  buildings  are  now  occupied,  four  are  in  process  of  construction, 
while  two  are  temporarily  used  for  other  purposes.  The  lumbermen's 
work  is  carried  on  each  Winter,  and,  in  direct  spiritual  results,  is  the  most 
satisfactory  of  any  department.  The  Bailroad  Branch  at  Milwaukee 
and  the  Bailroad  Association  at  Baraboo  have  both  suffered  by  the  with- 
drawal of  the  appropriations  of  the  railroad  companies.  At  Baraboo  the 
substantial  property  owned  will  insure  the  continuance  of  the  work,  and 
at  Milwaukee  a  lunch  counter  was  started  and  has  been  so  successful 
that  the  work  there  will  not  suffer .  The  work  among  the  colleges  is  in 


good  condition,  being  carried  on  with  an  aggressive  and  hopeful  spirit. 
The  annual  students'  gathering  at  Lake  Geneva  is  an  inspiration,  and  the 
occasional  visit  of  the  Interantional  College  Secretary  has  been  a  blessing. 
At  the  State  Convention  in  October,  1893,  a  new  State  constitution  was 
adopted,  involving  what  is  known  as  the  "group"  system.  It  is  too 
soon  to  know  whether  it  is  a  success  or  not,  but  it  seems  a  step  in  the 
right  direction.  District  work  has  been  carried  on  more  comprehensively 
than  ever  before,  and  the  results  have  been  all  and  always  good.  It  is 
the  intention  to  push  this  each  year  as  fully  as  possible.  The  financial 
condition  of  the  State  Board  (as  it  is  now  termed,  instead  of  State  Com- 
mittee) is  very  hopeful.  A  deficit  existing  for  two  or  three  years  past  has 
been  nearly  all  provided  for.  The  expenses  for  the  two  years  aggregate 
$9,922.40.  Our  work  has  suffered  from  the  seemingly  inevitable  frequent 
changes  in  the  secretarial  force.  Only  eight  men  are  in  the  positions 
they  occupied  two  years  ago,  and  four  of  these  are  in  Milwaukee. 

C.  B.  WZLUS,  Cor.  Mem.

TABLE  III.-CITY  AND  TOWN  ASSOCIATIONS. 

COMPILED  FHOM  OFFICIAL  REPORTS  RECEIVED  BY  THE  INTERNATIONAL  COMMITTEE  BETWEEN 
JANUARY  15  AND  MARCH  15,  1895. 

The  names  of  officers  are  the  most  recent  that  have  come  to  the  knowledge  of  the  Committee,  as 
far  as  convenience  of  printing  permits  their  insertion. 

Some  Associations  prefer  to  report  for  their  official  years,  closing  at  various  dates,  but  for  the 
most  part,  the  reports  are  for  the  calendar  year  1894 ;  a  number,  from  Associations  recently  organ- 
ized or  reorganized,  are  necessarily  incomplete.

saving  of  three 
cents  per  day  for  a  year 
will  provide  more  than

a  copy  of  the  Interna- 
tional. 


Every  Association 

should  have  this  work  in  its  Library.  It  answers  questions  con- 
cerning the  history,  spelling,  pronunciation,  and  meaning  of  words. 

It  is  a  Library  in  Itself. 

It  gives  the  often  desired  information  concerning  eminent  per- 
sons; facts  concerning  the  countries,  cities,  towns,  and  natural 
features  of  the  globe ;  particulars  concerning  the  noted  fictitious 
persons  and  places;  translation  of  foreign  quotations.  It  is  in- 
valuable in  the  home,  office,  study  and  school  room. 

It  is  the  Standard 

of  the  U.  S.  Supreme  Court ;  of  the  TJ.  S.  Government  Printing 
Office,  and  of  nearly  all  of  the  School  books.  It  is  warmly  com- 
mended by  every  State  Superintendent  of  Schools. 

A  College  President  writes : 

1 '  For  ease  with  which  the  eye  finds  the  word  sought,  for  accuracy 
of  definition,  for  effective  methods  in  indicating  pronunciation,  for 
terse  yet  comprehensive  statements  of  facts,  and  for  practical  use 
as  a  working  dictionary,  "  Webster's  International "  excels  any 
other  single  volume." 

It  is  the  One  Great  Standard  Authority. 

So  writes  HON.  D.  J.  BREWER,  Justice  of  the  U.  S.  Supreme

PEN-WRITTEN  COPIES  (Reproduced). 

The  books  enumerated  above  are  especially  adapted  for  use  in  Y.  M.  C.  A.  Educational 
Classes.    This  is  particularly  true  of  the 


owing  to  the  method  employed  in  presenting  and  treating  the  subject.  By  this  method 
the  pupil  is  initiated  into  the  science  in  an  easy,  natural  and  fascinating  way,  and  with 
little  or  no  assistance  from  the  teacher.  The  work  which  the  pupil  is  required  to  do 
is  of  the  most 

PRACTICAL    CHARACTER, 

and  is  so  arranged  that  bis  progress  depends  entirely  on  his  own  ability  and  the  time  he 
devotes  to  I  he  subject  By  the  use  of  varied  price  lists,  original  with  the  method,  results 
obtained  by  each  one  of  several  pupils  are  different  from  the  others,  thus  preventing  pupils 
from  copjing  or  getting  assistance  from  one  another,  while  at  the  s^me  time  it 

DEVELOPS   ACCURACY   AND   SELF-RELIANCE. 

As  no  class  work  is  necessary  by  this  method,  the  labor  of  the  teacher  is  reduced  to  a 
minimum,  and  consists  chiefly  in  examining  the  pupils'  work  and  rendering  them  such 
assistance  individually  as  they  may  require  to  obtain  accura'e  results. 

The  introduction  of  this  system  ot  bookkeeping  is  greatly  facilitated  by  the 

TEACHER'S  REFERENCE  BOOK  AND  TEACHER'S  KEY, 

a  copy  of  each  of  which  is  supplied  to  Associations  adopting  the  work.  The  Reference 
Book  contains  all  of  the  entries  which  the  pupils  make  in  their  books,  and  the  key 
contains  their  results,  which  are  arranged  in  convenient  form  for  quick  and  easy  reference. 
Among  the 

ASSOCIATIONS  THAT  HAVE  ADOPTED 

this  system  of  bookkeeping  may  be  mentioned  the  following:  New  York,  Chicago, 
Baltimore,  Washington,  Detroit,  Providence,  Hartford  and  Atlanta. 

An  examination  of  the  work  will  convince  any  progressive  teacher  of  its  superior  merits. 


Specimen  pages  of  any  of  the  above  publications  and  illustrated  cataloge  vrill  be  sent  free  to 
Association  officers  and  teachers.    Low  rates  are  made  for  introduction.

vision, and  are  not  (like  others)  dependent  on  the  open  market  for  a  miscellaneous  assort- 
ment of  crude  material,  which,  in  connection  with  75  years'  experience,  enables  them  to 
turn  out  a  product  of  a  very  superior  quality,  second  to  none,  and  at  the  same  time  the 
different  grades  of  Steel  are  always  of  the  same  uniform  quality.

xvin 


THOROUGH  THEORETICAL  AND  PRACTICAL 
TRAINING  FOR  ASSOCIATION  WORK 


The  Young  Men's  Christian  Association  Training  School, 

CHICAGO,  ILL. 

AND  THE 

Western  Secretarial  Institute  of  the  Young  Men's  Christian 
Associations,  Lake  Geneva,  Wis* 

The  Training  School  was  Established  and  Incorporated  in  June,  1890,  and 

endorsed  as  an  INTERNATIONAL  TRAINING  SCHOOL  by  the  International 

Convention,  at  its  meeting  in  Kansas  City,  May,  1891. 

OBJECT. 

To  educate  young  men  for  the  duties  of  the  General  Secretaryship,  Physical  Directorship 
and  other  Association  offices. 

COURSES  OF  STUDY. 

The  complete  courses  cover  two  years,  and  comprise  in  both  Secretarial  and  Physical 
Departments:  First— Thorough  and  systematic  courses  of  study,  covering  every  phase  of 
Association  work.  Second — A  practical  training,  each  student  being  assigned  to  regular 
duties  in  one  of  the  nine  departments  of  the  Chicago  Association.  Third— A.  comprehensive 
study  of  the  Bible,  and  how  to  use  aud  teach  it.  Fourth— Instruction  in  the  conduct  of  the 
Bible  Training  Class  aud  how  to  do  Personal  Work.  Fifth— Daily  instruction  and  practice 
in  gymnastics.  Sixth— Courses  in  Christian  Sociology  in  the  work 
of  the  Educational  Department,  and  lectures  on  general  topics 
closely  allied  to  Association  work. 

UNSURPASSED  EQUIPMENT. 

The  school  is  now  located  in  the  elegant  new  Central  Building 
of  the  Chicago  Association,  where  it  has  the  free  use  of  ample 
class  rooms,  good  library  facilities,  and  the  finest  Association 
Physical  Department  on  this  continent.  This  greatly  adds  to  the 
efficiency  of  the  school,  and  gives  it  model  facilities  for  the  train 
ing  of  men  for  Association  work. 

CALENDAR,   SIXTH   SCHOOL   YEAR. 

FALL  TERM!— Begins  Wednesday  morning,  September  llth,  1895. 
WINTER  TERM— Begins  Tuesday  morning,  January  7th   1896 
SPRING  TERM— Begins  Wednesday  Morning,  April  1st,  1896. 

ESTIMATED  COST  FOR   SCHOOL  YEAR. 

Tuition,  $50.  Living  Expenses  for  the  School  Year,  including 
Board,  Room,  Association  Membership,  Gymnasium  Suit, 
Laundry,  Text  Books  and  attendance  upon  Conventions,  es- 
timated at  $235  to  $300.

The  above  illustration  is  an  exact  reproduction  of  the  four  mag- 
nificent volumes  of  THE  ENCYCLOPAEDIC  DICTIONARY,  bound  in  rich 
silk  cloth,  with  gilt  back  stamp,  handsomely  embossed  sides,  and 
marbled  edges.  Each  volume  9  inches  wide,  I1J  inches  long,  3  inches 
thick.  "Weight,  about  40  pounds. 

We  ask  every  purchaser  to  speak  of  the  work  to  his  or  her  friends. 

It  is  a  Complete  Dictionary,  containing  every  word  in  the  English  language  (250,000  in  all), 
which  no  other  dictionary  does.  Every  word  is  exhaustively  treated  as  to  its  origin,  history, 
development,  etymology,  pronunciation,  and  various  meanings. 

It  is  a  Thorough  Encyclopaedia  of  anatomy,  botany,  chemistry,  zoology,  geology,  art, 
music,  agriculture,  physics,  philosophy,  mechanics,  history,  mythology,  biblical  knowledge, 
and  every  other  subject  known  to  the  human  intellect. 

It  is  a  Superb  Library  Book,  being  substantially  and  attractively  bound,  printed  from  new 
plates,  in  large,  clear  type,  on  heavy  white  paper,  and  illustrated  with  hundreds  of  new  pictures 
made  especially  lor  this  work. 

The  Four  Volumes  aggregate  a  total  of  5,357  pages.  Contains  130,000  more  words  than  Worces- 
ter, 110,000  more  than  Webster,  35,000  more  than  The  Century,  and  costs  less  than  any  of  them. 

WHAT    GOOD    JUDGES    SAY    ABOUT    THE    WORK. 


I  prize  highly  The  Encyclopaedic  Dictionary 
for  the  number  of  words  it  contains,  for  accuracy 
of  definitions,  for  fullness  of  illustrations,  and  for 
encyclopaedic  comprehensiveness. 

BISHOP  SAMUEL  FALLOWS, 

Chicago,  111. 

I  have  Webster,  Worcester  and  The  Century, 
and  for  encyclopaedias  I  have  the  Britannica  and 
Appleton's.  It  is  but  simple  truth  to  say  that 
The  Encyclopaedic  Dictionary  is  a  magnificent 
substitute  for  all  of  them.  J.  H.  ATWOOD, 

Attorney,  Leavenworth,  Kan. 


My  library  contains  The  Century  and  the  latest 
Webster,  bnt  I  have  found  much  information  in 
"The  Encyclopaedic"  not  in  either  of  the  former. 
I  regard  the  work  as  invaluable. 

FRANK  W.  OWERS, 
Judge  5th  Judicial  District,  Col. 

I  consider  The  Encyclopaedic  Dictionary  su- 
perior to  Webster,  Worcester,  Century  or  Stand- 
ard. For  the  busy  lawyer,  who  wants  to  know 
things  quickly,  no  better  reference  book  could 
be  had.  BENJAMIN  F.  HUOHRS, 

Attorney  and  ex -State  Senator,  Philadelphia.
